rule: Make every tappable target large enough that users can select it accurately without careful aim.
why: Fitts's law ties acquisition time and error rate inversely to target size, so small controls cost users time and mistakes.
do: Give every button, icon button and tab a hit area of at least 44×44 CSS px on touch layouts.
dont: Ship a 16px close icon with no padding, so the tap area is only the glyph itself.
example: In a SaaS settings drawer on mobile, the row delete icon is padded to a 44×44 tap area even though the glyph is 20px.
source_quote: Touch targets should be large enough for users to accurately select them.
check: Measure each interactive element's rendered bounding box on a 375px-wide viewport; flag any with width < 44px or height < 44px.

rule: Separate adjacent interactive targets with enough dead space that a tap cannot land on the wrong one.
why: Ample spacing around a target keeps near-misses from turning into wrong-action errors.
do: Leave at least 8px of gap between neighbouring icon buttons in a toolbar, and more between destructive and safe actions.
dont: Stack Save and Delete as touching 32px buttons with zero gap between them.
example: In a dashboard table row, edit and delete icon buttons sit 12px apart so a thumb tap cannot hit both.
source_quote: Touch targets should have ample spacing between them.
check: Measure the pixel gap between each pair of adjacent interactive bounding boxes; flag any pair closer than 8px.

rule: Place frequent targets where the user can acquire them easily, not in hard-to-reach screen regions.
why: Acquisition time grows with distance, so controls parked far from the hand cost extra effort on every use.
do: Put primary mobile actions in the bottom thumb zone rather than pinned to the very top of the screen.
dont: Bury the only way to advance a mobile checkout in the top-left corner of a tall phone screen.
example: A mobile SaaS app keeps its New record button in a bottom bar within thumb reach instead of in the top header.
source_quote: Touch targets should be placed in areas of an interface that allow them to be easily acquired.
check: On a screenshot, is every high-frequency action inside the natural thumb zone (bottom half of the screen)?

rule: Keep task-related actions close to the content or attention area they act on.
why: Travel to a button adds to total task time, so long jumps to a distant control slow every repetition.
do: Put a row's edit action at the end of that row, and selection actions in a bar directly above the selected list.
dont: Require users to select a row, then travel to a fixed toolbar in the far corner of a wide admin screen.
example: In an admin table, per-row actions appear at the row's right edge on hover instead of in a global top-right toolbar.
source_quote: the distance between a user’s task/attention area and the task-related button should be kept as short as possible.
check: Is the action control within the same visual region as the content it acts on, with no more than one short cursor travel between them?

rule: Run a tree test on the proposed navigation hierarchy before designing layouts or content.
why: Tree testing exposes findability problems while changes still cost only spreadsheet edits, not design or code rework.
do: Put the menu hierarchy into a tree-testing tool and ask users to find a key resource in the clickable categories.
dont: Build page mockups first and ask users to judge navigation from screenshots.
example: A SaaS team testing a new admin settings menu runs a tree test on the category names before any dashboard screens are designed.
source_quote: Can be conducted well in advance of designing page layouts or navigation menus
check: Was the tree test completed before any layout or content mockups were produced? yes/no

rule: Write tree-test tasks that describe a scenario without repeating the target category label.
why: Repeating the label gives away the answer and inflates success rates.
do: You are considering opening a lawn-care service. See if there are any resources on this site that can help you begin the process.
dont: Find information about starting a business.
example: A SaaS product tests a Billing category with a task about updating a card after a failed charge, not a task that says find Billing.
source_quote: task instructions should avoid using terms that give away the answers
check: Does any task text repeat the target category label verbatim? yes/no

rule: Define the tree down to the lowest-level leaf that contains each resource users will find.
why: Tree-testing tools score only leaf items as correct answers, so shallow trees cannot accurately measure task success.
do: List every branch and leaf in a spreadsheet, such as Home > Citizen > Popular Online Services > MVD Online Services.
dont: Stop the tree at top-level categories like Services and Citizen.
example: A SaaS team building a help-center tree lists each article page under its parent topic instead of stopping at top-level topics.
source_quote: define your tree down to the lowest level of subcategories that will contain the resources you will ask study participants to find
check: Spreadsheet check: every task target appears as a leaf row with at least one parent column populated.

rule: Use a between-subjects design when testing multiple tree versions.
why: Seeing one tree can bias how a participant navigates the next tree.
do: Randomly assign each participant to Tree A or Tree B and analyze each group separately.
dont: Show the same participant both the old and new tree in one session.
example: A SaaS company compares two label sets for its navigation by assigning each research participant to only one tree.
source_quote: If you test multiple trees, use a between-subjects study design, in which each participant sees a single tree version in a session.
check: Does each participant record show only one tree version? yes/no

rule: Mark the correct answer for every task before launching the tree test.
why: The tool needs the correct location to compute success rates automatically.
do: In the task setup, select the target leaf node for a task about finding permit renewal information.
dont: Launch tasks with no answer key and interpret clicks manually after the study.
example: A SaaS team configures each help-center findability task with its correct leaf page before sending the study link.
source_quote: For each task you write, you should also define the correct answer(s), corresponding to where the information is located within the tree.
check: Count of tasks with no marked correct answer equals 0.

rule: Run a small moderated qualitative pilot before the full quantitative tree test.
why: The pilot reveals confusing task wording and labels that aggregate click data can hide.
do: Test 5 users in moderated sessions, revise unclear tasks, then launch the larger unmoderated study.
dont: Send a 200-participant unmoderated tree test without checking the tasks first.
example: A SaaS product team pilots a settings-navigation tree test with 5 users and fixes broad labels before the main study.
source_quote: We recommend beginning a quantitative tree test with a small qualitative study for two reasons
check: Pilot sessions completed and a task-revision log exists before the main launch.

rule: Use the layout and interaction patterns users already know from other products instead of inventing new ones.
why: Users spend most of their time elsewhere, so they expect your site to behave like the sites they already use.
do: Signup page with the logo top-left, email and password fields, one primary 'Create account' button.
dont: Signup built as a chat-style conversation that requires typing commands to set a password.
example: A B2B SaaS trial signup reuses the familiar email/password plus SSO button layout instead of a novel card-swipe flow.
source_quote: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.
check: Can a new user complete the primary task using patterns recognizable from mainstream products, with no custom interaction required?

rule: Copy the structural conventions of the dominant products in your category before adding your own ideas.
why: Users transfer the expectations they built in a familiar product to any product that looks similar.
do: Analytics dashboard with left sidebar navigation, top-bar search, and a date-range picker in the top right.
dont: Dashboard that hides all navigation behind a custom radial menu unique to your product.
example: A new project-management tool keeps list, board and calendar views plus a left sidebar because that is what Linear and Asana users already know.
source_quote: Users will transfer expectations they have built around one familiar product to another that appears similar.
check: Do primary navigation, list views and settings location match the category's dominant convention?

rule: Place features where users' existing mental models predict they belong so the work stays on the task.
why: Reusing existing mental models lets users focus on their tasks rather than learning a new model.
do: Invoices, payment method and plan changes all live under Settings > Billing.
dont: Invoices tucked inside a 'Growth Hub' tab alongside unrelated marketing tools.
example: A fintech web app keeps the refund action on the transaction detail page because users expect actions next to the record.
source_quote: By leveraging existing mental models, we can create superior user experiences in which the users can focus on their tasks rather than on learning new models.
check: Can a user predict where a given setting or action lives before searching, based on prior product experience?

rule: Style toggles, radios, checkboxes and buttons so they visually match their familiar physical counterparts.
why: These controls originated from tactile objects, so their shape carries the meaning users rely on.
do: On/off switch with a sliding knob, radio as a filled circle, button with a border and a visible pressed state.
dont: An on/off setting rendered as a clickable text label that only changes color with no switch affordance.
example: Notification settings in a SaaS app use a standard switch per channel instead of a grid of colored chips.
source_quote: Things like form toggles, radio inputs, and even buttons originated from the design of their tactile counterparts.
check: Are toggles, radios and buttons identifiable as their standard control type from a screenshot alone?

rule: Give existing users a reversible way to keep the familiar version for a limited period after a redesign.
why: Minimizing discord by letting users stay on a familiar version reduces resistance to change.
do: 'Try the new look' banner with a 'Switch back to classic' link kept available for 60 days.
dont: Hard cutover on Monday with no preview and no path back to the previous interface.
example: A dashboard redesign ships with an opt-in preview and a documented end date for the old UI.
source_quote: When making changes, minimize discord by empowering users to continue using a familiar version for a limited time.
check: Is there a visible control that returns a user to the previous interface, plus a stated end date for it?

rule: Roll out a redesign through an opt-in preview that lets users build familiarity and send feedback before the switch.
why: Previewing let YouTube users gain familiarity, give feedback and revert, avoiding mental-model discord.
do: A 'Preview the new design' toggle in the account menu that opens a two-question feedback form.
dont: Silent 100% rollout to all accounts on day one with no preview and no feedback channel.
example: A SaaS settings revamp is offered as a preview toggle to 10% of accounts, with an in-product feedback link and revert option.
source_quote: Users could preview the new design, gain some familiarity, submit feedback, and even revert to the old version if they preferred it.
check: Run the preview on a small cohort and count what share opt in and what share revert within the first week.

rule: Make the default first column a human-readable record identifier, never an auto-generated ID.
why: Users scan the first column to locate a record, and a mystery ID forces them to search other columns to identify what they are looking at.
do: The leftmost column reads 'Northwind Traders  -  Plan: Growth', with the internal account ID pushed into a hidden column.
dont: The leftmost column shows 'acc_9f2a8c31' so users must scan plan and email columns to guess which record is which.
example: In a billing admin table, the first column shows the customer name so an agent can find the account in one pass.
source_quote: The (default) first column should be a human-readable record identifier instead of a “mystery meat” automatically generated ID.
check: Count rows whose first cell matches a UUID/numeric-only pattern; the count must be 0 across all rows.

rule: Order columns by importance to the user and place related columns next to each other.
why: Users should not have to move their eyes between column 1 and column 20 to compare the fields that matter most.
do: Account, Plan, MRR, Renewal date, Owner sit side by side, with all billing fields adjacent.
dont: Owner in column 1, MRR in column 19, renewal date in column 7, forcing horizontal ping-pong to compare.
example: In a subscription dashboard, revenue and renewal date are adjacent so an account manager reads them in one glance.
source_quote: The default order of the columns should reflect the importance of the data to the user and related columns should be adjacent.
check: From a screenshot, can a reviewer name the three most decision-relevant columns and confirm they sit next to each other without scrolling?

topic: Freeze header row and first column
rule: Freeze the header row and the first column whenever the table is larger than the screen.
why: Frozen headers and identifiers let users keep their place and know which column and which record they are reading while scrolling.
do: Sticky header row and sticky first column with a subtle drop shadow so the identifier stays visible when scrolling right.
dont: Headers scroll out of view so users see unlabeled numbers and cannot tell MRR from renewal date.
example: In a 200-row orders table on a laptop, the customer name column stays pinned while users scroll to the invoice column.
source_quote: Freeze header rows and header columns (if the table is larger than the screen).
check: Scroll the table container 400px vertically and 300px horizontally, then measure the header row top offset and first column left offset; both deltas must be 0px.

rule: Use row borders, zebra striping, and full-row hover highlighting so users can track a record across wide tables.
why: These visual cues let users keep their place as their eyes move across many columns and rows.
do: Alternating row tint, 1px row separators, and hovering row 5 highlights the entire record across all columns.
dont: A borderless grid with no hover state, so a user comparing columns 3 and 14 loses which row they were reading.
example: In a wide inventory table, hovering a row lights the whole record so the user can compare price and stock without losing the line.
source_quote: Borders, zebra striping, and hover-triggered highlighting of a record can all help.
check: Hover over row 5 and count rows whose computed background color differs from the default; the count must be exactly 1.

rule: Provide easy column hiding and reordering with a clear indicator of the current hidden state.
why: Users need to bring compared columns into proximity, and without a visible state indicator they cannot tell data is missing.
do: A 'Columns' menu showing '3 of 15 hidden' with checkbox toggles plus drag handles, and reordering also possible from that list.
dont: Drag-only column reordering on the headers with no menu and no sign that three columns are hidden.
example: In a support ticket table, an agent hides six rarely used fields and the menu still shows '6 hidden' so they know to re-enable them later.
source_quote: Hiding and reordering columns must be easy to accomplish (low interaction cost and accessible for those that don’t use drag and drop interactions).
check: From a screenshot, can a reviewer see which columns are hidden and reorder columns without a drag-and-drop gesture?

rule: Show a clear, persistent visual indication whenever filters are active.
why: Users must be able to tell at a glance that they are looking at a filtered subset rather than the full dataset.
do: A chip row above the table reading 'Status: Overdue ×  Region: EU ×' plus 'Showing 24 of 318 records'.
dont: Filters applied from a side panel that is collapsed, leaving the table visually identical to the unfiltered view.
example: In an expense approval queue, an approver sees 'Filtered: Pending > 30 days' so they do not assume the queue only has 12 items.
source_quote: users should be able to easily understand that they are looking at filtered data (that is, there should be a clear visual indication that filters are active)
check: Apply one filter, capture the screenshot with the filter panel closed, and have a reviewer confirm the active filter and result count are visible.

topic: Nonmodal editing of a single record
rule: Open a single record for view or edit in a nonmodal side panel rather than a modal dialog.
why: Users routinely reference data from similar records while editing, and a modal covers the very rows they need to compare.
do: Clicking a row slides in a side panel with all fields editable while the table stays visible beside it.
dont: A modal dialog dims and covers the table, so the user cannot check the value ranges of a neighboring record.
example: In a vendor management table, an admin edits payment terms in a side panel while keeping the neighboring vendor's terms on screen.
source_quote: A nonmodal side panel allows for the full display (and editing) of a single record while still allowing the user to view the rest of the table’s data.
check: From a screenshot of the edit state, is the underlying table still fully visible and unblocked?

rule: Support batch actions with a per-record checkbox and a select-all control.
why: Selecting records and acting on them in bulk keeps many actions space-efficient and avoids cramming icon-only actions into each row.
do: A checkbox per row, a header checkbox for select-all, and an action bar with 'Export / Assign / Delete' appearing once a selection exists.
dont: Twelve unlabeled icon buttons crammed into every row, with no way to apply one action to 40 selected records.
example: In an invoice table, a finance user checks the header box to select all 40 overdue invoices and clicks 'Send reminders' once.
source_quote: Batch actions usually involve a mechanism for selecting records (e.g., a checkbox for each record) and then a series of action buttons or menus above or below the table.
check: Click the header checkbox, then verify the batch action bar appears and displays the selected record count as a number.

rule: Build every surface of a product from a single shared design system instead of per-surface component sets.
why: Shared primitives across surfaces are what make the product feel like one product rather than a set of unrelated tools.
do: Reuse the same button, input, and text primitives from one library on the admin home, the checkout panel, and the mobile POS view.
dont: Ship a custom React button on the admin page, a separately styled one in checkout, and a third hand-coded one in the mobile app.
example: A billing SaaS ships its dashboard, an embedded checkout widget, and a mobile companion using the same token set and button component.
source_quote: All app surfaces use Polaris, Shopify's unified UI framework built on web components, to deliver a consistent experience across the platform.
check: Count distinct component libraries imported in UI source files; the number must be 1 per surface set, and hardcoded hex colors must be 0.

rule: Restrict each surface's build to the components that surface actually publishes, and treat the rest as unavailable.
why: Every surface exposes a different subset, so a component that works on one screen may simply not exist where you assume it does.
do: Check the surface's published component list before building a data table, and swap in a supported list pattern if the table is absent.
dont: Assume a rich data table available in the admin home can be dropped unchanged into a checkout or customer-account extension.
example: A team building a cart extension finds the table component is not published there and falls back to a stacked list of line items.
source_quote: Each surface has its own extension APIs and its own subset of Polaris web components.
check: Diff the components imported by each surface bundle against that surface's published component list; unmatched imports must equal 0.

rule: Model each surface as its own integration with its own API contract, sharing design tokens but not implementation assumptions.
why: A product that spans several surfaces inherits several API surfaces, and portability assumptions break at the boundary.
do: Keep one token package shared by all surfaces while giving each surface its own entry point, data layer, and component mapping.
dont: Copy one surface's page component wholesale into another surface and patch the compile errors until it renders.
example: A reporting SaaS reuses its token package on web and in an embedded panel, but writes separate data adapters for each host.
source_quote: Shopify apps can appear across multiple surfaces in the Shopify platform. Each surface has its own set of available APIs and components.
check: Does each shipped surface have its own entry point and adapter, with a shared token package and no cross-surface component copies?

rule: Compose embedded UI from the host's rendered primitives rather than rebuilding page chrome yourself.
why: When the host renders the surrounding surface, custom chrome breaks visual continuity and fights the host's layout rules.
do: Render only the inner block content with the host's primitives and let the surrounding page supply headers, spacing, and navigation.
dont: Draw your own page header, sidebar, and modal shell inside an embedded extension slot.
example: A shipping app's order-page block uses host layout primitives for spacing and adds no custom top bar or back button.
source_quote: Extensions put your app's UI inside a surface that Shopify renders
check: From a screenshot of the embedded slot, is there zero custom page-level chrome such as headers, sidebars, or navigation?

rule: Always render an error summary at the top of the page whenever any validation error occurs, even a single one.
why: A lone inline message on a long form is easy to miss, so users need one place that lists every problem.
do: Show the 'There is a problem' summary listing 'Enter your full name' alongside the inline message when one field fails.
dont: Only turn the email field red and show no summary because just one field failed.
example: A SaaS signup form rejects a weak password; the page returns with an error summary listing that one error.
source_quote: Always show an error summary when there is a validation error, even if there’s only one.
check: Submit each form with invalid data and confirm an error summary is rendered on every failing response, including single-field failures.

topic: Summary and inline messages travel together
rule: Pair every error summary entry with an inline error message next to the field it belongs to.
why: The summary tells users what went wrong overall while the inline message tells them where to fix it.
do: Render the summary link 'Enter your full name' and an inline message under the full name input with the same text.
dont: Show a summary at the top but leave the offending field looking normal with no inline message.
example: A checkout form shows the summary plus a red inline 'Enter a valid expiry date' under the card date field.
source_quote: When a user makes an error, you must show both an error summary and an Error message component next to each answer that contains an error.
check: For each error listed in the summary, confirm a matching inline error element exists adjacent to the associated input.

topic: Focus the error summary on reload
rule: Move keyboard focus to the error summary when a page reloads with validation errors.
why: Screen reader and keyboard users otherwise stay at their old position and never hear that submission failed.
do: On a failed submit, set focus to the summary container so its contents are announced immediately.
dont: Reload the page with errors while focus stays on the submit button at the bottom of the form.
example: Submitting an invite form with a malformed email lands focus on the summary so a screen reader reads the problem list.
source_quote: move keyboard focus to the error summary (the govuk-frontend javascript will do this for you)
check: After submitting invalid data, measure document.activeElement and assert it is the error summary container (1 of 1 submissions).

rule: Word each summary link exactly as the inline message shown next to the input.
why: Different wording makes users work out whether the two messages describe the same problem.
do: Use 'Enter your full name' in both the summary list and the inline message.
dont: Have the summary say 'Name is required' while the field message says 'Enter your full name'.
example: A billing form's summary and inline messages both read 'Enter a valid VAT number'.
source_quote: make sure the error messages in the error summary are worded the same as those which appear next to the inputs with errors
check: Diff the text of each summary link against its matching inline error message and require 0 mismatches.

topic: Link each error to its answer
rule: Link every summary error to the specific field, radio or checkbox that needs fixing.
why: A link that goes nowhere forces users to hunt the page for the failing answer.
do: Point the summary link at #full-name-input, the id of the input that has the error.
dont: Use href="#" for every summary item so clicking does nothing.
example: Clicking 'Passport issue date must include a year' jumps to and focuses the year input.
source_quote: You must link the errors in the error summary to the answer they relate to.
check: Click each summary link and assert the browser focuses an element whose id matches the failing field (100% of links resolve).

rule: For multi-field answers, link to the first field containing an error, or the first field when unknown.
why: Users need to land at the right place instead of guessing which of several boxes failed.
do: For a day/month/year date, link the summary error to the year input when the year is the failing part.
dont: Link a date-of-birth error to the fieldset wrapper so nothing receives focus.
example: A KYC form's date-of-birth error jumps to the day input when the day is the first failing part.
source_quote: If you do not know which field contains an error, link to the first field.
check: Does each multi-field summary link resolve to the first field that contains an error (or the first field if unknown)?

rule: Place the error summary at the top of the main container, below any back link or breadcrumb and above the h1.
why: Putting it in the expected reading order means users hit the problem list before the form.
do: Render the summary inside the main container after the back link and before the page heading.
dont: Bury the summary below the form fields or push it above the breadcrumb in the header area.
example: A settings page shows the back link, then the error summary, then the 'Your details' heading.
source_quote: Put the error summary at the top of the main container. If your page includes breadcrumbs or a back link, place it below these, but above the <h1>.
check: In a screenshot, is the error summary below the back link/breadcrumb and above the h1?

topic: Announce failure in the page title
rule: Prefix the page title with 'Error: ' when the page reloads with validation errors.
why: Screen readers announce the title on page load, so the prefix signals failure immediately.
do: Set the document title to 'Error: Your details - Service name' after a failed submit.
dont: Keep the title 'Your details - Service name' unchanged on the error page.
example: A SaaS invite form's tab title reads 'Error: Invite teammate' after a failed submit.
source_quote: by adding ‘Error: ’ to the beginning of the page <title> so screen readers read it out as soon as possible
check: Submit invalid data and assert document.title starts with 'Error:' (1 of 1 error pages).

rule: Encode quantitative values with length or 2D position, not area or angle.
why: People judge length and 2D position accurately and preattentively, but area and angle poorly.
do: Use a horizontal bar chart for revenue by plan tier.
dont: Use a pie or donut chart to compare revenue across five plan tiers.
example: A SaaS billing dashboard compares monthly recurring revenue across plans using a sorted bar chart, not a pie chart.
source_quote: we are quite adept at estimating how lengths compare, and we can also accurately estimate position in a 2D space
check: Count pie, donut, treemap, and gauge charts used for quantitative metrics; the count should be zero.

rule: Use color to distinguish categories, not to encode quantitative magnitude.
why: People do not perceive color order, and color-only encoding fails for colorblind users.
do: Use blue vs. orange to separate two customer segments, with labels.
dont: Use a red-to-green gradient to represent revenue magnitude.
example: A SaaS ops dashboard colors support channels blue and orange but uses bar length for ticket volume.
source_quote: people do not perceive different colors as being in a particular order, so color should not be used to communicate information about quantitative values or magnitude
check: Is color absent as the sole encoding of any numeric value, and used only for categories or secondary reinforcement?

rule: Render charts in 2D rather than 3D to preserve accurate quantitative comparisons.
why: 3D perspective distorts shapes and alignment, making values harder to read.
do: Show quarterly sales as flat 2D bars aligned to gridlines.
dont: Show quarterly sales as a 3D bar chart with perspective.
example: A SaaS analytics page uses a flat bar chart so users can immediately see Q3 is lower than Q4.
source_quote: a 3D representation of a chart distorts and skews the shapes that represent the data
check: Count 3D chart instances in the dashboard; the count should be zero.

rule: Design dashboards as single-screen, at-a-glance views rather than exploratory data tools.
why: Dashboards are meant to communicate critical information quickly with minimal interaction or cognitive processing.
do: Fit the five key SaaS metrics on one screen without scrolling.
dont: Require users to open multiple tabs and filters to find the main metrics.
example: A SaaS health dashboard shows MRR, churn, active users, and incidents on one screen.
source_quote: Dashboards are collections of data visualizations, presented in a single-page view that imparts at-a-glance information on which users can act quickly
check: Can a user see all key metrics on one screen without scrolling or navigating?

rule: Match chart type to the data relationship: bar for category comparison, line for trends, scatter for correlation.
why: Length and 2D position support fast, accurate comparison and trend perception.
do: Use a line chart for weekly signups, a bar chart for signups by channel, and a scatterplot for spend vs. conversions.
dont: Use a pie chart to show weekly signups over time.
example: A SaaS growth dashboard uses a line chart for weekly active users and a bar chart for users by plan.
source_quote: Bar charts are a reliable means of representing quantitative data: we pre-attentively process the length of each bar efficiently, allowing for easy comparison of values
check: Does each chart type match its intended data relationship (comparison, trend, or correlation)?

rule: Reinforce category grouping with shape or proximity before relying on color alone.
why: Shape and spatial grouping are more reliable for colorblind users, and color works best as a secondary cue.
do: Use different icons and borders for call vs. chat channels, then add color.
dont: Use color alone to distinguish support channels.
example: A support dashboard uses square vs. circle markers plus color for chat and phone tickets.
source_quote: color properties such as hue or saturation are helpful as a secondary grouping cue, rather than as the main way of showing groups or categories
check: Can categories still be distinguished if the screenshot is viewed in grayscale?

rule: Sort bars by value in ascending or descending order to speed comparison.
why: Ordered bars let users compare lengths faster and spot the largest and smallest values.
do: Sort a bar chart of tickets by team from highest to lowest volume.
dont: List bar chart categories alphabetically when the goal is to compare values.
example: A SaaS incident dashboard sorts incident counts by service from highest to lowest.
source_quote: we pre-attentively process the length of each bar efficiently, allowing for easy comparison of values (especially if they are ordered in an ascending or descending pattern)
check: Verify bar values are monotonically increasing or decreasing in the chart data; fail if alphabetical or unsorted.

rule: Check text and icon contrast against every visible background behind a glass surface.
why: Translucent fills let text sit over multiple colors, so contrast can fail in some regions.
do: Run a contrast checker on the worst-case area of a frosted card over imagery and adjust fill opacity or blur until normal text passes 4.5:1.
dont: Place white 14px text on a 30%-opacity card over a busy photo without checking the busiest area.
example: A SaaS dashboard uses a frosted filter panel over a colorful chart; verify filter labels stay readable over the darkest chart bars.
source_quote: Ensure that text and graphical elements meet contrast requirements. Since glassmorphic components are translucent, textual elements can fall over multiple colors, which can affect readability.
check: A contrast checker samples the worst-case text region over the glass and reports a ratio; pass if normal text is at least 4.5:1 and large text is at least 3:1.

rule: Increase background blur when a glass element overlays photography, video, or animation.
why: Strong blur keeps busy backgrounds from competing with the foreground and protects text readability.
do: For a modal over a hero video, set a strong backdrop blur so the video reads as soft color rather than recognizable detail.
dont: Use weak blur over a busy showcase background so every background object stays identifiable behind the panel.
example: A web product opens a command palette over a photo-rich landing page; apply strong blur behind the palette.
source_quote: More background blur is better, especially with intricate backgrounds (e.g., video, photography, animations).
check: Does the glass surface blur intricate background detail enough that background elements are not easily identifiable behind the panel?

rule: Offer a reduce-transparency or increase-contrast setting when glass surfaces are part of the interface.
why: Low-vision users need a way to remove blur and translucency that harm readability.
do: Add an accessibility setting that replaces glass panels with solid backgrounds and verify it removes blur.
dont: Ship glass overlays with no accessibility toggle and rely only on default blur.
example: A SaaS app's settings include 'Reduce transparency' which turns frosted side panels into solid surfaces.
source_quote: If feasible, give users the option to control contrast or transparency settings.
check: Open accessibility settings, toggle reduce transparency, and confirm glass components render with solid backgrounds and no backdrop blur.

rule: Reserve glassmorphism for a few depth-creating elements rather than applying it across the UI.
why: Overuse causes accessibility and usability problems and weakens visual hierarchy.
do: Use a frosted overlay only for a navigation bar or modal while keeping main content surfaces opaque.
dont: Make every card, button, and sidebar translucent so the whole screen becomes competing layers.
example: A project management SaaS uses glass only for the floating command bar, not for task cards.
source_quote: Overall, glassmorphism is best when utilized sparingly to create an illusion of depth.
check: Are glass effects used on only a few depth or overlay roles rather than most components in the screenshot?

rule: Add a low-opacity or gradient stroke to a glass component when it sits on a simple or single-color background.
why: A subtle border creates an illusion of thickness and keeps the glass edge visible without a complex backdrop.
do: On a solid gray page, give a frosted card a 1px white 20% border or gradient stroke so its edge reads as glass.
dont: Place a translucent card on a flat white page with no stroke, making the glass effect nearly invisible.
example: A settings panel uses a frosted card on a plain background; a faint gradient border defines its edge.
source_quote: You can add a low-opacity or gradient stroke around a component to create an illusion of thickness.
check: Does the glass component on a simple background have a visible low-opacity or gradient border that defines its edge?

rule: Use simple or single-color backgrounds behind translucent components when you control that background.
why: Controlled simple backdrops preserve readability and let the glass treatment create depth without noise.
do: For an in-app modal, place it over a dimmed solid scrim instead of a busy screenshot collage.
dont: Put a frosted dropdown directly over a rotating carousel of detailed photos you control.
example: A SaaS onboarding modal uses a frosted panel over a plain dimmed backdrop, not the dashboard's live charts.
source_quote: On the other hand, if you have control of what appears behind a translucent component, opt for simple or single-color backgrounds.
check: In the screenshot, is the area directly behind the glass a simple or single-color surface when the team controls that backdrop?

rule: Start from an established glass material in a design system instead of inventing one from scratch.
why: Existing materials account for blur, transparency, and accessibility better than ad hoc styles.
do: Use Apple SwiftUI materials or Microsoft Acrylic tokens as the baseline for glass surfaces.
dont: Hand-roll a custom glass CSS recipe with random opacity and blur values for every component.
example: A cross-platform app uses the platform's native acrylic material for context menus rather than custom CSS.
source_quote: Consider using already established design systems, like Apple’s SwfitUI, to avoid any potential issues with creating glassmorphic materials from scratch.
check: Does the implementation reuse a documented material or design-system token instead of a one-off glass style?

rule: Branch every animation on the prefers-reduced-motion media query with gsap.matchMedia() and ship a simplified variant.
why: Users with vestibular disorders can get dizzy, headachey or nauseous from motion, and the OS setting is the only signal they can give you before the page loads.
do: let mm = gsap.matchMedia(); mm.add("(prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)", () => gsap.from('.card', {opacity:0, rotation:360, ease:'back.out'})); mm.add("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)", () => gsap.from('.card', {opacity:0}));
dont: gsap.from('.card', {opacity: 0, rotation: 360, ease: 'back.out'}) fired unconditionally on load.
example: A SaaS dashboard hero card spins in on first load; with reduced motion on it only fades in.
source_quote: We can listen to this user preference and adjust our animations accordingly with gsap.matchMedia().
check: Count gsap animation calls not nested inside a prefers-reduced-motion matchMedia branch; the number must be 0.

rule: Remove decorative animation entirely under reduced motion, and keep functional feedback while simplifying it.
why: Decorative motion carries no information worth the discomfort, but progress and status animations tell the user something happened.
do: Progress bar keeps a 200ms opacity fade under reduced motion; the confetti burst on completion is not rendered at all.
dont: Parallax hero, spinning logo and bouncing badge all keep their full motion because the team liked the feel.
example: In an upload flow, the progress bar still animates width but the pulsing glow and confetti are dropped.
source_quote: If it's just decorative, removing it entirely is the best option.
check: With reduced motion enabled, does each animated element either disappear or still serve an informational purpose?

rule: Replace large x/y swipes and hard color flashes in the reduced variant with a gentle opacity crossfade.
why: Fast color cuts can trigger seizures and large axis movements are the main vestibular trigger, while a crossfade still conveys spatial context.
do: Route change crossfades the incoming view's opacity over 250ms with no translate on the x axis.
dont: A 600px slide-in page transition plus a flash to white on submit, unchanged for reduced-motion users.
example: Switching tabs in a SaaS app slides the panel 600px; under reduced motion it crossfades in place.
source_quote: Big swiping motions on the x axis can be triggering, but the animation is important for spacial context
check: Measure the maximum translateX/translateY delta of the animated element while reduced motion is on; it must be 0px.

rule: Add a reduced-motion toggle in the UI, seed it from the system preference, and re-run matchMedia when it changes.
why: Many affected users never change their OS settings, so the toggle hands control back to them and must override the system default both ways.
do: checkbox.checked = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches; checkbox.addEventListener('change', gsap.matchMediaRefresh); then read checkbox.checked inside the matchMedia handler.
dont: Only reading the OS media query and giving motion-sensitive users no way to opt out in the product.
example: A settings page 'Reduced animation' switch that refires every gsap.matchMedia() animation immediately.
source_quote: it's a good idea to add a reduced motion toggle in the UI and put the power back in the user's hands to decide.
check: Flip the in-app toggle and confirm every matchMedia animation reverts and re-runs within the same interaction, with reduced motion on and off.

rule: Disable SplitText's built-in aria and ship an .sr-only duplicate whenever the split text contains links or emphasis.
why: The generated aria-label is a flat string, so nested links and strong/em semantics vanish for screen reader users.
do:
Text with a link

Text with a link

plus SplitText.create('.animate-me', {type:'words', aria:'hidden'}).
dont: Letting SplitText put aria-label on a heading whose only link is inside an aria-hidden child div.
example: A marketing headline with an inline signup link is split into words; the sr-only copy keeps the real anchor.
source_quote: we recommend disabling the default aria settings with aria:false, and creating a screenreader-only duplicate of your element instead.
check: Does the screen-reader-only duplicate contain the same links and emphasis markup as the visible animated text?

rule: Walk every animated flow with motion on and off, including a screen reader pass, before shipping.
why: Reduced-motion bugs and broken split text only surface when the alternate branch actually runs.
do: Record a run of onboarding, upload and settings flows with the OS preference toggled and with a screen reader reading the split headline.
dont: Shipping after checking only the default animated view on the designer's machine.
example: A checkout success animation is verified for reduced motion and for screen reader announcement before release.
source_quote: Treat text splitting with care and ensure you test thoroughly!
check: For each animated page, log one browser run with reduced motion on and one off, and confirm no animation or announcement is broken.

rule: Set one pair of 16-32px outer margins for the whole page and skip the centered max-width container.
why: Almost half the studied strong sites use margins of 32px or less, while the 1100-1300px centered container is the frame of the ones called stock.
do: A `.wrap` with `padding-inline: clamp(1rem, 2.2vw, 2rem)` so hero type and images run full width, with only paragraph measure capped in `ch`.
dont: Wrapping the whole page in `main { max-width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto }` so every section floats inside side gutters.
example: A SaaS pricing page where the hero headline and logo wall run edge to edge and only the body copy is capped at 62ch.
source_quote: About 45 of 114 use outer margins of 32px or less; only about 8 use 80px or more.
check: At a 1440px viewport, measure computed padding-left and padding-right on the page wrapper: both between 16 and 32px and within 2px of each other.

rule: Pick two or three anchor lines for the page and start the hero, section headings, pricing figures and footer on the same ones.
why: Six different start positions mean nothing was decided; forcing everything onto a few lines is what makes a page feel composed.
do: Hero headline, the 'Prices' heading and the footer wordmark all begin on the column-5 line.
dont: Hero starts at 8%, section headings at 0, pricing centered, footer links in three columns each at their own edges.
example: A dashboard marketing page where the h1, the feature section titles and the closing CTA all start on the same third-across line.
source_quote: If the hero headline starts at column 5, the section headings, the pricing figure and the footer links start there too.
check: On a full-page screenshot, do the hero headline, section headings and footer content share the same left edge within a few pixels?

rule: Decide where each large empty area sits and name the picture, type or ground change that closes it.
why: Readers judge every big blank either a rest that something closes or a hole, and strong sites keep the rests but get criticized for the holes.
do: A full-width product photograph sits under the statement and closes the band of ground below it.
dont: A 500px band of plain background between two sections with a faint caption floating in it and nothing else.
example: An analytics landing page leaves a wide dark gap after the hero, closed by a full-bleed product screenshot that rises into it.
source_quote: Decide where the void is and name what closes it. If nothing does, it is a hole
check: For every empty area over 40% of a screen, can you point to the image, headline, text pair or ground change that closes it in the screenshot?

rule: Space sections 120-240px apart on desktop and 72-112px on mobile, measured from the last line of one to the first line of the next.
why: The median gap in the study is about 230-250px, and more than roughly 40% of a screen of plain ground reads as a hole.
do: `--section-gap: clamp(120px, 14vw, 240px)` applied consistently between sections, tightened to 72-112px under 640px.
dont: `padding: 12rem 0` on alternating sections so some gaps land at 190px and others at 380px.
example: A SaaS feature page where each section's top margin is 160px at 1440px and 88px at 390px, on every section.
source_quote: Sections sit 120-240px apart on desktop, counted from the last line of one to the first line of the next
check: Measure the vertical distance from the bottom of the last text line in one section to the top of the first text line in the next: 120-240px at 1440px and 72-112px at 390px, with no gap over 40% of viewport height.

topic: Say what it is in the h1
rule: Write one first-screen `h1` at display size, two lines at most, that states what the product is and who it is for.
why: 15 of 97 studied first screens never say what the page is, and a display-size name alone does not do it.
do:
`

Invoicing for freelance designers

` at 72px, with one supporting line and a start button on the same screen.
dont:
`

Aperture

` at 120px with a hero image and no line explaining the product anywhere above the fold.
example: A SaaS homepage whose first screen reads 'Payroll for small studios' in 64px type, plus a one-line description and a start button.
source_quote: If the `h1` is the name, the line under it, at 18px or more, says what the thing is.
check: Within five seconds of looking at the first screen, can a stranger say what the product is and who it is for in words, from the h1 or the line under it?

rule: Keep navigation within about a tenth of the first screen on desktop and one row on mobile, and never let it sit over content.
why: Floating or oversized nav bars are where the panel most often recorded navigation covering text, costing a whole point of usability.
do: Wordmark left, three text links and one action right, on the page ground with no bar, sitting above the hero with nothing pinned over it.
dont: A fixed translucent pill bar that overlaps the h1 at the top of the scroll and stacks into a column of tabs on the phone.
example: A 390px screen showing wordmark plus 'Start' in one row, links in a full-screen sheet opened from a 'Menu' text button.
source_quote: On desktop it takes no more than about a tenth of the first screen; on a phone it is one row.
check: At 1440 and 390 widths, screenshot every 10% of scroll: the nav bounding box must not intersect any text element, and nav height must be ≤10% of viewport on desktop and one row on mobile.

rule: Design the 390px screen as its own composition with 16-20px margins, 16-18px body text and 44px touch targets.
why: A phone layout that is the desktop shrunk is one of the failures the panel logs, and small text and touch targets lose usability points.
do: At 390px: 20px side padding, 17px body, buttons 48px tall, headline re-broken onto two lines and the image re-cropped to portrait.
dont: The desktop hero scaled down at 390px, giving 11px copy, 30px buttons and a headline wrapped to four lines.
example: A SaaS sign-up page on a phone with 18px labels, 44px-tall inputs and a portrait crop of the dashboard screenshot.
source_quote: Margins 16-20px. Body text 16-18px. Touch targets at least 44px high.
check: At a 390px viewport, measure page side padding (16-20px), computed body and label font-size (≥16px) and the height of every button and link target (≥44px).

rule: Acknowledge every user action immediately with a visible state change or progress indicator.
why: Users need confirmation that their interaction succeeded so they do not repeat it or lose confidence.
do: Change the submit button label to “Sending…” and disable it while the request is pending.
dont: Leave the submit button unchanged and silent while the request is processing.
example: A SaaS “Invite teammate” button shows a spinner and “Sending…” until the invite succeeds.
source_quote: feedback can be as simple as a change of color once the user has clicked on a button
check: A browser test clicks a primary action and measures whether a visible pending state appears within 1000 ms.

rule: Show a progress indicator whenever a process takes longer than a moment.
why: Progress indicators reassure users that a longer wait is normal and that the system is still working.
do: Display a progress bar during a file upload and keep it visible until completion.
dont: Show a blank screen while an upload or import runs with no indication of activity.
example: A report export shows a progress bar and “Preparing download” until the file is ready.
source_quote: Progress indicators reassure the user that a longer wait is normal, and that the system is still working
check: A browser test triggers an operation longer than 1 second and verifies a visible progress or status element remains until completion.

rule: Expose the current system state that users need to choose their next action.
why: Only by knowing the current status can users decide what to do next and feel in control.
do: Show sync status, last updated time, and offline badges on a dashboard.
dont: Hide whether data is stale, syncing, or offline when users must act on it.
example: A project dashboard displays “Synced 2 min ago” and an offline badge when disconnected.
source_quote: Only by knowing what the current system status is can you change it
check: Can a reviewer identify the current system state from the screenshot without interacting?

rule: Explain consequential state changes and let users decide how to handle affected items.
why: Silent changes take control away from users and degrade trust in the product.
do: Mark unavailable wish-list items and offer choices to remove them or keep them for reference.
dont: Silently remove out-of-stock or discontinued items from a saved list.
example: A subscription billing failure banner explains the issue and offers “Update payment” or “Keep plan paused.”
source_quote: explicitly communicate the current system’s status  -  which items are no longer available  -  and then allow the user to either remove them
check: Does the screen explain the state change and offer a user choice to remove or keep affected items?

rule: Surface backstage events that affect users through notifications, indicators, or modal dialogs.
why: Users need to be informed when system-side changes significantly affect their work or account.
do: Show a modal explaining a failed payment and the next required step.
dont: Silently downgrade a subscription after a failed renewal with no on-screen notice.
example: A billing failure modal appears when a team’s plan is about to be downgraded.
source_quote: To communicate backstage events that may impact users, you can use either notifications or indicators.
check: Is each consequential backstage event visible to the user when it happens?

rule: Show low-stock and out-of-stock status only when it helps users act or avoid wasted effort.
why: Low stock can prompt action, while out-of-stock status prevents users from attempting unavailable purchases.
do: Display “Only 2 left” for low inventory and disable sold-out sizes before selection.
dont: Hide sold-out status until users try to add an unavailable item to cart.
example: A product page shows “Only a few left” for low-stock sizes and crossed-out sold-out sizes.
source_quote: When there are no items in stock: This information can save the users the effort of trying to add to cart products that are no longer available.
check: Are low-stock and out-of-stock states shown before the user attempts to buy?

rule: Provide at least minimal feedback when a command is received on a screenless device.
why: A perceptible acknowledgement assures users that the system heard the command.
do: Flash a light ring when a smart speaker hears a voice command.
dont: Accept a voice command silently with no light, sound, or other acknowledgement.
example: A smart-home app’s device flashes once when it receives “Set a timer.”
source_quote: a minimum feedback that the command was heard is essential
check: Send a voice command and observe whether a perceptible acknowledgement appears within 1 second.

rule: Fill heroes, buttons and glow layers with flat colour from the dealt palette, never a violet or indigo gradient.
why: The indigo gradient hero is the most-produced default of generated pages, so it reads as generated before the content is read.
do: Hero ground #111111 with a solid #1A7F5A primary button labelled 'Start a project'.
dont: Hero with `linear-gradient(90deg,#7C3AED,#4F46E5)` behind the headline and a radial violet glow under the CTA.
example: A SaaS pricing page keeps its hero on a flat off-white field; the CTA is a solid ink button reading 'Start free trial'.
source_quote: Violet / indigo gradients on hero, buttons and glows
check: Lint counts elements on the hero, buttons and glow layers whose computed background-image is a gradient; the page fails above 0.

rule: Replace the three identical feature cards with one composed section instead of three rounded-square icons in a row.
why: Three equal cards each carrying a rounded-square icon are the default feature section a generator emits with no argument behind it.
do: A feature section built as one lead statement plus a large annotated interface shot with three named capabilities stacked beside it.
dont: Three equal cards, each with a 48px icon in a 12px-radius square, a heading and a two-line paragraph.
example: A project-management SaaS features page leads with one large workflow screenshot and a stacked list of three capabilities next to it.
source_quote: Three identical feature cards, each with an icon in a rounded square
check: Count feature-section children that share identical dimensions and each contain an icon inside a rounded square; must be 0.

rule: Delete the tiny tracked uppercase eyebrow above headings and fold its words into the heading or the sentence below.
why: The kicker is applied above every heading by default, so it reads as a template rather than a decision.
do: Heading 'Invoices that reconcile themselves' followed by the sentence 'Built for finance teams closing the month.'
dont: 'BILLING' in 11px uppercase with 0.18em tracking sitting above the heading 'Invoicing you can trust'.
example: A payments dashboard section header reads 'Payouts land the same day' with no small label above it.
source_quote: Eyebrow / kicker: tiny tracked uppercase label above every heading
check: Lint counts elements with uppercase transform, letter-spacing at or above 0.1em and font-size at or below 12px positioned above a heading; must be 0.

rule: Take warmth from a low-chroma stone, a deep ink or a photograph, not a yellow-cream ground with a terracotta accent.
why: The warm editorial remedy was adopted wholesale and is now the most recognisable generated look of all.
do: An off-white #F7F5F1 ground with ink #1C1A17 and one deep green accent.
dont: Cream #F5EFE6 ground with terracotta #C96F4A buttons, rust headings and clay-tinted card borders.
example: A B2B analytics landing page uses stone-grey grounds and a near-black footer; the only warm note is a photograph of the team.
source_quote: Yellow-cream ground + terracotta / rust / clay accent
check: Sample the rendered palette and fail if the ground hue sits in the cream band (40-55 degrees) and any accent sits in the terracotta/rust/clay band (10-30 degrees) above 0.05 chroma.

rule: Set labels and captions in the text face, keeping monospace for tabular figures in data only.
why: Mono labels are the first thing a generator copies from award galleries and they carry no information.
do: A section label 'Method' set in the body sans at 14px, with monospace kept only for a data table's numeric columns.
dont: A section marked '// 03 - METHOD' in 11px monospace above the heading.
example: A reporting SaaS labels chart axes in the UI sans and keeps monospace only for the numeric columns of its tables.
source_quote: Monospace micro-labels, mono as a "technical" voice, mono captions
check: Lint counts monospace font-family declarations used outside data tables and code blocks; must be 0.

rule: Separate content with space, tone steps or filled shapes instead of hairline dividers and 1px outlined boxes.
why: Hairline rules and outlined tiles are gallery-fashion structure markers a generator copies without a reason.
do: Sections divided by a tone step from #FFFFFF to #F4F2EE with 64px of space between blocks.
dont: Every section under a 1px #E5E5E5 rule and feature tiles boxed with 1px outlines at 8px radius.
example: A settings page groups rows into a filled card on a tinted ground rather than drawing a 1px box around each row.
source_quote: Thin rules: hairline dividers, ruled grids, 1px outlined boxes and tiles
check: Lint counts borders of width 1px or less used as dividers or box outlines; the page fails at 3 or more outlined boxes.

rule: Write the hero headline as a title of about five words and push the rest of the sentence below it.
why: A display-size full sentence running three or four lines is a structural tell that buries the actual claim.
do: An H1 reading 'Close the books faster' with the supporting line 'Month-end in three days, not three weeks.'
dont: An H1 reading 'We help finance teams close the books faster with automated reconciliation and real-time reporting' at 64px across four lines.
example: A payroll SaaS hero reads 'Payroll without the paperwork' with all the detail in the paragraph beneath it.
source_quote: Headline as a full sentence at display size, three or four lines
check: Script counts h1 words at or below 8 and rendered h1 line count at 1440px width at or below 2.

rule: Use one signature motion move and drop the identical fade-up applied to every block.
why: The same fade-and-rise everywhere plus staggered hero entrances is the motion default that makes a page read as generated.
do: A single deliberate reveal on the hero product shot while every section below it appears static.
dont: Every section wrapped in a fade from opacity 0 to 1 with translateY(24px), each delay 100ms longer than the last.
example: A dashboard marketing page animates one chart building once on load and leaves the feature sections untouched.
source_quote: Identical fade-up on every block; a dozen staggered hero entrances; hover lift on every card
check: Lint counts distinct entrance animation patterns and elements with scroll-triggered translateY; any pattern repeated on more than one section fails.

topic: Never ship a totally empty container
rule: Design an explicit message for every container that can render with no content instead of leaving it blank.
why: A blank region leaves users unsure whether the system is working, still loading, or broken, which erodes confidence.
do: A 'Recent views' panel with no items shows 'Items you open will appear here.'
dont: A 'Recent views' panel renders as an empty white box with no text at all.
example: A SaaS dashboard ships with the Favorites tab empty on day one and shows a one-line explanation inside the panel.
source_quote: Do not default to totally empty states. This approach creates confusion for users, who may be left wondering if the system is still loading information or if errors have occurred.
check: Does every container that can render with zero items show a text message rather than blank space?

rule: Show a progress indicator while a process runs and reserve the no-data message for after it completes.
why: Declaring 'no records' mid-load makes trigger-happy users abandon the screen before the content ever appears.
do: The table shows a spinner or skeleton rows until the fetch resolves, then states 'No records for the selected date range.'
dont: The table flashes 'No records' on load, then replaces it with rows a few seconds later.
example: An employee-management list briefly shows 'No records' before populating, so users refresh and lose their place.
source_quote: When a process is running, use progress indicators to increase visibility of system status.
check: Throttle the network, load the screen, and confirm zero-result text never renders before the data request resolves.

topic: Name the state and its cause
rule: Write the empty-state message so it names the missing content and the filter or scope that produced it.
why: Without that framing users rerun queries repeatedly, unsure whether an error occurred or the filters were wrong.
do: 'There are no records to display for the selected date range.'
dont: An empty log-details table with no message after a date-range query.
example: A log viewer's details dialog returns nothing for a date range and explains why instead of showing silence.
source_quote: If there is no relevant data to display after a process has completed, use the empty space to provide a system-status message
check: Does the empty-state copy name both what is missing and the filter or scope that caused the empty result?

topic: Teach the feature in the empty state
rule: Use the empty state to explain what would appear there and how the user creates it.
why: In-context help shown at the moment of need is remembered better than a tutorial pushed at first login.
do: The favorites panel reads 'Star your favorites to list them here.'
dont: The Alerts panel shows nothing when no alerts exist, so users never learn what alerts do.
example: An ERP alerts panel with no configured alerts explains the feature and how to trigger one.
source_quote: When content does not yet exist for a screen, page, or panel, use the empty state to provide help cues.
check: Does the empty state explain both what will appear in this area and how the user adds that content?

topic: Put the first action inside the empty state
rule: Place a primary button or link that starts the populating task directly inside the empty state.
why: Telling users what to do without showing where to do it stalls them at the exact moment they should be onboarded.
do: The empty alerts panel offers a 'Create' button plus a 'Learn more' link, and the log tool offers two starter paths.
dont: The message says 'Send a request to view details in the workspace' with no link or button.
example: A cloud log tool's empty state offers 'Add log source' and 'Explore demo data' as two direct entry points.
source_quote: Provide direct pathways (i.e., links) to getting started with key tasks related to populating the empty state.
check: Does the empty state contain at least one clickable action that starts the task which fills this container?

rule: Verify the empty-state label matches the true system state before shipping it.
why: A false 'no records' message makes users distrust the product or abandon work they assume is impossible.
do: Show 'No alerts configured yet' only after the alerts query has returned empty.
dont: Show 'No records' during fetching and swap it for rows seconds later.
example: An HR tool shows 'No records' on screen entry and then loads the actual list, so users learn to distrust the label.
source_quote: Inaccurate system-status messages for empty states are particularly harmful.
check: Reviewing a record of the screen over time, does the empty-state copy ever contradict what the system is actually doing?

rule: Build a full palette of greys, primary and accent families instead of picking five swatches from a generator.
why: Real interfaces need many shades for text, surfaces, controls and states, so a five-color scheme forces compromises everywhere.
do: Ship a tokens file with grey, primary and accent families, each as a numbered scale, before styling any component.
dont: Use a generator's five perfect swatches as the whole color system and then invent new hexes ad hoc per component.
example: A SaaS onboarding app defines grey-100…900, blue-100…900 and red/green/yellow scales in tokens.json before the first screen is styled.
source_quote: You can’t build anything with five hex codes. To build something real, you need a much more comprehensive set of colors to choose from.
check: Parse the palette/token file and count distinct color values: expect at least 20 across at least 3 color families.

rule: Create 8-10 grey shades from a very dark grey up to white rather than starting at pure black.
why: Almost every surface, text and control is grey, and true black looks unnatural against real screens.
do: Define grey-900 as a dark charcoal such as #1F2933 and step evenly to grey-50 as #FFFFFF.
dont: Set the darkest text color to #000000 and jump straight to white with only two stops in between.
example: A dashboard uses grey-900 for headings, grey-600 for body text, grey-100 for panel backgrounds and grey-50 for the page.
source_quote: True black tends to look pretty unnatural, so start with a really dark grey and work your way up to white in steady increments.
check: Count stops in the grey scale (target 8-10) and compute the darkest stop's relative luminance: it must be above pure black.

rule: Give each primary color 5-10 lighter and darker shades, not a single brand hex.
why: Primary colors carry actions and navigation, and they need light tints for backgrounds and dark shades for text.
do: Define primary-100 through primary-900 with the brand blue at 500, using 100 as a tinted alert background.
dont: Hardcode one brand blue for every button, link, badge and background regardless of context.
example: A landing page uses primary-500 for the CTA button, primary-700 for link text on white and primary-100 behind a callout.
source_quote: Just like with greys, you need a variety (5-10) of lighter and darker shades to choose from.
check: Count shades in each primary family in the token file: the number must fall between 5 and 10.

rule: Add accent families with multiple shades for semantic states, and use them sparingly.
why: Users read color as meaning, so destructive, warning and success states each need their own scale, not a borrowed primary.
do: Define danger, warning and success scales with at least three shades each, using yellow-100 for the warning banner tint.
dont: Reuse the primary blue for a delete confirmation and a success toast so the states look identical.
example: A project tool shows red-600 for a delete action, yellow-100 background with yellow-800 text for a warning, green-600 for a positive trend.
source_quote: You’ll want multiple shades for these colors too, even though they should be used pretty sparingly throughout the UI.
check: Check tokens for danger, warning and success families and count shades in each: at least 3 per family.

rule: Define a fixed numbered shade set up front instead of generating variants with lighten or darken at build time.
why: On-the-fly functions produce dozens of near-identical blues that all look the same and cannot be governed.
do: Reference only tokens like primary-600 and primary-300 from components, with every value present in the palette file.
dont: Write lighten($primary, 10%) in a button hover state and another lighten() elsewhere with a slightly different amount.
example: A web app's CSS only uses var(--blue-600) / var(--blue-700) for hover states, never a filter or color function.
source_quote: don’t get clever using CSS preprocessor functions like "lighten" or "darken" to create shades on the fly.
check: Grep stylesheets/tokens for lighten(, darken(, color-mix( and filter: brightness on color: count must be 0.

rule: Pick the base shade so it would work well as a button background.
why: The middle of the scale is the most-used shade, and a button is its most common real context.
do: Test candidate blues behind white button label text and keep the one that reads clearly as a filled button.
dont: Choose the base shade from a brand guideline swatch that is too light to carry white text.
example: A signup form's primary button uses the base shade, which passes contrast with white text without needing a darker hover.
source_quote: for primary and accent colors, a good rule of thumb is to pick a shade that would work well as a button background.
check: Looking at the button in the palette sheet, is the base (500) shade obviously usable as a filled button background with white text?

rule: Use a nine-step scale numbered 100 to 900 and fill shades 700 and 300 before the remaining gaps.
why: Nine divides evenly, and picking the midpoints first gives a balanced ramp that still leaves enough options.
do: Set 900 darkest, 500 base, 100 lightest, then choose 700 and 300 as visible compromises, then fill 800, 600, 400, 200.
dont: Freehand eight arbitrary stops so 600 and 700 are nearly identical while 300 to 500 jumps sharply.
example: A design system's blue ramp has nine tokens where each step looks like an even midpoint of its neighbors.
source_quote: Start by picking shades 700 and 300, the ones right in the middle of the gaps.
check: Squinting at the rendered ramp, does each shade look like a believable midpoint of the two shades beside it?

rule: Avoid adding new shades once the palette is in use; tweak existing ones instead.
why: An unbounded palette with one-off hexes is effectively no color system at all.
do: If a shade feels wrong, adjust the existing token and let every component inherit the change.
dont: Add a sixteenth blue for one hero section because the nearest token is slightly off.
example: A marketing page team changes blue-600 globally rather than introducing a new hero-only blue.
source_quote: Just try to avoid adding new shades too often if you can avoid it.
check: Grep component files for hex color literals outside the token file: the count must be 0, or no growth vs the previous commit.

rule: Define or redefine the information architecture before designing any navigation components.
why: Navigation designed before the IA is scoped cannot accommodate the real content set and forces costly redesign or cramming.
do: Run a content inventory, group content, and draft a sitemap diagram before wireframing the top bar or sidebar.
dont: Pick an inverted-L layout from a template and only later discover that many sections run more than four tiers deep.
example: A SaaS admin console redesign starts with a spreadsheet of every settings page and its parent node before anyone opens Figma to draw the sidebar.
source_quote: When approaching a design or redesign project, it is important to take a look under the hood and start by defining or redefining the IA.
check: An IA diagram or spreadsheet exists whose last-modified date precedes the first navigation wireframe file.

rule: Document the information architecture in spreadsheets and diagrams, not in wireframes or prototypes.
why: IA is the structural backbone behind the UI, so it needs an artifact that can be inspected and revised independently of visual layout.
do: Keep a spreadsheet listing every content object, its parent node, and its standardized label.
dont: Treat the clickable prototype as the only record of site structure.
example: The content team maintains a sitemap spreadsheet for the marketing site; the Figma file only shows the resulting nav bar.
source_quote: The IA is documented in spreadsheets and diagrams, not in wireframes, comprehensive layouts (known as comps), or prototypes.
check: Is there a spreadsheet or diagram artifact that records the site structure separately from any wireframe or prototype?

rule: Size navigation patterns to the full depth and breadth of the content, not to how they look.
why: Navigation that cannot hold the real content scope forces either a redesign or cramming content into too few tiers.
do: Count the deepest content tier and the number of top-level sections before choosing global nav, megamenu, or left rail.
dont: Choose an inverted-L layout because it looks clean, then discover sections run more than four tiers deep.
example: A dashboard product maps six top-level areas and five levels of settings before picking a sidebar plus top bar pattern.
source_quote: An inverted-L can accommodate sites that are no more than 4 tiers deep.
check: Measured max content depth in tiers and count of top-level sections are recorded, and the chosen nav pattern's stated tier capacity is at least the measured depth.

rule: Decide usage priority, placement, and pattern explicitly for every navigation component.
why: Each component exists to help users find content or take action, and those decisions differ per component.
do: Write one line per component: who relies on it, which pages it appears on, and which pattern it uses.
dont: Add breadcrumbs, filters, and a fat footer by default with no stated reason or placement rule.
example: In a SaaS app spec, the left nav is primary, breadcrumbs appear only on detail pages, and related links sit in the right rail.
source_quote: Usage Priority: How much will users rely on this navigation component?
check: Does the spec list usage priority, page placement, and pattern for each navigation component shown?

rule: Inventory and audit existing content before grouping it or naming navigation labels.
why: User-centered groupings and a controlled vocabulary depend on knowing what content exists and whether it is any good.
do: List every page and object, evaluate its usefulness and tone, then group and standardize labels.
dont: Invent top-level nav labels before anyone has listed what pages the site actually has.
example: Before renaming the support section in a SaaS help center, the team lists all 140 articles and flags 30 outdated ones.
source_quote: Content inventory: Examination of a website to locate and identify existing site content
check: A content inventory file exists listing every known page or object, with audit status recorded per item.

rule: Get a first-pass IA done before wireframing, but do not block wireframes until it is final.
why: A rough IA is enough to gauge content volume and complexity, and waiting for a perfect IA stalls the project.
do: Publish a v0 sitemap with known content volumes, then start wireframes while refining groupings.
dont: Block all wireframing until the taxonomy is fully signed off.
example: A B2B site starts wireframes with a draft four-section sitemap and updates it after card sorting.
source_quote: The IA doesn’t need to be final before beginning to wireframe and prototype
check: Is there a draft IA artifact, and did wireframing begin before the IA was marked final?

rule: Put a product outcome - a customer behavior or sentiment - at the top of every opportunity solution tree.
why: Product outcomes are within the team’s control, unlike business metrics, and traction metrics are too narrow for discovery.
do: Top the tree with 'Increase % of first-session users who reach the aha moment from 22% to 25%'.
dont: Top the tree with 'Increase revenue by 20%' or 'Drive adoption of the new export button'.
example: A SaaS onboarding trio maps opportunities under a product outcome about first-session aha reach, not a revenue target.
source_quote: As a general rule, I like to see a product outcome at the top of an opportunity solution tree.
check: Does the top of the tree state a product outcome measuring a customer behavior or sentiment rather than a business or traction metric?

rule: Collect three to four story-based customer interviews before mapping the opportunity space.
why: Three to four stories prevent overreacting to one story while avoiding analysis paralysis.
do: Run four 'Tell me about the last time…' interviews, then map top-level moments from those stories.
dont: Start the tree from a single support ticket or from opportunities you brainstormed from memory.
example: A web app team logs four interview transcripts before drawing the first opportunity branches.
source_quote: I encourage teams to start mapping the opportunity space after collecting three to four customer stories.
check: Count story-based interview transcripts or notes logged before the first opportunity map; pass if the number is at least 3.

rule: Put only opportunities heard in customer interviews on the tree; use sales, support, and analytics as leads for interviews.
why: Opportunities generated from memory or secondhand sources lack context and risk addressing the wrong need.
do: Trace each top-level opportunity to a named interview story about past behavior.
dont: Add 'users want SSO' from a sales call directly as an opportunity without interviewing about the underlying need.
example: A B2B SaaS team treats a feature request for bulk editing as a prompt to interview admins, not as a tree opportunity.
source_quote: When we limit the opportunities on the opportunity solution tree to just the opportunities we hear in customer interviews
