check: Does every top-level opportunity on the tree trace to a specific customer interview story rather than a ticket or request?

rule: Test each opportunity by asking whether more than one solution could address it; reframe single-solution statements.
why: If only one solution fits, the statement is a solution in disguise and narrows discovery prematurely.
do: Reframe 'I want a CSV export' by asking why, uncovering 'I need to reconcile usage in my finance tool'.
dont: List 'I want a CSV export button' as an opportunity because only building that button addresses it.
example: A dashboard team reframes a requested filter into an unmet need to compare segments quickly.
source_quote: Is there more than one way to address this opportunity?
check: Can a reviewer name at least two distinct solutions that would address the stated opportunity?

rule: Choose a target opportunity as soon as the opportunity space has a crummy first draft.
why: Most discovery learning happens once solutions and assumptions are explored, so don't wait for a polished map.
do: Sketch top-level moments, pick one target opportunity, and start solution exploration the same week.
dont: Spend days perfecting the opportunity branches before selecting any target.
example: A SaaS trio selects one onboarding opportunity from a rough map and begins assumption tests.
source_quote: Choose a target opportunity as soon as you have a first draft of the opportunity space.
check: Was a target opportunity selected from a first-draft map before the team spent hours refining the opportunity space?

rule: Generate and compare more than one solution for the chosen target opportunity, not solutions across the whole tree.
why: Compare-and-contrast decisions improve when teams explore multiple options for one opportunity.
do: For one target opportunity, sketch three distinct solution concepts and list their riskiest assumptions.
dont: Brainstorm one pet feature across every branch of the opportunity space.
example: A SaaS team explores three ways to help admins find stale accounts before testing assumptions.
source_quote: I recommend that teams consider more than one solution for their target opportunity.
check: Does the record show at least two distinct solution concepts considered for the same target opportunity?

rule: Assess opportunities by sizing, market, company, and customer factors - not by solution effort.
why: Any opportunity can have easy or hard solutions, and early effort assumptions can wrongly rule out valuable needs.
do: Score an opportunity on how many customers are affected, how often, and how important it is to them.
dont: Drop an opportunity because the team assumes it will take too much engineering effort.
example: A SaaS team keeps an opportunity about reconciling billing data even though the first imagined fix seems hard.
source_quote: Solutions take effort. But we aren’t exploring solutions yet.
check: Does the opportunity assessment exclude engineering effort estimates and include sizing, market, company, or customer factors?

rule: Revisit and refine the opportunity space every three to four customer interviews.
why: Three to four interviews add enough new data to refine the tree without over-indexing on a single conversation.
do: After every fourth interview, add or regroup opportunities on the tree.
dont: Freeze the tree after the first batch of interviews while continuing to interview for months.
example: A product trio schedules a tree-refinement session every four weekly interviews.
source_quote: I recommend you revisit the opportunity space every three to four customer interviews.
check: Count interviews completed since the last opportunity-space update; pass if the count is 4 or fewer.

rule: Define evaluation goals before starting any competitive usability work.
why: Clear goals keep the evaluation tied to the design challenges and features you actually need to compare.
do: Write a one-page brief naming the design challenge, the competitor features to compare, and your own features to benchmark before collecting screenshots.
dont: Start reviewing competitor dashboards because one competitor launched a new navigation, then decide later what question the review answers.
example: A B2B SaaS team planning a billing-settings redesign first writes the challenge - reduce failed payment-method updates - then selects features to compare.
source_quote: The goals of the competitive evaluation should be clear before any work is started.
check: Does the evaluation brief name the design challenge and comparison targets before evidence collection begins?

rule: Limit a competitive evaluation to 2 to 4 competitor sites.
why: More than a few competitors makes the analysis expensive and overwhelming without adding proportionate insight.
do: Choose three direct competitors for a pricing-page review and list why each is included.
dont: List every competitor in the market and attempt a full site review of ten products.
example: A SaaS pricing-page evaluation includes three competitors: two direct and one innovative self-serve peer.
source_quote: A typical competitive evaluation focuses on 2 to 4 competitors’ sites. Any more than that can be too expensive and too overwhelming to analyze.
check: Count the competitor sites named in the evaluation plan; pass if the count is 2 to 4.

rule: Include smaller, innovative, or tangentially related competitors, not only the largest direct ones.
why: Useful insights can come from companies that solve the same user need with different practices or industry traditions.
do: Add one smaller or adjacent product that solves the same job differently to the evaluation set.
dont: Benchmark only the three largest vendors and ignore an innovative niche tool customers mention.
example: A project-management SaaS review includes a tiny vertical tool known for onboarding alongside the enterprise leaders.
source_quote: While larger competitors may seem like natural benchmarks, valuable insights can also be gleaned from examining smaller or more innovative companies.
check: Does the competitor set include at least one smaller, innovative, or tangentially related product, not only the largest direct competitors?

rule: Identify key focus areas before conducting a broad competitive review.
why: A broad review needs focused areas so the findings are analyzable and relevant to your design questions.
do: For a broad checkout review, name cart, payment, and confirmation as focus areas before writing notes.
dont: Browse five sites top to bottom and produce a long unstructured list of observations.
example: An ecommerce SaaS team scopes a broad onboarding review to activation emails, setup checklist, and first-project creation.
source_quote: In any broad evaluation, it is best if some key areas are identified to focus the review and its results.
check: Does the review plan name the key focus area or areas before site-by-site notes begin?

rule: Cap each participant at 2 or 3 competing sites in a competitive test.
why: Testing too many sites with any one participant overwhelms them and weakens the data.
do: Assign each participant tasks on two sites and reserve a third for a follow-up session if needed.
dont: Run one participant through five competitor signup flows in a single session.
example: A SaaS usability test has each participant compare its signup flow with two competitor flows, not all five.
source_quote: Each study participant typically completes a series of tasks on 2 or 3 different sites. Testing more than 3 sites with any given participant can overwhelm the study participants.
check: Review the test protocol and count sites per participant; pass if no participant is assigned more than 3.

rule: Randomize site pairing and test order across participants.
why: Alternating order and pairings prevents learnability effects from biasing the study results.
do: Build a test schedule that rotates which site is first and which sites are paired across participants.
dont: Test your product first for every participant against the same competitor.
example: In a competitive test of three billing flows, the schedule alternates the first site so no product always benefits from primacy.
source_quote: Alternate which sites are paired together and which is tested first for each user. This helps prevent learnability effects biasing your study results.
check: Inspect the test schedule and count distinct first-tested site orders; pass if more than one order is used across participants.

rule: Ask participants to compare the sites at the end of each session.
why: A final comparison helps users verbalize what was clear or confusing across the designs.
do: End the session with a side-by-side question about which site was clearer and why.
dont: Finish immediately after the last task and rely only on task-success numbers.
example: After testing two expense-reporting tools, the moderator asks each participant which was easier to submit and what caused confusion.
source_quote: ask participants at the end of the session to compare the sites they used.
check: Does the session script include a final side-by-side comparison question after task completion?

rule: Translate competitive findings into design recommendations instead of only naming a winner.
why: The main value of the evaluation is improving your own design, not producing a ranked scorecard.
do: Write findings as recommendations tied to specific design changes, with competitor evidence attached.
dont: Publish only a scorecard declaring your product the winner and stop there.
example: A dashboard evaluation reports that filters confused users on two competitors and recommends a persistent filter bar for the redesign.
source_quote: However, the main goal of a competitive evaluation is not to declare a winner. The goal is to improve your design.
check: Does the report include concrete recommendations for our product, not only rankings or scores?

rule: Size every pointer target at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
why: Small controls are hard to hit accurately for people with hand tremors, spasticity, or limited dexterity.
do: Icon buttons in a table row use a 24×24 CSS pixel hit area, filled out with padding around the glyph.
dont: A 16×16 SVG close icon with no padding, sitting flush against the next icon.
example: A SaaS data table's row actions (edit, delete) are built as 24×24 targets instead of bare 16px icons.
source_quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:
check: Measure each interactive element's width and height in CSS pixels with getBoundingClientRect; count how many fall below 24×24.

rule: Keep a 24px-diameter clearance circle around each undersized target so it never intersects a neighbor.
why: Sufficient spacing works as well as a larger target for preventing accidental activation of the adjacent control.
do: 20×20 icon buttons separated by a 4px gap so their imaginary 24px circles clear each other.
dont: 20×20 icon buttons placed edge to edge with zero gap between them.
example: A SaaS editor toolbar of 20px icon buttons uses 4px gaps so the row still passes the spacing exception.
source_quote: the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target
check: For each target under 24×24, compute the shortest gap between its bounding-box center circle (24px diameter) and any adjacent target; count any intersections.

rule: Leave links inside sentences at text size and set line-height for readability instead of padding them.
why: Text reflow moves inline links unpredictably, and padding them into blocks damages reading flow.
do: Body paragraph links stay inline within 1.5 line-height body text.
dont: Inline links padded into 24×24 blocks that break the sentence apart and shove words onto new lines.
example: A SaaS marketing page keeps terms-and-conditions links inline in body copy rather than turning them into buttons.
source_quote: The success criterion does not apply to inline targets in sentences, or where the size of the target is constrained by the line-height of non-target text
check: Are links inside paragraphs and sentences left inline with a readable line-height, without forced 24×24 padding?

rule: Do not rely on page zoom to make an undersized target count as compliant.
why: The CSS pixel size of an element does not change when the user zooms, so the target stays just as small.
do: Ship the icon button at 24×24 CSS pixels in the base layout at default zoom.
dont: Ship a 16×16 button and note in review that users can just zoom in.
example: A SaaS settings panel's toggle is 24×24 at default view, not a 16px control justified by zoom.
source_quote: The requirement is independent of the zoom factor of the page; when users zoom in, the CSS pixel size of elements does not change
check: Measure each target's CSS-pixel bounding box at default and at 200% zoom; the count of targets below 24×24 must stay the same (zero).

rule: Meet the 24×24 minimum outright rather than leaning on the spacing exception.
why: Spacing alone still leaves tiny, difficult controls, so meeting the size itself helps more people.
do: Make important controls larger still, aiming at the stricter 2.5.5 enhanced size for primary actions.
dont: A 14px icon that technically passes only because its 24px circle happens to miss its neighbors.
example: A SaaS checkout's primary pay button is comfortably larger than 24×24 while secondary link icons are merely spaced.
source_quote: As a best practice it is recommended to at least meet the minimum size requirement of the Success Criterion, regardless of spacing
check: Do important controls reach at least 24×24 on their own size, with primary actions visibly larger?

rule: Offer a way to enlarge active target areas or switch layout density.
why: Different users have different needs, from condensed layouts to large controls for low vision.
do: A comfort/compact density setting that changes row height and icon hit areas without changing the visible glyph.
dont: One fixed dense layout with 16px controls and no alternative for users who need bigger targets.
example: A SaaS dashboard ships a density toggle that expands table row heights and action hit areas for users who need it.
source_quote: It can be beneficial to provide an option to increase the active target area without increasing the visible target size
check: Is there a user-facing setting that increases target area or layout density, and does toggling it visibly change measured target sizes?

rule: Set a time appetite for an idea before discussing how to build it.
why: Naming how much time and attention an idea deserves stops the team from over-investing or drifting into endless solution debates.
do: Before wireframing, write 'Small batch: 2 weeks, 1 designer + 1 dev' and design inside that box.
dont: Open a two-hour brainstorm about notification features with no agreed time budget.
example: A SaaS team receives a 'group notifications' request and agrees it is a two-week small batch before anyone draws a UI.
source_quote: We call this the appetite. You can think of the appetite as a time budget for a standard team size.
check: Does the project brief state an explicit time appetite (e.g., 2 weeks or 6 weeks) before any solution description?

rule: Hold the deadline fixed and cut scope instead of extending time.
why: A fixed time box forces real trade-offs about what is core to the project and what is peripheral.
do: With one week left, drop the extra settings panel and spend the time fixing typos.
dont: Push the ship date out two weeks so every planned feature fits.
example: A dashboard team ships v1 without saved-view sharing to hit the six-week cycle, then adds it in a later batch.
source_quote: If the scope wasn’t variable, I’d have to include the extra section. Then there’d be no time to fix the quality issues.
check: When the deadline is at risk, does the record show a feature being cut rather than the ship date moving?

rule: Interview for the moment the need arose instead of asking what the feature should look like.
why: The triggering situation reveals the specific pain, which shrinks scope far more than a feature wish list does.
do: Ask 'What were you doing when you wanted this?' and record the concrete workflow breakdown.
dont: Ask 'What should the calendar view include?' and collect a list of desired features.
example: A customer asks for a calendar; the interview reveals she only needs to see free meeting-room slots from home.
source_quote: Instead of asking her why she wants a calendar and what it should look like, we asked her when she wanted a calendar.
check: Does the research record quote a specific triggering situation from the user rather than a feature wish list?

rule: Reject 'redesign X' and 'X 2.0' requests until they are tied to one specific problem.
why: Without a single driving problem you cannot tell where the work starts, where it ends, or what done looks like.
do: Rewrite 'rethink Files' as 'sharing multiple files takes too many steps' before scoping anything.
dont: Kick off a 'Files 2.0' project on enthusiasm and discover mid-way that 'done' is undefined.
example: A team starts 'Settings 2.0', stalls, then splits it into 'custom folder colors' and 'better previews', each with its own appetite.
source_quote: When someone proposes something like “redesign the Files section,” that’s a grab-bag, not a project.
check: Is the project framed as one named problem with a stated context, rather than a section-wide redesign or version label?

rule: Answer new ideas with a soft 'maybe some day' and keep them out of the backlog.
why: Committing too early either shuts down an idea you don't understand or promises work you may never fund.
do: Log the request in a parking-lot note with its context and no delivery promise.
dont: Add every incoming request to the sprint backlog and tell the requester it is planned.
example: A PM replies 'Interesting  -  maybe some day' to a Slack feature request and notes the customer's situation for later.
source_quote: Our default response to any idea that comes up should be: “Interesting. Maybe some day.”
check: Are unvalidated incoming requests kept out of the committed backlog and recorded without a delivery promise?

rule: Break off a meaningful part of an oversized project that fits a six-week appetite.
why: A project too big to shape in one appetite never gets defined, while a carved-out slice can be shaped and shipped.
do: Split 'full calendar' into 'see free spaces' and shape that slice within the cycle.
dont: Keep a six-month calendar redesign as one project and stall on shaping it.
example: A team carves 'see free meeting-room slots' out of a full calendar rebuild and ships it in one six-week cycle.
source_quote: If we still can’t shrink the scope, we’ll break off a meaningful part of the project that we can shape to a six-week appetite.
check: Does every shaped project fit a stated appetite, with oversized efforts split into a named, shippable slice?

topic: Critique the screenshots, not the code
rule: Review the rendered screenshots page by page, never the source code.
why: You wrote the code, so you will read your intentions into it instead of what actually shipped.
do: Open desktop-fold.jpg, then the desktop-page sheets, then mobile-fold.jpg and write findings from those images only.
dont: Open index.html and conclude the hero is fine because the markup says so.
example: Reviewing a B2B SaaS pricing page, the reviewer judges the exported PNGs of the pricing screen, not the JSX component.
source_quote: Use it on the screenshots, never on the code: you wrote the code, so you will read your intentions into it.
check: Did the reviewer write every finding from a screenshot with no reference to source files?

rule: Make the first screen say what this is, who it is for and what to do next within five seconds.
why: A title that only makes sense after scrolling is not a title, and a visitor who cannot orient leaves.
do: Hero headline names the product and audience, with a real primary button visible above the fold.
dont: A moody slogan whose meaning is only revealed by a paragraph three screens down.
example: A scheduling SaaS hero reads 'Shift scheduling for hospital teams' with a 'Start free' button in the first viewport.
source_quote: can you say what this is, who it is for and what to do next? If the title only makes sense after scrolling, it is not a title.
check: Shown only the first-screen screenshot for five seconds, can a stranger name what it is, who it is for, and the next action?

rule: Swap the logo and the headline noun; if the page still works for a competitor, the hero has no idea.
why: A page whose concept survives the name swap belongs to the category rather than to this product.
do: Keep a hero built on a specific object, motion or claim that only makes sense for this product.
dont: A generic 'Work smarter' hero that would be equally valid for six other companies.
example: A payments dashboard hero uses a live transaction-feed motif that would break if pasted onto a CRM.
source_quote: If swapping the name and the noun in the headline would produce an equally valid page, the page has no idea.
check: Swap the product name and headline noun for a competitor's and re-read the hero: if it still reads as a complete valid page, the test fails.

topic: Two or three shared left edges
rule: Align all text blocks to two or three shared left edges reused across the page.
why: Six distinct left edges mean elements were placed one at a time instead of composed.
do: Have every section of the marketing page start its text on the same two or three grid lines.
dont: Nudge each card, quote and paragraph to its own left offset.
example: On a SaaS marketing page the hero, feature rows and footer all align to a single container edge.
source_quote: Follow the left edge of every text block down the page. Count the distinct x positions. A composed page has two or three, reused on purpose.
check: Measure the left x of every text block across the desktop-page sheets; the number of distinct values must be 3 or fewer.

topic: Decisive type scale, five sizes max
rule: Make the headline jump at least three times the body size and use no more than five type sizes on the page.
why: Without a decisive jump everything reads as medium, so nothing leads the eye.
do: Use 16px body with a 56px headline, five sizes total, and cap the measure near 75 characters.
dont: Use six sizes between 14 and 30px, with the headline only one step above the body.
example: A pricing page uses one 52px section headline, 16px body and 13px labels, and nothing else.
source_quote: Is the jump from body text to headline decisive (three times or more)? Do you see more than five sizes?
check: Compare computed headline and body font sizes (ratio at least 3.0) and count distinct font sizes on the page (5 or fewer).

rule: Write one layout word per section and break any run where the same word appears twice in a row.
why: Repeated identical layouts reveal the template and make the page feel machine-assembled.
do: Alternate split, full-bleed, statement and list sections so no layout word repeats consecutively.
dont: Stack three split-image-and-text sections in the middle of the page.
example: A feature tour goes full-bleed screenshot, then two-column split, then a statement quote, never split three times.
source_quote: Write one word for each section's layout (split, list, full-bleed, grid, statement, index …). The same word twice in a row, or three times on the page, is the template showing.
check: Does the reviewer's section-by-section layout list contain no identical consecutive words and no layout word appearing three times?

rule: Remove anything that overlaps a headline, statement or button at any scroll position, and wrap rows that run off the phone screen.
why: Overlaps and sideways-scrolling rows read as broken to visitors and as cut off in screenshots.
do: Stack or wrap the mobile row so every card is fully visible inside the viewport.
dont: Leave a decorative badge across the hero headline, or a horizontally scrolling feature row cut at the phone edge.
example: The mobile testimonial carousel wraps to two rows instead of bleeding past the right edge.
source_quote: Is anything lying on top of a headline, a statement or a button at any scroll position? Does any element run off the edge of the phone screen?
check: At every scroll position and at 375px width, no element's bounding box intersects a headline or button, and no element's right edge exceeds the viewport width.

topic: Fix order: idea first, motion last
rule: Fix problems in order of idea, hierarchy, composition, typography, imagery, colour, detail, motion, and stop after three rounds.
why: Later items cannot rescue earlier ones, so polishing detail while the concept fails wastes the round.
do: Rebuild the hero concept when the cover-the-logo test fails, before touching spacing.
dont: Tweak button shadows while the page could belong to any competitor.
example: Round one of a SaaS landing critique changes the hero idea, not the card hover states.
source_quote: Fix in this order; later items cannot rescue earlier ones.
check: Does the fix list address a higher-order item (idea, hierarchy or composition) before any typography, imagery, colour or motion item?

rule: Gate decorative animations behind prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference and remove them when reduce matches.
why: Users who set reduced motion may experience distraction or motion sickness from non-essential movement.
do: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { .signup-cta { animation: vibrate .3s linear infinite both; } } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .signup-cta { animation: none; } }
dont: .signup-cta { animation: vibrate .3s linear infinite both; }
example: A SaaS signup button pulses only for users who have not opted out; reduced-motion users see a static button.
source_quote: The prefers-reduced-motion media query detects whether the user has requested the operating system to minimize the amount of animation or motion it uses.
check: In DevTools, emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and measure the CTA's computed animation-duration; it must be 0s or no animation-name.

rule: Make the base experience static and opt into motion only for no-preference users.
why: Browsers that do not understand the media query should not get animations just because they cannot match reduce.
do: button { animation: none; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { button { animation: vibrate .3s linear infinite both; } }
dont: button { animation: vibrate .3s linear infinite both; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { button { animation: none; } }
example: A dashboard's "new" badge does not animate in older browsers, but bounces for users who explicitly allow motion.
source_quote: as a good web citizen I will only play it for those users who are explicitly OK with animations, but not everyone else
check: Load the page in a browser without prefers-reduced-motion support and assert the badge has 0 computed animations.

rule: For JS-driven animations, listen for matchMedia change events and stop or restart in-flight animations.
why: CSS media queries update dynamically, but Web Animations API code must react on its own.
do: const mq = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)'); mq.addEventListener('change', () => { if (mq.matches) chartAnimation.cancel(); else chartAnimation.play(); });
dont: const chartAnimation = element.animate(keyframes, timing); // no preference listener
example: A SaaS dashboard's onboarding chart reveal stops instantly when the user flips the OS reduce-motion setting.
source_quote: for JavaScript animations I have to listen for changes myself, and then manually stop my potentially in-flight animations (or restart them if the user lets me)
check: Browser check: start the JS animation, toggle reduce, and assert element.getAnimations() has 0 running animations within 100ms.

rule: Pass the full media query string with parentheses to window.matchMedia.
why: The parentheses are required syntax, so omitting them breaks the preference check.
do: window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')
dont: window.matchMedia('prefers-reduced-motion: reduce')
example: A SaaS app's animation controller reads the motion preference correctly instead of silently failing.
source_quote: Note that the parentheses around the actual media query are obligatory
check: Static check: grep JS for matchMedia calls and confirm every prefers-reduced-motion query starts with an opening parenthesis; fail on 1 or more unparenthesized matches.

rule: Use picture source media to serve animated AVIF/WebP/GIF only under no-preference and a static image otherwise.
why: Animated media can trigger motion sickness and should respect the user's explicit reduced-motion setting.
example: A SaaS help-center hero shows an animated demo for motion-safe users and a still frame for reduced-motion users.
source_quote: If (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) evaluates to true, it's safe to display the animated version, else the static version
check: Browser check: emulate reduce and assert the hero img currentSrc ends in the static .png, not .gif/.avif.

rule: Remove or flatten parallax and scroll-linked background motion when reduced motion is requested.
why: Background elements moving at a different rate than foreground can cause vestibular symptoms.
do: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .hero-bg { transform: none; background-attachment: scroll; } }
dont: window.addEventListener('scroll', () => { heroBg.style.transform = `translateY(${scrollY * 0.5}px)`; });
example: A SaaS landing page keeps its hero background fixed for reduced-motion users instead of parallax scrolling.
source_quote: parallax scrolling animations can cause vestibular disorders because background elements move at a different rate than foreground elements
check: On a screenshot or recording with reduce enabled, does the background stay visually fixed while foreground content scrolls?

topic: Near-zero duration instead of animation none
rule: Use near-zero animation durations instead of animation:none when product logic waits on animationend.
why: Some flows depend on animation completion events, so removing the animation entirely can break them.
do: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .modal { animation-duration: 1ms !important; animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; } }
dont: .modal { animation: none !important; } /* step never advances if it waits for animationend */
example: A SaaS onboarding modal still advances to the next step when reduced motion is on.
source_quote: As some websites depend on an animation to be run in order to work correctly (maybe because a certain step depends on the firing of the animationend event)
check: Interaction test: with reduce emulated, open the modal and confirm the onboarding step advances within 1s.

rule: Choose a user journey for goals that span multiple channels or products, and a user flow for interactions inside one product.
why: The two artifacts differ in scope, so using the wrong one hides either cross-channel context or the exact steps users take.
do: Map a new-patient experience across website, phone, email, office visit, and portal as one journey.
dont: Draw a single flow chart for the entire multi-channel patient experience.
example: A SaaS team maps 'evaluate and buy' across marketing site, sales call, and trial as a journey, then maps in-app invite setup as a flow.
source_quote: User journeys are best for capturing activities dispersed over multiple channels; user flows are well-suited for interactions within one product.
check: Does the map include at least two distinct channels or products and a timeframe longer than one day?

rule: Keep user flows limited to user actions and system responses; do not add emotions, thoughts, or channel context.
why: Flows zoom in on discrete product interactions, and extra experiential detail blurs the granularity.
do: Wireflow: click 'Invite teammate' then modal appears then enter email then send invitation then confirmation toast.
dont: Flow chart node: 'User feels unsure whether inviting is safe.'
example: A signup flow in a B2B SaaS product shows only screens, clicks, and system responses.
source_quote: These maps capture key user steps and system responses; they do not contextualize the process with emotions and thoughts like a journey map does.
check: Does every node in the flow describe only a user action or a system response, with no emotion or thought annotations?

rule: Represent a user flow with a wireflow, flow chart, or task diagram rather than a narrative journey map.
why: These artifacts capture key steps and system responses at the micro level without overloading the flow with journey-style context.
do: Use a low-fidelity wireflow with screens, decision points, and system responses for password reset.
dont: Use a rich journey map with emotion curves to document password reset.
example: An onboarding flow is drawn as a wireflow from account creation to first dashboard view.
source_quote: User flows can be represented with artifacts such as low-fidelity wireflows, simple flow charts, or task diagrams.
check: Does the artifact show screens or task steps and system responses rather than a time-based journey narrative?

rule: Attach a detailed user flow to each high-level journey stage that involves a product interaction.
why: Flows act as a deep dive into specific areas of the journey, connecting macro context to micro steps.
do: For the 'access results' journey stage, link a portal-login and results-viewing flow.
dont: Leave the journey map at high-level stages with no supporting product flows.
example: A healthcare SaaS journey maps patient intake, then links a flow for portal registration.
source_quote: User flows can be thought of as a deep dive into specific areas of the high-level user journey.
check: Is each journey stage that uses the product linked to a separate detailed flow?

rule: Base journey maps on field studies or diary studies, optionally supplemented by user interviews.
why: Journeys require longer-term goals and behaviors in context, which usability tests alone rarely capture.
do: Run a two-week diary study plus interviews before drawing the customer journey.
dont: Build the customer journey only from a one-hour usability test of the checkout page.
example: A subscription SaaS team uses diary study entries to map renewal anxiety across billing emails and support calls.
source_quote: The best research methods for journey mapping are usually context methods, such as field studies and diary studies
check: List the research inputs: does at least one input come from a field study or diary study?

rule: Match the map type to the goal's time horizon: use journeys for days-to-months goals and flows for minute-to-hour tasks.
why: Journeys communicate activities over longer periods, while flows suit relatively short-term goals.
do: Use a journey for 'choose a doctor over several weeks'; use a flow for 'reset password in two minutes'.
dont: Use a user flow to represent a months-long onboarding and renewal relationship.
example: A SaaS admin's quarterly security review is a journey; adding an API key is a flow.
source_quote: User journeys are better for communicating activities over longer periods of time; user flows are better for relatively short-term goals.
check: Does the chosen artifact's time scale match the stated goal duration?

rule: Create both a journey map and supporting user flows instead of forcing one artifact to cover macro and micro views.
why: Examining journeys and flows together gives greater context and understanding of users' experiences.
do: Keep a journey map for the account lifecycle and separate flows for signup, invite, and billing.
dont: Stretch one flow diagram to cover the entire customer lifecycle across channels.
example: A SaaS company pairs a renewal journey with flows for invoice download and plan upgrade.
source_quote: Examining user journeys and user flows together provides greater context and understanding of users’ experiences.
check: Are both a high-level journey and at least one product-level flow present in the same project?

rule: Present the problem and the solution together in every pitch.
why: A solution without a stated problem gives no basis for judging fitness.
do: Open with the customer story, then show the fat-marker solution.
dont: Pitch a feature such as “add tabs to the iPad app” with no problem attached.
example: A SaaS team proposing an onboarding checklist first shows a new admin failing to invite teammates.
source_quote: It’s critical to always present both a problem and a solution together.
check: Does the pitch state a specific problem before or alongside the proposed solution?

rule: Write the problem as one specific story that shows the status quo failing.
why: A single story gives readers a baseline to test the solution’s fitness against.
do: Describe one customer, one task, and the exact point where the current product breaks down.
dont: Write “Users want better search” with no concrete situation or consequence.
example: In a project tool, a PM cannot find the one comment where a client approved the budget.
source_quote: The best problem definition consists of a single specific story that shows why the status quo doesn’t work.
check: Can a reader point to one named customer situation that explains why the current product fails?

rule: State a fixed time appetite before proposing the solution.
why: A fixed appetite prevents open-ended scope debates and forces a simpler idea.
do: Write “Appetite: two weeks” and constrain the solution to one screen.
dont: Say the team will “figure out scope as we go” with no time box.
example: A dashboard team limits a filter redesign to two weeks rather than a three-month platform rewrite.
source_quote: You can think of the appetite as another part of the problem definition.
check: Does the pitch name a specific time appetite before describing solution scope?

rule: Use labeled fat-marker sketches instead of wireframes or high-fidelity mocks.
why: Over-specified design boxes in designers and pulls the discussion into color and layout.
do: Draw the dashboard change with a thick marker and short labels.
dont: Include a pixel-perfect Figma mock of the new screen.
example: A SaaS pitch for a billing page uses a rough box sketch with three call-outs, not a polished mock.
source_quote: We need more concreteness, but we don’t want to over-specify the design with wireframes or high-fidelity mocks.
check: Does the pitch avoid wireframes and high-fidelity mocks in favor of low-detail sketches?

rule: Label fat-marker sketches cleanly with call-outs and separated colors.
why: Readers without shaping-session context need to understand the idea from the sketch alone.
do: Redraw on an iPad with one color for labels and one for the material parts.
dont: Paste an unlabeled soup of words and arrows from the whiteboard.
example: A mobile app pitch labels each new notification control with a short call-out.
source_quote: Fat marker sketches can be very effective in a pitch; you just need to take more care to label them cleanly.
check: Are sketch elements labeled with call-outs that explain their role?

rule: Call out each known rabbit hole and the specific decision that avoids it.
why: Spelling out a non-central risk patches it before it derails the project.
do: Write “URLs won't live on custom domains for v1” as a short note.
dont: Leave domain handling ambiguous for the build team to discover later.
example: A form-builder pitch states that custom domains are excluded from v1.
source_quote: This is the kind of thing that’s not central to the concept, but spelling it out patches a potential rabbit hole.
check: Does the pitch name each known risk and the decision that resolves it?

rule: List explicit no-gos for functionality and use cases excluded from the concept.
why: Visible exclusions keep the solution inside the appetite and make the problem tractable.
do: Write “No WYSIWYG editing; users can only set a logo and header text.”
dont: Leave WYSIWYG editing implied and let scope expand later.
example: A payment-form pitch excludes inline rich-text editing for the first release.
source_quote: if there’s anything we’re not doing in this concept, it’s good to mention it here.
check: Does the pitch include a no-gos section listing excluded functionality?

rule: Post the complete pitch for asynchronous reading before any live bet discussion.
why: Stakeholders can read on their own time and the betting table stays short and productive.
do: Post all five ingredients in a searchable pitch category before the meeting.
dont: Open a decision meeting with an unprepared verbal pitch.
example: A product team posts a Shape Up pitch in Basecamp and collects comments before the betting table.
source_quote: the first step for presenting a pitch is posting the write-up with all the ingredients above somewhere that stakeholders can read it on their own time.
check: Was the full pitch posted where stakeholders could read it before the decision meeting?

rule: Start with a problem you personally have, not with an idea you try to think up.
why: Ideas invented for their own sake often solve problems no one actually has.
do: List three annoyances from your own workflow before brainstorming any product concept.
dont: Brainstorm 'a social network for pet owners' without checking if anyone urgently needs it.
example: A SaaS tool for freelance designers: start from your own pain of chasing invoices, not from 'Uber for X'.
source_quote: The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas. It's to look for problems, preferably problems you have yourself.
check: Does the project brief name a specific problem the founder personally experiences, rather than a generic market opportunity?

rule: Validate that a small group urgently needs the product, not that many people are mildly interested.
why: Good startup ideas are narrow and deep; broad, shallow interest yields zero users.
do: Ask five target users: 'Would you use a crappy v1 today?' and require at least three yeses.
dont: Accept 'Yeah, maybe I could see using that' as validation.
example: A dashboard for indie coffee shops: find 10 owners who say they'd pay today, not 100 who say it's interesting.
source_quote: When you have an idea for a startup, ask yourself: who wants this right now?
check: Can the team name at least five specific users who urgently need the product today, not just say the market is large?

rule: Design the first version for a narrow beachhead that has a clear path to a larger market.
why: A well-shaped demand is necessary but not sufficient; great ideas start small but can expand.
do: For a college-focused app, ensure the same design can extend to all colleges without a rewrite.
dont: Build something that can only ever appeal to one tiny, non-adjacent group.
example: A task manager for wedding planners, designed so it can later serve all event planners.
source_quote: Facebook was a good idea because it started with a small market there was a fast path out of.
check: Does the design brief describe a credible next segment beyond the initial beachhead and show how the same product architecture serves it?

rule: Look for messy, tedious, or unsexy problems that others avoid.
why: The schlep and unsexy filters keep most people away, leaving valuable problems unaddressed.
do: List three tedious workflows in your industry (e.g., payment reconciliation) and design for them.
dont: Skip a painful payment integration because it feels like a schlep.
example: A SaaS for freelancers: tackle invoicing and tax paperwork instead of a shiny social feed.
source_quote: The schlep filter is so dangerous that I wrote a separate essay about the condition it induces, which I called schlep blindness.
check: Does the problem list include at least one tedious, unsexy task that competitors avoid?

topic: Notice gaps by questioning the status quo
rule: Pay attention to things that annoy you and ask why they work that way.
why: Annoyances often signal a missing product that will seem obvious in retrospect.
do: Keep a running list of 'this is stupid' moments in your daily workflow.
dont: Accept the current way of doing things without asking if it could be software-generated.
example: You hate manually copying data between tools; that's a potential integration product.
source_quote: Pay particular attention to things that chafe you.
check: Does the discovery log contain at least three specific 'this annoys me' observations tied to the product idea?

rule: Build things that seem cool or toy-like, and don't force them to be startups immediately.
why: Toys often have everything an idea needs except perceived importance, and they can grow into big companies.
do: Prototype a fun tool for yourself with no business model, then see if others love it.
dont: Discard an idea because it seems inconsequential or like a hobby project.
example: A simple internal tool for your team that later becomes a SaaS product.
source_quote: Just as trying to think up startup ideas tends to produce bad ones, working on things that could be dismissed as "toys" often produces good ones.
check: Is there at least one prototype or project in the portfolio that was built for intrinsic interest rather than a business case?

rule: Interview users about what's missing and what they wish they could do.
why: Direct conversations reveal unmet needs you might not notice alone.
do: Ask five users: 'What's tedious or annoying in your work?' and record exact phrases.
dont: Assume you know the user's pain without talking to them.
example: For a project management tool, ask freelancers what they hate about tracking time.
source_quote: Try talking to everyone you can about the gaps they find in the world. What's missing?
check: Does the research plan include at least five open-ended interviews about missing capabilities, not just feature requests?

rule: Don't discard an idea just because competitors exist; instead, articulate what they're overlooking.
why: Worrying you're late is a sign of a good idea, and a crowded market signals demand.
do: Write a one-sentence thesis about what incumbents miss, then design around it.
dont: Abandon a good problem because a quick web search finds someone else working on it.
example: A CRM for solo lawyers: competitors exist, but none handle court-date reminders well.
source_quote: Worrying that you're late is one of the signs of a good idea.
check: Does the competitive analysis include a specific, non-generic thesis about what existing solutions overlook?

rule: Set each early user up in person during the first session instead of sending them a link to try later.
why: Agreeing to try is the moment of highest intent, and a link lets that intent decay into nothing.
do: The founder joins a screen share, creates the account, imports the data, and leaves the user with a working project before hanging up.
dont: A signup modal that says 'Thanks! We'll email you an invite link within 24 hours.'
example: A two-person analytics SaaS onboards its first 20 beta accounts by having the founder paste the tracking snippet live on the customer's own site.
source_quote: When anyone agreed to try Stripe they'd say "Right then, give me your laptop" and set them up on the spot.
check: Does at least one onboarding path end with the user holding a working, populated account inside the same session, with a named human responsible?

rule: Track weekly growth rate as the primary progress number, not cumulative signups.
why: Small absolute numbers hide the compounding that decides whether the product ever gets big.
do: A dashboard tile reading 'weekly active growth: 11% (110 vs 100 last week)' next to the raw count.
dont: A proud '10,000 signups all time' counter that hides the fact the last four weeks added 30 users.
example: A seed-stage invoicing tool sets a 10%-per-week target for accounts that send at least one invoice.
source_quote: If you have 100 users, you need to get 10 more next week to grow 10% a week.
check: Compute week-over-week growth of activated accounts for the last 4 weeks; each week's figure must be displayed and the median must be at or above 10%.

rule: Give each of the first users one personal, human gesture the product could never automate.
why: Attention is the one advantage a small team has over large incumbents, and it is what early users remember.
do: A hand-written note or a personal video for each of the first 50 signups, sent within 24 hours.
dont: An auto-generated 'Welcome aboard!' email illustrated with a smiling stock photo.
example: A tiny scheduling SaaS where the founder records a 40-second Loom naming the customer's team and showing how their account was set up.
source_quote: Wufoo sent each new user a hand-written thank you note. Your first users should feel that signing up with you was one of the best choices they ever made.
check: Is there at least one touch in the user's first week that is clearly authored by a specific human and could not be sent at 100,000 users?

rule: Ship the core loop as soon as it delivers one unit of real value, then watch what users do with it.
why: Perfectionism is often an excuse for procrastination, and the first model of users is always inaccurate.
do: Release a single flow that takes a real input and produces the real output, even if settings and billing are stubs.
dont: Holding the whole release for six weeks to finish the settings page and brand polish.
example: A CSV-cleanup tool launches with one upload-fix-download screen and no accounts at all.
source_quote: it usually works best to get something in front of users as soon as it has a quantum of utility, and then see what they do with it.
check: Measure steps from landing to first real output; the core path must complete in 3 steps or fewer with zero 'coming soon' or disabled states.

rule: Pick the narrowest subset of users who will feel the product is really for them, and build for that group first.
why: A contained fire gets hot, so a critical mass of the right users signs up and treats the product as their natural home.
do: Headline and copy that name one segment, e.g. 'invoicing for freelance illustrators in the EU'.
dont: 'The all-in-one platform for every team' with five audience tabs above the fold.
example: A note-taking app launches only for one university's design school, with that school's course lists baked in.
source_quote: It's always worth asking if there's a subset of the market in which you can get a critical mass of users quickly.
check: Does every page speak to one named audience, with no sentence that would read identically to a different segment?

rule: Do by hand what you plan to automate later, and keep the manual step invisible to the user.
why: Manual work launches you faster and gives you muscle memory of exactly what to automate.
do: A request triggers a founder-run script plus a personal reply, while the UI simply shows the finished state.
dont: Blocking launch until the self-serve admin panel and automated provisioning are fully built.
example: A B2B SaaS shows an 'instant approval' screen while the founder activates each new merchant account by hand behind it.
source_quote: When you only have a small number of users, you can sometimes get away with doing by hand things that you plan to automate later.
check: Is every manual step hidden behind the same UI state a user would see if it were automated, and logged in enough detail to script it later?

rule: Plan the launch as a way to get a small core of users, not as a broadcast event.
why: Months later your results depend on how happy those first users were, not on how many people heard the announcement.
do: One channel, one date, and a list of 30 people the founder personally invites and follows up with.
dont: Coordinating embargoes across eight publications on an 'optimal' Tuesday.
example: A developer tool ships quietly with a single Hacker News post and a founder-written email to 25 former colleagues.
source_quote: All you need from a launch is some initial core of users.
check: Does the launch plan name a single channel plus a manual follow-up list, with no dependency on press coverage for success?

rule: Write each product idea as a pair: what you build plus the unscalable thing you will do to get it started.
why: If the second half is empty there is no way to find users, and the idea is probably bad for that founder.
do: One-pager line: 'Build: X. Unscalable start: founder visits 20 agencies and sets the tool up for them.'
dont: 'Build: X. Growth: viral loops, SEO, and a big partnership.'
example: A B2B tool's concept doc names 'founder does the data migration for the first 10 customers' as its second half.
source_quote: Instead we should try thinking of them as pairs of what you're going to build, plus the unscalable thing(s) you're going to do initially to get the company going.
check: Does the concept doc name one specific unscalable action, with a named owner and a first-week date attached to it?

rule: Keep recognizable clickability signifiers such as underlined links and shaped buttons even in flat layouts.
why: Flat surfaces strip away cues and leave users guessing what is interactive.
do: Style inline links blue and underlined, and give primary actions a filled button shape.
dont: Render navigation and actions as plain black text with no underline, shape, or hover state.
example: A SaaS marketing site restyles its top nav as plain text; visitors cannot tell the links apart from headings.
source_quote: One of the biggest usability issues introduced by flat design is the lack of signifiers on clickable elements.
check: Can a reviewer identify every clickable element from a static screenshot without hovering?

rule: Use subtle shadows, highlights, and layering to restore hierarchy and interactivity in mostly flat interfaces.
why: A little depth preserves simplicity while making controls and layers legible.
do: Add a soft shadow to the floating add button and slight elevation to cards.
dont: Flatten every card, button, and panel to the same white surface with zero elevation.
example: A dashboard uses flat white cards on a light gray background but adds a 1px border and faint shadow so panels are distinguishable.
source_quote: This design style is mostly flat, but it makes use of subtle shadows, highlights, and layers to create some depth in the UI.
check: Does the screenshot show at least one subtle elevation cue that distinguishes an interactive or layered element?

rule: Apply 3D effects only when they communicate interaction or hierarchy, never as pure decoration.
why: Aesthetic-only shadows add noise and do not help users understand the interface.
do: Use an inset shadow on a search field to show it accepts input.
dont: Use long-shadow icons whose depth conveys no state or affordance.
example: A settings page decorates icons with long shadows while the actual Save button remains flat and easy to miss.
source_quote: Long shadows are one example of flat 2.0 gone wrong  -  the 3D effects are purely aesthetic and don’t add any meaningful information for users.
check: Can a reviewer name the interaction or hierarchy meaning conveyed by each shadow or depth effect?

rule: Make buttons look raised and input fields look sunken so users can tell pressable controls from fillable ones.
why: Users infer pressability from raised shapes and fillability from hollow shapes.
do: Give the primary button a filled raised surface and the search box an inset border or shadow.
dont: Style the Save button and the search field as identical flat rectangles.
example: In a SaaS settings form, the Save button and search input look the same, so users try to type into the button.
source_quote: Elements that appear sunken or hollow look like they could be filled. This technique is often used as a signifier for input fields, like search tools.
check: From a screenshot, are buttons and input fields visually distinguishable as pressable versus fillable?

rule: Validate clickability with real users instead of trusting your own familiarity with the interface.
why: Designers know what each element does, but users do not share that context.
do: Run a first-click test on the main task and measure correct first-click rate.
dont: Ship a fully flat redesign because it looks modern and assume users will figure it out.
example: A team launches an icon-only nav after internal review; analytics show users repeatedly opening the wrong section.
source_quote: Don’t forget that  -  unless you’re designing only for other designers  -  you are not the user.
check: Run a 5-user first-click test on the primary task; record the percentage of correct first clicks.

rule: Combine at least two independent clickability cues on each interactive element.
why: Users rely on a mix of convention, resemblance, and context to decide what is clickable.
do: Use a colored, filled button with an action label plus a visible hover state.
dont: Rely on a single brand-color change as the only signal that text is a link.
example: A pricing table uses colored plan buttons but also adds borders, action labels, and underlines on secondary links.
source_quote: Traditional, externally consistent signifiers (such as the blue, underlined text or raised buttons)
check: Does each interactive element carry at least two independent cues such as shape, color, underline, or action label?

rule: Set a fixed six-week cycle and follow every cycle with a two-week cool-down.
why: Six weeks is long enough to finish something meaningful but short enough to see the end from the beginning, and cool-down gives the team breathing room between bets.
do: Calendar a six-week build cycle, then two weeks of unscheduled cool-down for bug fixes and exploration.
dont: Run back-to-back two-week sprints with sprint-planning meetings every other Monday.
example: A B2B SaaS team plans a new reporting module; it blocks six weeks for the build and two weeks after for cleanup before the next bet.
source_quote: Therefore, after each six-week cycle, we schedule two weeks for cool-down.
check: Does the calendar show a fixed six-week cycle followed by a two-week cool-down with no scheduled project work?

rule: Bet only one cycle ahead from a short list of shaped pitches, keeping the slate clean.
why: A clean slate preserves future options and avoids committing to old work that has not been freshly shaped and considered as a new bet.
do: Bring three freshly shaped pitches to the betting table and choose one; start the cycle with only that.
dont: Maintain a 60-item groomed backlog and pull the top ticket every sprint.
example: A SaaS product team replaces its backlog with three pitches for the next cycle and chooses one at the betting table.
source_quote: The key to managing capacity is giving ourselves a clean slate with every cycle.
check: Is the next cycle chosen from a few shaped pitches rather than a groomed backlog or carried-over work?

rule: Protect the committed team from every interruption for the full cycle.
why: Momentum is a second-order effect, so pulling someone away for a day costs more than a day and breaks the bet.
do: Send a request for a small fix to the next betting table instead of tapping the committed engineer.
dont: Borrow the only back-end programmer for a day to help another team.
example: A sales team asks for a one-day data-export tweak; the PM queues it for the next cycle instead of interrupting the billing project.
source_quote: We do not allow the team to be interrupted or pulled away to do other things.
check: Count mid-cycle pull-aways per committed team from calendar or ticket history; target 0.

rule: Apply a circuit breaker: grant no extensions and re-shape any project that misses its cycle.
why: The circuit breaker caps downside risk, prevents runaway projects, and forces the team to reframe the problem instead of funding a bad approach.
do: At the end of week six, ship the working slice or stop the project and write a new pitch.
dont: Grant a two-week extension to finish the original scope.
example: A billing redesign misses its six-week deadline; the team stops and re-shapes rather than extending the original bet.
source_quote: If they don’t finish, by default the project doesn’t get an extension.
check: Compare each project's planned cycle end date with its actual ship date and count extensions granted; target 0.

rule: Staff each bet with one designer plus one or two programmers, adding QA for integration testing.
why: Standard team shapes make capacity predictable and keep the bet small enough to finish inside one cycle.
do: Staff the next bet with one designer and two programmers; add a QA engineer for integration testing later in the cycle.
dont: Assign five engineers and no designer to the project.
example: A SaaS company limits its new onboarding project to one designer, two engineers, and later QA.
source_quote: Our project teams consist of either one designer and two programmers or one designer and one programmer.
check: At kickoff, does each project have one designer and no more than two programmers assigned?

rule: Treat bugs as normal work rather than automatic interrupts; route them to cool-down, the betting table, or a bug smash.
why: Bugs are not automatically more important than everything else, and most can wait six weeks without stopping committed work.
do: Add a non-crisis bug to the cool-down list or shape it as a pitch for the betting table.
dont: Pause the six-week cycle whenever a customer reports a UI bug.
example: A dashboard team collects minor bugs during the cycle and fixes them in the two-week cool-down.
source_quote: There is nothing special about bugs that makes them automatically more important than everything else.
check: Were non-crisis bugs kept out of the active cycle and handled in cool-down, at the betting table, or in a bug smash?

rule: Define a concrete payout for each bet and cap the downside at one cycle.
why: A bet should finish something meaningful, and the most the company should lose on it is the single cycle committed.
do: Write a pitch that names the shippable outcome and states the six-week cap.
dont: Approve repeated two-week extensions on a project that blew its appetite.
example: An analytics feature pitch promises a working export by week six and caps spend at one cycle.
source_quote: If we bet six weeks on something, the most we can lose is six weeks.
check: Does the pitch state a specific shippable outcome and a hard cost cap of one cycle?

rule: Do not use AI to generate user data, research findings, or personas.
why: Generating synthetic user data is unethical and can mislead the product team.
do: Write personas from five real interview transcripts and quote participants.
dont: Ask ChatGPT to invent three SaaS buyer personas with pain points.
example: A SaaS team needs personas for a new dashboard; they synthesize real interviews instead of prompting an LLM.
source_quote: Do not use AI to generate user data, user-research findings, or user personas.
check: Are all personas and research findings traceable to real participant data rather than AI-generated content?

rule: Lean on existing design methods for wireframes and visual workflows instead of AI generators.
why: AI wireframing tools produced generic, templated layouts even with detailed prompts.
do: Sketch dashboard wireframes in Figma using your own layout patterns and content hierarchy.
dont: Generate a Figma wireframe from a prompt and ship the templated result.
example: A B2B SaaS team designs a settings page by hand instead of using an AI wireframe plugin.
source_quote: Lean on existing methods for design tasks. Current AI offerings cannot meaningfully enhance those visual and design-heavy workflows.
check: Were the wireframes and visual screens produced with established design methods rather than an AI design generator?

rule: Use AI as a brainstorming partner only for low-precision text tasks like naming and approaches.
why: AI is most reliable for low-precision text tasks where a human can judge suggestions.
do: Prompt ChatGPT for ten feature-name options, then shortlist three with the team.
dont: Use an AI answer as the final research approach without review.
example: A product team brainstorms onboarding email subject lines with AI and edits the best ones.
source_quote: AI tools are also helpful as a brainstorming partner, providing suggestions for feature names, research approaches, or anything else that doesn’t require absolute precision or trust.
check: Is AI used only for low-stakes ideation or drafting that a human reviews before it enters the design?

rule: Test AI design tools with repeated prompts before trusting them for replicable design work.
why: Probabilistic LLM output means the same prompt can produce wildly different designs, breaking reproducibility.
do: Run the same prompt three times and compare the resulting layouts before trusting the tool.
dont: Promise stakeholders identical brand-compliant screens from one AI prompt.
example: A SaaS team evaluating an AI UI generator sees three different dashboard layouts from one prompt.
source_quote: a single ChatGPT 4 prompt for an example of front-end design featuring Google’s Material Design components resulted in three drastically different designs.
check: Run the same prompt three times and count distinct layout structures; more than one distinct structure means the tool is not deterministic.

rule: Assess copyright and ethical risk before using AI-generated content in shipped designs.
why: AI-generated content can carry copyright and legal exposure for the organization.
do: Log the source and license for each AI-generated image before using it on a landing page.
dont: Paste Midjourney images into a shipped landing page without a rights review.
example: A marketing team checks provenance before using AI hero art on a SaaS pricing page.
source_quote: He also worried about ethical and legal risk if his team used AI-generated content in designs, due to potential copyright issues.
check: Does the asset log show licensing or provenance for every AI-generated visual shipped in the design?

rule: Evaluate design-specific AI tools on real tasks before adopting them into the workflow.
why: NN/g found no design-specific AI tool in serious use or worth recommending.
do: Pilot one AI design plugin on a low-risk page and measure time saved.
dont: Roll out an AI design tool across the design org based on vendor hype.
example: An agency tests a Figma AI plugin on one client mockup before buying seats.
source_quote: existing AI tools that are advertised for design are lacking, and the vast majority are not ready to be used in design workflows.
check: Pilot the tool on one real task and record net minutes saved versus the existing method; keep it only if the net is positive.

rule: Draft UX copy with AI only when a human edits it for voice and accuracy.
why: AI can fill copy gaps quickly, but the output still needs human editing for product voice.
do: Draft form microcopy with ChatGPT, then rewrite it to match the product's voice.
dont: Paste AI-generated error messages into the production form unchanged.
example: A SaaS team drafts onboarding tooltips with AI and edits them before the prototype test.
source_quote: a UX designer may turn to a text-based AI tool to generate UX copy for a prototype instead of reaching out to a copywriter and waiting for a response.
check: Has every AI-drafted UX string been edited by a human for voice and accuracy before it appears in the prototype?

rule: Show primary navigation on large screens instead of hiding it behind a hamburger menu.
why: Visible menus help users find content and understand the product’s scope without opening an extra control.
do: Put Dashboard, Reports, and Settings links directly in a desktop SaaS header.
dont: Hide all top-level app sections behind a desktop hamburger icon in the corner.
example: A B2B analytics product shows its top navigation links across the desktop header at 1440px.
source_quote: This means that the hamburger menu (or any form of hiding the navigation categories under a single menu) is not appropriate for desktop websites and apps.
check: On a desktop screenshot, is primary navigation visible without opening a hamburger menu?

rule: Place primary navigation in the header for websites and on the left side for applications.
why: Users look for menus in predictable screen locations, so matching those expectations makes navigation faster.
do: Use a top header nav on a marketing website and a left sidebar nav in the logged-in app.
dont: Put primary navigation in a floating bottom-right widget on desktop.
example: A SaaS marketing site has header links, while its app dashboard uses left-side sections.
source_quote: Users expect to find specific menus in specific areas of the screen. Make these expectations work in your favor.
check: Are primary menus located in the header for web pages and on the left for application screens?

rule: Show the user’s current page or section with a distinct active state in the menu.
why: Users need menu cues to answer “Where am I?” and orient themselves after landing on an internal page.
do: Highlight “Reports” in the left sidebar and show a breadcrumb from Home > Reports.
dont: Render all navigation links identically so the current section is indistinguishable.
example: A SaaS reporting page highlights Reports in the sidebar and shows Home > Reports above the title.
source_quote: One of the top jobs that navigation menus have is to orient users, since visitors often don’t enter from the homepage.
check: In a screenshot, is the active menu item visibly different from inactive menu items?

rule: Use familiar, descriptive link labels instead of internal jargon or clever category names.
why: Menus work best when labels clearly describe the content or features users will find.
do: Label a billing page “Billing” and a usage page “Usage.”
dont: Label a billing page “Revenue Ops Hub” or “Moneyverse.”
example: A SaaS admin sidebar uses “Billing,” “Usage,” and “Team” instead of invented internal terms.
source_quote: Stick to terminology that clearly describes your content, features, or resources.
check: Would a new user understand each top-level menu label without internal company context?

rule: Open submenus on click or tap rather than relying on hover only.
why: Touchscreen and keyboard users cannot access content hidden only under hover.
do: Make “Products” a button that expands a submenu when clicked and supports keyboard focus.
dont: Show the “Products” submenu only when a mouse hovers over it.
example: In a SaaS header, a keyboard user tabs to Products and presses Enter to open its menu.
source_quote: Hover is not universally available: users on touchscreens or those who interact primarily through a keyboard do not have access to content hidden under hover.
check: Trigger every submenu by keyboard focus and click; count submenus that fail to open (target: 0).

rule: Replace deep cascading dropdown submenus with a mega menu or an intermediate landing page.
why: Multilevel cascading menus cause accidental selections and make users fall out of the menu.
do: Use a two-tier mega menu with grouped links for a large product catalog.
dont: Nest Reports > Revenue > Forecast > Q3 in a hover dropdown that closes when the pointer slips.
example: A SaaS reporting menu groups report categories in one mega menu instead of three hover levels.
source_quote: A simple dropdown menu works well for one-tier navigation but becomes frustrating with two tiers.
check: Does any open submenu require a third level of cascading dropdown to reach a destination?

rule: Make menu links large enough and spaced enough to be easily tapped or clicked.
why: Links that are too small or too close together frustrate mobile users and complicate large-screen use.
do: Give each mobile menu row at least 44px height with clear gaps between links.
dont: Stack 12px navigation links tightly in a footer-like list on mobile.
example: A mobile app settings menu uses full-width rows with 44px tap targets.
source_quote: Links that are too small or too close together are a huge source of frustration for mobile users
check: Measure each menu link’s clickable box and spacing; count links below 44×44 CSS px or overlapping a neighbor’s hit area (target: 0).

rule: Keep navigation visible with a sticky or partially sticky header on long pages.
why: Users at the bottom of a long page otherwise face tedious scrolling to reach menus at the top.
do: Pin the primary header to the top while users scroll a long pricing or docs page.
dont: Require users at the bottom of a long page to scroll all the way back up to reach navigation.
example: A long documentation page keeps a slim sticky header with Docs, API, and Support links.
source_quote: Menus that remain visible at the top of the viewport even after scrolling can solve that problem and are especially welcome on smaller screens.
check: Scroll three viewport heights down; count visible primary navigation links in the viewport (target: at least one).

rule: Honor prefers-reduced-motion by default and make programmatic scrolls jump instantly when reduce is set.
why: Users with vestibular sensitivity can get motion sickness from smooth scrolling, and Lenis already exposes the preference live.
do: new Lenis({ respectReducedMotion: true }) and read lenis.prefersReducedMotion before animating parallax.
dont: new Lenis({ respectReducedMotion: false }) or forcing duration/easing on reduced-motion users.
example: A SaaS marketing site's pricing anchor still scrolls smoothly for a visitor who set Reduce Motion on macOS.
source_quote: By default, Lenis honors the user's prefers-reduced-motion setting: when it is set to reduce, smoothing is disabled
check: With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce emulated, does a scrollTo or anchor-link click land instantly with no eased animation?

rule: Drive Lenis from one requestAnimationFrame loop and add lenis.raf to GSAP's ticker instead of starting a second loop.
why: Two rAF loops fight each other and cause jitter, doubled speed, and inconsistent scroll-driven animations.
do: const lenis = new Lenis(); gsap.ticker.add((time) => lenis.raf(time * 1000)); gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0);
dont: Calling new Lenis({ autoRaf: true }) while also calling requestAnimationFrame(raf) with lenis.raf.
example: A dashboard's scroll-linked chart stutters because the app starts its own rAF loop and GSAP also ticks Lenis.
source_quote: Add Lenis's requestAnimationFrame (raf) method to GSAP's ticker
check: Does the codebase contain exactly one rAF/ticker loop that calls lenis.raf, rather than autoRaf plus a manual loop?

rule: Mark modals and nested scrollable panels with data-lenis-prevent instead of enabling allowNestedScroll globally.
why: allowNestedScroll checks the DOM tree on every scroll event, which can create performance problems.
do: ...
dont: new Lenis({ allowNestedScroll: true }) on a page with a long list of nested scroll areas.
example: A SaaS app's settings drawer scrolls natively while the page behind it stays put, with no dropped frames.
source_quote: However, this can create performance issues since Lenis needs to check the DOM tree on every scroll event.
check: Count nested scrollable containers/modals without data-lenis-prevent or a prevent callback; target is 0.

rule: Import lenis/dist/lenis.css whenever you use autoToggle or the one-line no-code setup.
why: autoToggle reads the wrapper's overflow, and the recommended CSS is what makes that state reliable across browsers.
do: import 'lenis/dist/lenis.css' in the app entry, then new Lenis({ autoToggle: true }).
dont: new Lenis({ autoToggle: true }) with no Lenis stylesheet linked, so modals don't stop the page scroll.
example: Opening a pricing modal in a Vue SaaS app stops background scroll because the Lenis CSS toggles overflow correctly.
source_quote: Automatically start or stop the lenis instance based on the wrapper's overflow property, ⚠️ this requires Lenis recommended CSS.
check: Count Lenis CSS references (import or <link>) in the built page; target is at least 1 when autoToggle is enabled.

rule: Set anchors: true (or pass ScrollToOptions) so in-page anchor links scroll under Lenis instead of being blocked.
why: Lenis prevents anchor links from working while scrolling unless you explicitly enable them.
do: new Lenis({ anchors: { offset: 80, onComplete: () => track('anchor') } })
dont: Shipping Lenis with default options and leaving nav links dead on the pricing page.
example: A documentation site's table of contents jumps to the right heading with a sticky-header offset.
source_quote: By default, Lenis will prevent anchor links from working while scrolling. To enable them, you must set anchors: true.
check: Clicking an in-page anchor scrolls to the target with offset and does not leave the URL hash stuck without movement; yes/no.

rule: Choose either lerp or duration/easing for a Lenis instance, never both.
why: The duration and easing options are ignored once lerp is defined, so a config with both hides which feel actually ships.
do: new Lenis({ lerp: 0.1 }) for a responsive feel, or new Lenis({ duration: 1.2, easing: easeOutExpo }) when you need exact timing.
dont: new Lenis({ lerp: 0.1, duration: 1.2, easing: easeOutExpo }) and assuming the duration applies.
example: A design-system team's scroll config is reviewed and the unused duration value is removed so tuning is predictable.
source_quote: The duration of scroll animation (in seconds). Useless if lerp defined.
check: Count Lenis configs that define both lerp and duration/easing; target is 0.

rule: Use the lenis/snap plugin for section snapping instead of CSS scroll-snap.
why: Lenis has no support for CSS scroll-snap, so the browser and the smooth scroll will fight.
do: Install lenis/snap and configure snap points for full-screen sections.
dont: Putting scroll-snap-type: y mandatory on the scroll container that Lenis is smoothing.
example: A product launch page snaps between three feature panels without the scroll stuttering.
source_quote: no support for CSS scroll-snap, you must use (lenis/snap)
check: Count CSS scroll-snap declarations on the Lenis wrapper/content; target is 0 when snapping is needed, and lenis/snap is present.

rule: Cap each usability test round at five participants and run multiple small rounds instead of one large study.
why: After the fifth user you mostly see repeated findings, so extra participants yield diminishing new insight.
do: Run three rounds of five users each across redesigns of the onboarding flow.
dont: Recruit fifteen users for a single marathon study before making any design changes.
example: A SaaS team testing a new signup form schedules five sessions, fixes the top issues, then tests again with five new users.
source_quote: The best results come from testing no more than 5 users and running as many small tests as you can afford.
check: Count participants per test round in the research plan; each round must be at most 5 and there must be at least 2 rounds.

rule: Re-test the redesigned interface with a fresh set of five users before shipping.
why: Fixes are assumptions, and a second study verifies they worked and surfaces the remaining problems.
do: Schedule a second five-user round after the redesign to confirm the top issues are resolved.
dont: Ship the redesign on the assumption that the first round's fixes worked.
example: After fixing navigation labels, the team runs another five-user test and finds two new issues introduced by the change.
