source_quote: A second test will discover whether the fixes worked or whether they didn't.
check: Does the research plan include a follow-up test round after the redesign?

rule: Never run a usability test with a single user; use at least three to see behavioral diversity.
why: One person's accidental or unrepresentative behavior can mislead the team.
do: Recruit three to five participants so you can distinguish unique behavior from generalizable patterns.
dont: Base design decisions on a single test participant's session.
example: A PM wants to test with just one colleague; instead the team recruits three users for the round.
source_quote: There is always a risk of being misled by the spurious behavior of a single person who may perform certain actions by accident
check: Count participants per study; any round with fewer than 3 participants fails.

rule: Run separate test rounds for each highly distinct user group, using three to four users per group.
why: The five-user curve holds only for comparable users, since distinct groups behave differently.
do: Test three parents and three children separately for a family account feature.
dont: Average findings from children and parents into one mixed five-user test.
example: A B2B marketplace tests three purchasing agents and three sales reps separately rather than one mixed group of five.
source_quote: You need to test additional users when a website has several highly distinct groups of users.
check: Does the test plan list distinct user segments with at least 3 participants per segment?

rule: Split the research budget across multiple small studies instead of one elaborate study.
why: Fixed study overheads depreciate across users, and iterative rounds improve the design more than one big study.
do: With budget for fifteen users, run three studies of five rather than one fifteen-user study.
dont: Blow the entire research budget on a single elaborate fifteen-user study.
example: A startup allots its research budget to three five-user rounds over three sprints.
source_quote: it is better to distribute your budget for user testing across many small tests instead of blowing everything on a single, elaborate study
check: Does the research plan show at least 2 small test rounds rather than one large study?

rule: Plan usability tests to improve the design, not merely document its weaknesses.
why: The real goal of usability engineering is improvement, which requires acting on findings and re-testing.
do: End each test round with a prioritized fix list and a scheduled redesign.
dont: Deliver a forty-page findings report with no design changes planned.
example: After round one, the team fixes the three worst issues in the checkout flow before the next round.
source_quote: the real goal of usability engineering is to improve the design and not just to document its weaknesses
check: Does each test round have a documented fix list and a redesign step before the next round?

rule: Design monitoring dashboards to prominently display the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
why: These four signals provide comprehensive coverage of user-facing system health.
do: A dashboard showing latency percentiles, request rate, error rate, and resource saturation for each service.
dont: A dashboard that only shows CPU usage and memory without latency or error rates.
example: A SaaS analytics platform's status page displays real-time latency, request volume, error counts, and database load.
source_quote: The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
check: Does the dashboard include all four golden signals?

rule: Only page a human for urgent, actionable, and user-visible problems, ensuring high signal and low noise.
why: Frequent or non-actionable pages cause alert fatigue and can lead to missed critical issues.
do: An alert that fires when the checkout page error rate exceeds 5% for 5 minutes, with a runbook link.
dont: An alert that fires for a single failed login attempt or for a non-critical disk usage warning.
example: A SaaS project management tool pages on-call only when the API returns 500 errors for >1% of requests, not for slow background jobs.
source_quote: Effective alerting systems have good signal and very low noise.
check: Are alerts configured to be actionable and urgent, avoiding noise?

rule: Keep monitoring and alerting rules simple, predictable, and reliable.
why: Complex rules are fragile and harder to maintain, leading to false positives or missed incidents.
do: A rule that alerts when HTTP 5xx rate > 1% for 5 minutes.
dont: A rule that uses machine learning to detect anomalies with multiple nested conditions.
example: A SaaS CRM sets an alert for when average response time exceeds 2 seconds over a 10-minute window.
source_quote: The rules that catch real incidents most often should be as simple, predictable, and reliable as possible.
check: Are monitoring rules simple and easy to understand?

rule: Design monitoring to clearly distinguish between symptoms (what's broken) and causes (why).
why: Focusing on symptoms for paging reduces noise and ensures user-impacting issues are addressed first.
do: A dashboard section for 'User-facing symptoms' (e.g., error rate, latency) and a separate 'Diagnostics' section (e.g., CPU, DB connections).
dont: A single alert that fires when CPU is high without indicating whether users are affected.
example: A SaaS file-sharing service shows 'Upload failures' as a symptom on the main dashboard, with cause details like 'Storage cluster latency' available on a drill-down page.
source_quote: Your monitoring system should address two questions: what’s broken, and why?
check: Does the monitoring UI separate symptom alerts from cause diagnostics?

rule: Measure and display latency distributions (e.g., percentiles) rather than just averages to capture tail latency.
why: Averages can hide slow requests that affect user experience, especially in distributed systems.
do: A latency histogram showing 50th, 90th, 95th, and 99th percentiles over time.
dont: A single line showing average latency over the last hour.
example: A SaaS payment gateway dashboard shows P99 latency alongside P50, revealing that 1% of transactions take over 5 seconds.
source_quote: The simplest way to differentiate between a slow average and a very slow "tail" of requests is to collect request counts bucketed by latencies
check: Does the dashboard show latency percentiles or histograms?

rule: Use dashboards to monitor ongoing subcritical problems instead of sending email alerts.
why: Email alerts often become noisy and ignored, while dashboards provide a persistent, filterable view.
do: A 'Warnings' dashboard panel showing non-urgent issues like disk usage at 80% or minor error rate increases.
dont: Sending an email for every minor threshold breach, cluttering inboxes.
example: A SaaS HR platform displays a 'Service Health' dashboard with yellow warnings for degraded features, without paging anyone.
source_quote: Email alerts are of very limited value and tend to easily become overrun with noise; instead, you should favor a dashboard that monitors all ongoing subcritical problems
check: Are subcritical issues shown on a dashboard rather than sent as emails?

rule: Reserve user interviews for exploratory questions about attitudes and problems, not for settling specific UI decisions.
why: Users cannot reliably evaluate concrete design alternatives they have not used.
do: Ask 'What was hard about reconciling last month's invoices?' in an interview.
dont: Ask 'Should the Buy button be red or orange?' in an interview.
example: A SaaS team choosing between a dropdown and radio buttons runs a usability test on both prototypes instead of asking interviewees to pick one.
source_quote: Most specific design questions can't be answered by interviewing users.
check: Does every interview question target a user problem or attitude rather than a specific UI element choice?

rule: Do not ask users to predict how they would use a feature or system in the future.
why: Users cannot envision something that does not exist, so predictions are weak and often misleading.
do: Build a clickable prototype and watch users attempt the task.
dont: Ask 'Would you use this feature if we built it?'
example: A SaaS team considering bulk-edit mode builds a prototype and runs a task test rather than asking interviewees whether they would use it.
source_quote: you can't ask "Would you use (potential future) feature X?" because users can't predict something they haven't seen.
check: Does the research plan replace every hypothetical future-use question with an observed prototype task?

rule: Ask users to recall a specific difficult or successful instance instead of describing their usual workflow.
why: Extreme concrete cases are more vivid and reveal real deviations that generalized answers hide.
do: Ask: 'Tell me about the last time a payroll run went wrong.'
dont: Ask: 'How do you usually run payroll?'
example: A finance SaaS team asks 'Tell me about a time a vendor payment was rejected' to uncover workflow shortcuts and workarounds.
source_quote: Ask users to recall specific instances in which they faced a particularly difficult case or when something worked particularly well.
check: Does each interview guide include at least one critical-incident question asking for a specific episode?

rule: Treat prompted opinions as unreliable and act only on comments users volunteer while using the product.
why: People invent opinions about anything when asked, so leading questions can drive false design changes.
do: Log unprompted remarks made while a user works through checkout.
dont: Send a poll asking 'Do you like this color?' and change the palette from the answers.
example: A team ignores a survey where users rate colors, but investigates when two users spontaneously mention the neon accent during onboarding.
source_quote: People can make up an opinion about anything, and they'll do so if asked.
check: Are design changes justified by comments users made unprompted during use rather than by direct opinion questions?

rule: Evaluate feature usefulness by having users attempt real tasks, not by asking whether they would use it.
why: Users cannot predict or judge features they have not seen or used.
do: Run a task where a user creates a recurring invoice in the feature.
dont: Ask interviewees 'How useful is the recurring-invoice feature?'
example: A SaaS team building reports ships a paper prototype of the export flow and watches five users try it instead of surveying demand.
source_quote: The way to assess features is to have people use them.
check: Run five observed task attempts per feature before deciding, and record the pass rate.

rule: Combine interviews with user testing instead of relying on any single research method.
why: Each method has blind spots, and triangulating findings guards against misleading conclusions.
do: Pair five usability-test sessions with three exploratory interviews on the same billing problem.
dont: Redesign checkout from interview quotes alone.
example: A SaaS team runs usability tests for checkout speed and interviews to learn brand impressions, then reconciles both.
source_quote: Interviews are great supplements to other usability methods. If you could do only one thing, I would always recommend user testing.
check: Does the research plan include at least one observational usability method alongside interviews?

rule: Include one or two nonexistent features in feature-opinion interviews to calibrate how much users invent feedback.
why: If users give copious feedback on fake features, their opinions about real ones are suspect.
do: Add an imaginary 'AI invoice whisperer' to a feature list and note user enthusiasm.
dont: Take rave reviews of real features at face value with no fake-feature baseline.
example: A PM interviewing customers about a roadmap includes an imaginary Slack integration; when users rave about it, she discounts the rest of the wishlist.
source_quote: be sure to include a few nonexistent features to collect a baseline.
check: Does each feature-opinion interview include at least one nonexistent feature?

rule: Model the product around three default environments: Local, Preview, and Production.
why: Separating local, pre-production, and live states keeps testing from leaking into user-facing behavior.
do: Show Local, Preview, and Production as distinct tabs in project settings.
dont: Use one generic environment selector with no local, preview, or production distinction.
example: A SaaS deployment settings page lists three environments and scopes secrets to each.
source_quote: Vercel provides three default environments (**Local**, **Preview**, and **Production**):
check: Can a reviewer identify Local, Preview, and Production as separate environment choices in the screenshot?

rule: Keep preview deployments isolated from the production site.
why: Preview work must be testable without changing what live users see.
do: Serve preview builds on a generated URL with a visible Preview badge.
dont: Point a preview build at the production domain or production database.
example: A QA reviewer opens a preview URL while the main app stays on the production domain.
source_quote: **Preview** environments allow you to deploy and test changes in a live setting, without affecting your production site.
check: Does the screenshot show preview access on a URL or label distinct from production?

rule: Give a named staging environment its own branch tracking, domain, and variables.
why: A staging workflow needs isolated routing, URL, and credentials to verify changes realistically.
do: Configure staging branch tracking, assign staging.example.com, and add staging-only secrets.
dont: Reuse the production domain and production variables for staging verification.
example: A SaaS team pushes to staging and tests at staging.example.com with a staging database.
source_quote: You need a named environment with its own branch tracking, domain, and variables.
check: Can a reviewer confirm branch tracking, domain, and variables are all defined for the staging environment?

rule: Require manual promotion before a staged production build serves production domains.
why: A final check should happen with production configuration before live traffic is switched.
do: Disable auto-assign custom production domains and promote only after verifying the generated URL.
dont: Auto-assign production domains to every production-branch deployment before verification.
example: A release manager checks the deployment URL, then promotes it to production without rebuilding.
source_quote: Deployments from your production branch then wait for manual promotion before serving traffic on your production domains.
check: Browser check counts whether the production domain is assigned before the manual promote action is recorded (expected: 0 before promotion).

rule: Offer custom named environments for long-running pre-production workflows.
why: Some teams need specialized staging or QA lanes beyond a single preview environment.
do: Let Pro and Enterprise projects create a staging or QA environment with its own settings.
dont: Force every pre-production workflow into one shared preview bucket.
example: A SaaS admin creates a QA environment separate from staging and production.
source_quote: Custom environments are useful for longer-running pre-production environments like `staging`, `QA`, or any other specialized workflow you require.
check: Does the settings screenshot show a custom environment name beyond Local, Preview, and Production?

rule: Let each environment define its own environment variables and credentials.
why: Database connections and API keys should differ between preview, staging, and production.
do: Scope a staging database URL and API key to the staging environment only.
dont: Expose production API keys or database URLs to preview deployments.
example: A SaaS project stores separate DATABASE_URL values for preview and production.
source_quote: Every environment can define its own unique environment variables, like database connection information or API keys.
check: Test that a preview or staging deployment reads a different database URL and API key than production.

rule: Show a visible state change the instant a user submits an action, before any server result appears.
why: Without immediate visual acknowledgment, users assume the action was not registered and retry.
do: On a SaaS 'Create project' click, immediately disable the button and show 'Creating project…'.
dont: Leave the form unchanged for 3 seconds while the request runs, then show a success toast.
example: A billing portal shows a pressed button state the moment 'Pay invoice' is clicked.
source_quote: Always give some type of immediate feedback. A user’s wait time begins the moment when she initiates an action
check: Click a submit control and measure milliseconds until any visible DOM/state change; pass if the first feedback appears within 100 ms.

rule: Add a progress indicator to every action that may take longer than about one second.
why: After a few seconds attention wanders, and users may abandon the task.
do: Show a spinner or progress bar when saving a report that can take 2-5 seconds.
dont: Silently block the interface for 4 seconds while a dashboard filter reloads.
example: A CRM shows a busy indicator while a saved view loads longer than a second.
source_quote: Use a progress indicator for any action that takes longer than about 1.0 second.
check: Does every recorded action that exceeds 1 second show a visible progress indicator?

rule: Use looped animations such as spinners only for fast waits of roughly 2-10 seconds.
why: Looping feedback reassures for short waits but gives no sense of progress for long waits.
do: Show a circular spinner for a 4-second comment load with text 'Loading comments…'.
dont: Keep a spinner rotating for a 45-second file import with no percentage or step count.
example: A support inbox spins briefly while fetching a new ticket, but switches to progress once the wait grows.
source_quote: This indicator should be reserved for actions that take between 2-10 seconds.
check: Time simulated 3s and 15s operations; record indicator type; pass if the spinner appears only for the short operation and a percent-done/step indicator for the long one.

rule: Use a percent-done or step-count indicator for operations that take 10 seconds or more.
why: Percent-done feedback shows how much is accomplished and how much remains, reducing uncertainty.
do: Show 'Updating address 3 of 50' with a filling bar during a bulk record update.
dont: Use an indefinite spinner for a 30-second export.
example: A SaaS invoice export shows 42% complete instead of only 'Working…'.
source_quote: Generally, percent-done progress indicators should be used for longer processes that take 10 or more seconds.
check: Time a simulated 15-second operation; record whether a percent-done bar or step count is visible before completion.

rule: Pair each progress indicator with specific text explaining what is loading or which step is in progress.
why: Text clarifies the reason for waiting and helps users form a time estimate.
do: Label a spinner 'Loading comments…' and a bar 'Updating address 3 of 50.'
dont: Show only an unlabeled spinner with no context about the operation.
example: A project tool shows 'Importing tasks: 12 of 80' beside the bar.
source_quote: include a text explanation of the process, for example “Updating address 3 of 50.”
check: Does every progress state include specific text naming the operation or showing step/percent progress?

rule: Give users a visible way to stop any operation that takes a little while.
why: Without a cancel control, the design leaves users powerless when they cannot wait.
do: Show a 'Cancel import' button during a 30-second CSV upload.
dont: Lock the screen with a spinner and no escape until a slow bulk action finishes.
example: A reporting tool lets users cancel a slow PDF generation and return to the dashboard.
source_quote: For actions that take a little while, give users the option to stop the process
check: Does every operation longer than a few seconds show a clear cancel/stop control during the wait?

rule: Replace static 'Loading…' text with an animated or percent-done indicator.
why: Static indicators do not show whether the system is progressing or stuck.
do: Swap 'Please wait' for a spinner with 'Loading invoices…' after a slow filter request.
dont: Show only 'Please wait while we process your request' with no motion or progress.
example: A SaaS settings page changes static 'Saving…' text to an animated progress state.
source_quote: Avoid using static progress indicators, which do not give enough feedback about the status of the action.
check: Is any wait state limited to static text or an unmoving image without animation or progress?

rule: Avoid warnings telling users not to click again; show that the first click was accepted instead.
why: Users rarely read such warnings before acting, and threats do not prevent duplicate submissions.
do: After 'Place order' is clicked, disable the button and show 'Submitting order…'.
dont: Show 'Clicking again may create an extra order' next to an active submit button.
example: A checkout page disables 'Pay now' immediately instead of warning about duplicate payments.
source_quote: Do not use warnings that instruct users not to click again.
check: Does the interface avoid copy warning about double-clicking and instead show a visible accepted/working state after the first click?

rule: Write card labels that share no repeated brand or product words, so participants group by meaning rather than by word match.
why: Identical words in labels cause automatic grouping and hide deeper relationships such as size or capacity.
do: Label cards by distinct customer tasks: 'Compare plans', 'Invite teammates', 'Export invoices'.
dont: Label cards 'Acme Starter', 'Acme Pro', 'Acme Enterprise' and watch everyone pile them together.
example: A car-rental site sorts vehicles by 'fits 5 with luggage' vs 'seats 7' instead of three Toyota model names.
source_quote: Avoid using identical words in labels for different cards because participants will automatically group those instead of thinking about deeper relationships between items.
check: Run a script that flags any two card labels sharing a non-trivial content word; pass if zero pairs are flagged.

rule: Have participants form their groups first and name each group only afterwards.
why: Showing or requesting category names up front limits participants to those categories while they sort.
do: Instruct: 'Step 2: organize the cards into groups. Step 3: label each group.' with grouping strictly before naming.
dont: Show a dropdown of your existing menu categories next to each card during sorting.
example: A dashboard redesign tool locks the naming step until the participant clicks 'Done grouping'.
source_quote: It's essential to do this step after (rather than before) they form groups, so participants don't limit themselves to specific categories during the sorting process.
check: In the session recording or tool flow, do category names appear only after the participant finished forming groups?

rule: Run an open card sort with no predefined categories to map a new IA, and use tree testing instead of a closed sort to validate an existing one.
why: Open sorts reveal users' own mental models, while predefined categories bias the groupings they produce.
do: Give participants a blank canvas and free-text group names when organizing a new product's content.
dont: Provide your current five menu categories and ask users to slot cards into them to design a new IA.
example: A SaaS team open-sorts onboarding topics to build a new help center, then tree-tests the resulting menu.
source_quote: Open card sorting is the most common type of card sort. Users create their own groups with no predefined categories.
check: Does the study plan show an open sort with no predefined categories for new IA work, or tree testing where an existing IA is being validated?

rule: Recruit at least 15 participants for a qualitative card sort and 30-50 for a quantitative one.
why: Qualitative sorts need enough voices to explain groupings, while quantitative sorts need larger samples to be generalizable.
do: Book 16 moderated sessions when you need to hear why users grouped 'Billing' with 'Security'.
dont: Run 6 unmoderated sessions and report the resulting percentages as representative of your user base.
example: A fintech team runs 15 moderated sorts for rationale, then a 40-person unmoderated sort to confirm patterns.
source_quote: Researchers need to recruit at least 15 participants for this approach.
check: Count recruited participants per study type in the plan file; pass if qualitative ≥15 and quantitative ≥30.

rule: Pilot the card sort with a small group before launch to confirm the deck size and that every label is understandable.
why: A pilot surfaces confusing labels and an unwieldy deck size before you spend the full recruiting budget.
do: Run 3 pilot sessions and rewrite any label that more than one pilot participant asked about.
dont: Launch the full 45-person study with labels nobody outside the product team has ever read.
example: A SaaS team pilots 35 settings cards with 3 colleagues, renames 4 jargon labels, then recruits.
source_quote: Conduct a pilot test with a smaller group of participants to assess the appropriate number of cards and whether the card labels are easy to understand.
check: Run a 3-5 person pilot and count how many cards each pilot participant left unsorted or asked about; revise any label flagged by 2 or more pilots.

topic: Validate with inline message plus error summary
rule: Show an error message next to the failing field and repeat it in an error summary at the top of the page on validation failure.
why: Users need the message where they are looking plus a page-level summary so they can see every problem at once.
do: A date input submits with a past-dated passport issue, so the field shows the error text and the same line appears in the summary linking back to it.
dont: Only turning the field border red with no text, or flashing a toast that disappears after three seconds.
example: A SaaS invoice form rejects a bad VAT number and shows it both inline and as a link in the top summary.
source_quote: Follow the Validation pattern and show an error message when there is a validation error.
check: On a failed submit, count the field's inline error elements and matching summary items; both counts must be 1 and their text must be identical.

topic: Say what went wrong and how to fix it
rule: Write each error message in plain, positive language that states the problem and the fix in one sentence.
why: A message that only reports failure leaves the user with no path forward.
do: Enter a date after 31 August 2017 for when you started the course
dont: Invalid input. Please try again.
example: A password reset form rejects a weak password with 'Enter a password with at least 10 characters'.
source_quote: Describe what has happened and tell them how to fix it. The message must be in plain English, use positive language and get to the point.
check: Does each error message state both what is wrong and what the user must do, with no jargon, 'please', 'sorry', or 'invalid'?

topic: Keep entered values after an error
rule: Preserve every field value, passing or failing, when you re-render the form with an error.
why: Users can then see what went wrong, edit their previous answer and avoid retyping everything.
do: After a failed submit the National Insurance field still holds the value the user typed.
dont: Clearing the whole form and showing an empty state under a red banner.
example: A checkout address form keeps all address lines filled when the postcode fails validation.
source_quote: Do not clear any form fields when showing the Error message component. Keep both passing and failing answers.
check: After a failed submit, compare each field's value to its pre-submit value; the number of fields that changed or emptied must be 0.

rule: Reuse the exact words from the field's label or question inside its error message.
why: Shared wording lets users match the message to the right field even when it is read out of context.
do: Label 'How many hours do you work a week?' pairs with 'Enter how many hours you work a week'.
dont: Label 'How many hours do you work a week?' paired with 'Field must contain a number'.
example: A billing form labelled 'Company VAT number' errors as 'Enter a company VAT number in the correct format'.
source_quote: Error messages should directly include language from the question or fieldset label.
check: Does each error message repeat key words from the label or question of the field it belongs to?

rule: Write a distinct message for each failure case instead of one generic 'required' or 'invalid' string.
why: Generic messages do not explain the situation and make no sense on their own.
do: Enter a National Insurance number in the correct format
dont: This field is required
example: A signup email field says 'Enter an email address' when empty and 'Enter an email address in the correct format, like name@example.com' when malformed.
source_quote: An error for a specific situation is more helpful. It will tell someone what has happened and how to fix it.
check: Is every error message unique to its failure case, with no 'required field' or 'an error occurred' text anywhere on screen?

rule: Use the same wording next to the field and in the error summary so both say the same thing.
why: Users see one message rather than two competing versions, which lowers the effort to understand what happened.
do: Both the inline message and the summary link read 'Enter a National Insurance number in the correct format'.
dont: Inline says 'Enter a NI number' while the summary says 'Invalid National Insurance number'.
example: A settings form shows 'Enter a phone number in the correct format' beside the field and in the summary link.
source_quote: Use the same message next to the field and in the Error summary component
check: Compare each inline error string to its matching summary item string; the number of differing characters must be 0.

rule: Use error messages only for problems with what the user entered, not for eligibility, permission or service failures.
why: An error tells the user to fix their input, which is impossible when the problem is with the service.
do: Send a non-eligible user to a page that explains why they cannot apply and what to do next.
dont: Showing 'Error: you are not eligible for this account' next to a form field.
example: A trial signup that finds an already-used domain redirects to an explanatory page instead of flagging a field.
source_quote: Do not use error messages to tell a user that they are not eligible or do not have permission to do something.
check: Is every visible error message about the user's own input, with no eligibility, permission, capacity or system-failure messages?

rule: Prefix every error message with a visually hidden 'Error:' (translated for other languages) so assistive tech announces it.
why: Screen reader users hear 'Error' before the text and know the message is a failure rather than a hint.
do: Error: Enter your full name
dont: A red message with no hidden prefix, so screen readers read it as ordinary body copy.
example: A payment form's card-number error carries a visually hidden 'Error:' span before the text.
source_quote: To help screen reader users, the error message component includes a hidden ‘Error:’ before the error message.
check: Count error message nodes that lack a visually hidden child containing the localised 'Error' label; the count must be 0.

rule: Use animation only as brief, unobtrusive feedback rather than decoration.
why: Motion grabs peripheral attention involuntarily, so decorative animation distracts from the user's task.
do: Animate a cart badge with a short pulse when an item is added.
dont: Add a constantly wiggling squiggle beside article text.
example: In a SaaS billing dashboard, a brief highlight on the invoice row confirms payment was recorded.
source_quote: Animation in UX must be unobtrusive, brief, and subtle.
check: Does every animation on the screen communicate feedback, state change, or navigation, with none purely decorative?

rule: Animate feedback when the system acknowledges a user action.
why: Change blindness causes static feedback to be missed, so motion increases the chance users notice it.
do: Animate the cart badge updating after 'Add to cart' is clicked.
dont: Silently swap the badge number with no visual change.
example: In a project tool, a saved-status pill briefly pulses when a task autosaves.
source_quote: Animations are often helpful as a form of noticeable feedback that an action has been recognized by the system.
check: After a primary action, is a motion cue visible confirming the system received it?

rule: Animate mode and state changes so users notice the switch.
why: Modes are hard to communicate, and motion makes the transition noticeable and gives it a conceptual metaphor.
do: Morph a pencil icon into a checkmark after the user enters edit mode.
dont: Instantly swap icons with no transition when switching modes.
example: In a design tool, the edit toolbar morphs into a save toolbar when editing ends.
source_quote: Motion can be used to indicate that the interface switched to a different state  -  for example, because of a mode change.
check: When the UI changes mode, does it animate the transition instead of swapping instantly?

rule: Use zoom animations to show whether users move up or deeper in a hierarchy.
why: Zooming out reveals more objects while zooming in reveals detail, giving a spatial metaphor for navigation.
do: Animate zoom-out when moving from a month view to a year view.
dont: Jump instantly between hierarchy levels with no zoom transition.
example: In a file manager, moving from a folder to its parent zooms out slightly.
source_quote: Zooming out shows less detail, but more objects, thus suggesting that the user travels up into the hierarchy
check: Does moving between hierarchy levels use a directional zoom rather than an instant cut?

rule: Match animation direction to the gesture that dismisses or reveals an element.
why: The direction of motion acts as a signifier of which interaction the element accepts.
do: Slide a card up from the bottom so users infer it can be pulled down to close.
dont: Animate a card from the bottom but require a swipe from the left edge to dismiss.
example: In a mobile app, a 'Now Playing' panel rises from the bottom and is dismissed by dragging down.
source_quote: a card that expands from the bottom of the screen towards the top signals to the user that it can be closed by pulling down.
check: Does the animation direction match the gesture that actually dismisses the element?

rule: Animate accordions, anchor links, and overlays so users know they remain on the same page.
why: Instant changes can look like a new page, prompting users to press Back and lose their place.
do: Smooth-scroll to an anchor target and animate the accordion expanding.
dont: Instantly render accordion content at the top of the screen with no motion.
example: In a help center, clicking an FAQ anchor scrolls smoothly to the answer on the same page.
source_quote: Accordions, anchor links, and menu overlays can be disorienting or confusing if the change appears instantaneously
check: Do in-page accordions, anchors, and overlays animate rather than appear instantaneously?

rule: Limit simultaneous animations so each cue keeps its power to attract attention.
why: Competing animations overwhelm users and diminish the attention each one earns.
do: Show one loading indicator plus a progress bar, not five separate animations.
dont: Animate a mascot, counter, progress bar, and placeholder all at once.
example: In a SaaS search results page, a single skeleton shimmer communicates loading while other changes stay still.
source_quote: the number of simultaneous animations is overwhelming: the power of any of these animations to pull the user’s attention is diminished by competition from all the others.
check: Count animations visible in one viewport at the same time; target is 1-2 concurrent cues, never more than 3.

rule: Never animate to hijack attention or trigger fear of loss.
why: Using motion to force attention or urgency is an unethical dark pattern.
do: Use a single subtle pulse on a new message icon.
dont: Add a flashing countdown timer to pressure purchases.
example: In an e-commerce SaaS, avoid pulsing 'sale ends soon' badges; use static text instead.
source_quote: using animation to hijack the users’ attention or create a fear of loss is a dark pattern
check: Would a reviewer flag any animation as pressuring, flashing, or unrelated to the user's task?

rule: Animate element movement with transform translate or rotate instead of top or left.
why: Transform-only movement can stay off the layout and paint stages, so the animation remains smooth.
do: @keyframes slide-in { 0% { transform: translateY(-1000px); } 100% { transform: translateY(0); } }
dont: @keyframes move { 50% { top: calc(90vh - 160px); left: calc(90vw - 200px); } }
example: A SaaS onboarding panel slides in from the right using transform: translateX(100%) to 0 instead of animating left.
source_quote: To move an element, use the translate or rotation keyword values of the transform property.
check: Chrome Performance Summary for the animation window must show Rendering = 0 ms and dropped frames below 1%.

rule: Resize animated elements with transform scale instead of animating width or height.
why: Scaling with transform avoids layout work that width and height animations can trigger.
do: @keyframes scale { 50% { transform: scale(0.5); } 100% { transform: scale(1); } }
dont: @keyframes resize { 50% { width: 50%; height: 50%; } 100% { width: 100%; height: 100%; } }
example: A pricing card pulses on hover using transform: scale(1.05) rather than changing width and height.
source_quote: To resize an element, use the scale keyword value of the transform property.
check: Keyframe inspection must show transform: scale and no width/height animation; Performance Rendering time must be 0 ms.

rule: Fade elements in and out with opacity instead of animating display or visibility in keyframes.
why: Opacity is a compositor-friendly property that avoids layout and paint work for visibility changes.
do: @keyframes fade { 0% { opacity: 0; } 100% { opacity: 1; } }
dont: @keyframes hide { 0% { visibility: visible; } 100% { visibility: hidden; } }
example: A toast notification fades in with opacity from 0 to 1 and fades out to 0 without toggling display.
source_quote: To show or hide an element, use opacity.
check: Does the keyframe animation change opacity while leaving display and visibility out of the animated properties?

rule: Avoid animating any property that triggers layout or paint unless it is absolutely necessary.
why: Non-composited properties can force layout or painting and make the animation slow or glitchy.
do: Animate transform and opacity; if a blur or shadow effect is needed, profile it and choose a cheaper substitute when possible.
dont: Continuously animate box-shadow blur or filter on a large hero area without profiling.
example: A dashboard KPI card animates transform: translateY instead of box-shadow blur when it appears.
source_quote: Avoid any property that triggers layout or paint unless it's absolutely necessary.
check: Chrome Performance Summary must show Rendering = 0 ms and paint flashing must show 0 full-screen flashes during the animation.

rule: Use will-change sparingly, and only after observing a graphics or performance issue.
why: Layer creation can cause other performance issues, so preemptive will-change can make performance worse.
do: .sidebar { will-change: transform; } only on a sidebar that frequently slides in and out.
dont: .card, .button, .modal { will-change: transform; } added to every animated element up front.
example: A SaaS app adds will-change: transform to its slide-out sidebar after profiling shows compositing issues, not to every card.
source_quote: Use the will-change property sparingly, and only if you encounter a performance issue.
check: Was will-change added only after a documented graphics or performance issue rather than preemptively?

rule: Remove will-change when the change stops, and apply it shortly before infrequent changes via JavaScript.
why: Timely application and removal gives the browser time to optimize without keeping unnecessary layers.
do: On pointerenter, set el.style.willChange = 'transform'; on transitionend, set el.style.willChange = 'auto'.
dont: .modal { will-change: transform; } left in the stylesheet permanently for a modal that opens rarely.
example: A settings drawer sets will-change: transform just before opening and clears it on transitionend.
source_quote: Make sure to give the browser enough time to perform the necessary optimizations, and remove the property when the change has stopped.
check: After transitionend, getComputedStyle(element).willChange must be 'auto' with 0 persistent will-change layers.

rule: Record animations in Chrome DevTools Performance and fix any animation that shows nonzero Rendering time.
why: Rendering time in the Summary tab can indicate the animation is forcing the browser to do layout work.
do: Record the animation, open Summary, and keep the animation only when Rendering is 0 ms.
dont: Ship an animation that shows nonzero Rendering time because it looks acceptable on a fast laptop.
example: A SaaS modal entrance using top/left shows Rendering 80 ms; rewrite it with transform until Rendering is 0 ms.
source_quote: If you see a nonzero value for Rendering in the Summary tab, it might mean your animation is making the browser do layout work.
check: Chrome Performance Summary: Rendering time must be 0 ms for the recorded animation window.

rule: Verify animation smoothness with the FPS meter and target a high kept-frame percentage such as 99%.
why: A high kept-frame percentage means few frames are dropped and the animation looks smooth.
do: Enable Rendering > FPS meter and accept only animations showing about 99% frames kept.
dont: Accept an animation showing 50% of frames dropped because the code looks optimized.
example: A checkout progress bar animation is reworked until the FPS meter shows 99% frames kept instead of 50% dropped.
source_quote: A high-performance animation has a high percentage, such as 99%, meaning that few frames are being dropped and the animation looks smooth.
check: Chrome Rendering FPS meter: dropped frames must be at most 1% (kept frames at least 99%) during the animation.

rule: Adopt OWASP Top 10 as the security-risk baseline in every SaaS page scope.
why: It is the reference standard for the most critical web application security risks.
do: In the page-scope doc, list the page's auth, data, and input paths against OWASP Top 10 categories.
dont: Scope the page only by layout, components, and happy-path user stories.
example: Before building an admin user-management page, the scope doc flags broken access control and injection risks.
source_quote: The OWASP Top 10 is the reference standard for the most critical web application security risks.
check: Does the page-scope document reference OWASP Top 10 risks for the page's auth, data, or input flows?

rule: Cite the current OWASP Top 10 release, version 2025, when defining security risks.
why: OWASP identifies 2025 as the most current released version.
do: Write "OWASP Top 10 2025" in the security section of the page brief.
dont: Use a 2017 PDF as the primary risk list without noting that a newer version exists.
example: A SaaS checkout page brief cites OWASP Top 10 2025, not an older 2017 PDF.
source_quote: The most current released version is the OWASP Top 10 2025.
check: File check counts occurrences of "OWASP Top 10 2025" in the page-scope document; require at least 1.

rule: Use OWASP Top 10 as an awareness baseline, not as the only security test plan.
why: OWASP describes it as a standard awareness document for developers and web application security.
do: Label the scope's risk list "awareness baseline" and add page-specific security test items.
dont: Treat a checked OWASP Top 10 list as proof the page is fully secure.
example: A SaaS settings page uses OWASP Top 10 for awareness, then adds tests for file upload and session expiry.
source_quote: The OWASP Top 10 is a standard awareness document for developers and web application security.
check: Does the scope document call the OWASP Top 10 an awareness baseline and list additional page-specific security tests?

rule: Make OWASP Top 10 adoption an early step in the SaaS development process, not a late QA add-on.
why: OWASP presents it as a first step toward a culture focused on producing secure code.
do: Add a security-risk review at page scoping and again before build.
dont: Wait until penetration testing after implementation to consider OWASP Top 10 risks.
example: A new billing page gets an OWASP Top 10 review during scoping before any UI is built.
source_quote: Using the OWASP Top 10 is perhaps the most effective first step towards changing the software development culture within your organization into one that produces more secure code.
check: Does the project record an OWASP Top 10 review at scoping or design stage before implementation?

rule: Combine at least two research methods on a project instead of defaulting to the one or two your team already knows.
why: Each method answers a different question, so combining them covers the blind spots a single familiar method leaves behind.
do: Pair five moderated usability sessions with a funnel analytics review before redesigning onboarding.
dont: Run only a survey because the team has always run surveys, and treat the results as the full picture.
example: A SaaS team pairs 6 usability tests with a clickstream review before rebuilding the signup flow.
source_quote: nearly all projects would benefit from multiple research methods and from combining insights
check: Does the research plan list at least two distinct methods with different data types (e.g., qualitative sessions plus analytics or survey)?

rule: Base usability conclusions on observed behavior, and treat self-reported beliefs as supporting context only.
why: Attitudinal data is limited by what people are aware of and willing to report, and often diverges from what they actually do.
do: Record where users click and hesitate in a task, then use survey comments only to explain those moments.
dont: Ship a navigation change solely because focus-group participants said the current menu was 'fine'.
example: A dashboard team watches 8 task recordings before trusting a survey that says the filters are easy to use.
source_quote: The purpose of attitudinal research is usually to understand or measure people's stated beliefs, but it is limited by what people are aware of and willing to report.
check: Are the stated findings backed by observed task behavior (recordings, metrics) rather than only survey or interview opinions?

rule: Choose qualitative methods for why and how-to-fix questions, and quantitative methods for how-many and how-much questions.
why: The two families answer different question types, so mismatching them yields data that cannot settle the decision.
do: Run 5 moderated sessions to find why users abandon checkout, then an A/B test to size the fix's impact.
dont: Send a 2000-response survey to discover why users are confused by a specific form field.
example: A SaaS team interviews churned accounts to find causes, then measures churn-rate change after the fix ships.
source_quote: qualitative methods are much better suited for answering questions about why or how to fix a problem
check: Does each research question in the plan map to a method that can actually answer that question type (why vs how many)?

rule: Pick generative methods when choosing direction, formative methods while designing, and summative methods once the product can be measured.
why: Research goals change across the development process, so a method aimed at the wrong phase produces answers nobody can act on.
do: Use diary studies and interviews during strategy, then usability tests during design, then benchmarking after launch.
dont: Run a competitive usability benchmark on a feature that is still a rough concept with no defined flow.
example: A SaaS team runs concept tests before building a new billing page, then benchmarks it three months after launch.
source_quote: methods at this stage are often generative in nature, because they help generate ideas and answers about which way to go
check: Does the research plan label each study as generative, formative, or summative and match it to the current development phase?

rule: Script benchmark studies tightly with predetermined tasks and metrics so results stay comparable across participants and runs.
why: Consistency across participants is what makes usability metrics reliable enough to compare over time or against competitors.
do: Fix the task list, success criteria, and time-on-task measures before running 20 benchmark sessions across two quarters.
dont: Let each moderator improvise tasks during a benchmark, then compare success rates between versions.
example: A SaaS team reuses one frozen onboarding task script to benchmark each quarterly release against the last.
source_quote: a benchmarking study is usually very tightly scripted, so that it can produce reliable usability metrics by ensuring consistency across participants
check: Compare the task scripts and metric definitions across two benchmark runs; count the number of differing tasks or measures (target: 0).

rule: Validate navigation structure with card sorting and tree testing before locking an information architecture.
why: These methods expose users' mental models so the hierarchy matches how people actually group and look for things.
do: Run an open card sort on 40 items, draft the IA, then confirm findability with a tree test on the top tasks.
dont: Approve a new sidebar taxonomy in a stakeholder meeting without testing whether users can find items in it.
example: A SaaS settings menu is reorganized after a card sort, then tree-tested to confirm admins find billing faster.
source_quote: This method helps create or refine the information architecture of a site by exposing users’ mental models.
check: Is there a card sort or tree test record backing the proposed navigation structure before it ships?

rule: Test concepts with a rough approximation that conveys the value proposition, not a polished detail-level prototype.
why: Concept tests are meant to find out whether users want the product at all, and detail distracts participants from that judgment.
do: Show a one-page value-prop mock and ask whether and when participants would use it, before designing screens.
dont: Build a clickable high-fidelity prototype just to learn whether the core idea is worth pursuing.
example: A SaaS team tests a pricing-model concept as a single annotated slide before committing engineering time.
source_quote: employ an expression of the idea of a product or service that gets at the heart of what it would provide
check: Does the concept stimulus show only value-proposition level detail, with no interaction-level fidelity?

rule: Fit every block the brief names, header plus first rows or figure, into a 1440×900 first screen.
why: In blind testing screens lost because half the requested blocks started below the fold.
do: A headline block sized 200-360px tall, long lists capped at 4-6 rows with a 'View all' link.
dont: One full-width flat chart filling the screen while the required table begins below the fold.
example: A deploy overview at 1440×900 shows the error-rate chart, the failed build row and its log link without scrolling.
source_quote: At 1440×900, every block the brief asks for shows its header and its first rows or its figure.
check: Screenshot at 1440×900 and list each brief-named block: mark yes/no whether its header and first row or figure are visible without scrolling.

topic: Primary job is one click away
rule: Place a control for the screen's most frequent job next to the answer it acts on.
why: A screen with rows and numbers but no action reads as a report rather than a tool.
do: A 'Redeploy' button on the failed build row and 'Pack orders' in the title row.
dont: A queue screen listing waiting replies with no approve, reply or assign control anywhere.
example: An inbox puts 'Reply' on the row of the oldest unanswered thread, level with its waiting time.
source_quote: A screen with no control for its main job reads as a report, not as a tool.
check: Name the screen's most frequent job, then ask: is a control for that job visible on the first screenshot next to where its answer appears?

rule: Put the product's own mark and name at the top of the sidebar or rail and show its scope.
why: A screen with no name, workspace or mark could belong to anyone and reads as a template.
do: A monogram drawn from the product's name in the accent, with a workspace switcher beneath it.
dont: A black rounded square with a letter, no product name, and no workspace or account shown.
example: A scheduling tool's shell shows its mark, 'Shiftly' and 'Riverside Bakery' above the navigation.
source_quote: The product's mark and name sit at the top of the sidebar or rail
check: From the first screenshot alone, can a reviewer name the product and the workspace or account the screen is scoped to?

rule: Choose one product-specific face before building: a tinted ground, a characterful figure face, or the brand hue on the main data element.
why: The judges' top complaint was a well-applied kit rather than a product with its own identity.
do: A bakery dashboard on a ground tinted from its world, with a sell-out strip as its signature element.
dont: Stock Inter on #f8f8f8, white 12px cards and lime on black, identical for every product.
example: An energy home's overview carries a power-flow element and a hue on today's line, noted beside the screen's question.
source_quote: The style's tokens make a screen correct; these make it this product's, and choosing them is a step of the run, not a finish
check: Does the first screenshot show one written-down identity choice (tinted ground, characterful typeface, or hue on the main data element) recorded next to the screen's question?

rule: End the breadcrumb trail with the current page and render that last item as non-link text.
why: A link that points to the page the user is already on is a dead click that muddles their sense of location.
do: Reports > Analytics > Funnels, where 'Funnels' is plain bold text with no underline or hover state
dont: 'Funnels' styled in the same blue underlined link style as its ancestors and clicking back to the same URL
example: A SaaS analytics app ends its trail with 'Weekly report' as plain text after 'Home > Reports'.
source_quote: You should never have a link that does nothing. The last breadcrumb (denoting the current page) should not be a link.
check: Does the final breadcrumb render as non-link text and look visually different from the linked crumbs before it?

topic: Only real pages in the trail
rule: Link every breadcrumb item except the current page to an ancestor page that actually exists.
why: Users read breadcrumbs as places they can click to, so a label with no page behind it breaks that promise.
do: Trail reads Networking > Wired Networking because the intermediate 'Commercial Networking' label has no page, so it is left out
dont: Inserting 'Commercial Networking' as plain text (or a dead link) because it appears as a menu grouping in the global nav
example: A SaaS admin console skips the 'Billing settings' grouping label from the trail because only the inner pages exist as routes.
source_quote: If some of the subcategory labels in the global navigation don’t have a separate page dedicated to them do not include these subcategories in the breadcrumb trail.
check: For every breadcrumb item except the last, assert it is an anchor with an href returning HTTP 200; count of non-linked non-final items must be 0.

rule: Expose a Home link in either the breadcrumb trail or the global navigation, but not in both.
why: Users still need a way back to the root, but duplicating the same destination twice wastes space and adds noise.
do: Breadcrumb trail starts at 'Home' on a site whose top nav has no Home item
dont: Top nav shows 'Home' and the breadcrumb trail also starts with a 'Home' crumb linking to the same place
example: A marketing site keeps Home in the global nav only, so its trail on a pricing subpage begins at 'Plans > Enterprise'.
source_quote: duplicating the Home link in both the global navigation and the breadcrumb trail is not recommended  -  one or the other is fine.
check: Is the Home destination reachable exactly once across the global nav and the breadcrumb trail (no duplicate Home entries)?

rule: Build breadcrumbs from the site's information hierarchy, never from the sequence of pages the user visited.
why: A history trail grows long and repetitive and tells users nothing when they land deep from an external link.
do: Trail shows Docs > API > Authentication regardless of whether the user came from search or the pricing page
dont: Trail reads Pricing > Blog > Docs > API > Authentication because that is the order the user clicked through
example: A SaaS help center shows Support > Billing > Invoices even when the visitor arrived straight from a Google result.
source_quote: Breadcrumbs are not intended to show the history of pages traversed during a session on the site
check: Does the trail list the page's parent chain in the IA rather than the order of pages the user visited?

rule: For a page with multiple parents, show exactly one canonical breadcrumb path.
why: Two parallel trails confuse users and eat scarce space at the top of the page.
do: Pick Jobs > Design as the canonical trail for a listing page that is also reachable via Companies > Careers
dont: Rendering 'Home > Jobs > Design' and 'Home > Companies > Careers > Design' stacked above the same page
example: A SaaS marketplace page reachable from two category trees shows only the primary category in its trail.
source_quote: we do not recommend showing two or more breadcrumb trails reflecting the different paths in the polyhierarchy
check: Does the page show exactly one breadcrumb trail rather than two parallel trails?

rule: Keep breadcrumbs as a supplement to global and section navigation, not a replacement for them.
why: Breadcrumbs only point up the hierarchy, so removing lateral navigation traps users in the current branch.
do: Breadcrumb sits below a full global nav plus a left-hand section nav listing sibling pages
dont: Breadcrumb crumb opens a dropdown of sibling pages, standing in for a missing section nav
example: A SaaS dashboard keeps its left sidebar section nav and adds a small trail above the page title.
source_quote: Breadcrumbs augment but do not replace those main forms of navigation.
check: Is there still a global nav and/or section nav on the page in addition to the breadcrumb trail?

rule: On mobile, keep the breadcrumb trail to a single line by shortening it to the last level or two.
why: A wrapped trail consumes crowded screen space and can push the page's main content below the fold.
do: Mobile product page shows just 'Back to Outdoor Gear' as the single upward crumb
dont: Five crumbs wrapping onto three lines above the product name on a 375px screen
example: An ecommerce product page shows one parent crumb on mobile and the full trail on desktop.
source_quote: on mobile, breadcrumbs can take up too much space or can be hard to tap; consider shortening the breadcrumb trail if your users’ tasks allow it
check: At a 375px viewport, measure the breadcrumb container: scrollHeight must equal clientHeight (no wrap to a second line) and it must sit above the page heading without pushing it past the fold.

rule: Size each breadcrumb link's tap target to at least 1 cm by 1 cm on touchscreens.
why: Shrinking crumbs to save space makes them nearly untappable on a phone.
do: Each crumb rendered with padding so its hit box measures ~40x40px on a 375px viewport
dont: 12px text links packed edge to edge with 2px gaps to keep the trail narrow
example: A mobile SaaS app gives each crumb a padded hit area so users can tap a parent page on the first try.
source_quote: tap targets need to be at least 1 cm X 1 cm
check: Measure each breadcrumb link's bounding box at a 375px viewport: width and height must each be at least 38px, with at least 8px spacing between adjacent targets.

rule: Write each persona as a fictional but realistic description of a typical or target user.
why: That definition keeps personas grounded in target-user traits while avoiding the false authority of a real individual.
do: Persona doc: 'B2B ops lead, 35-50, manages 15 vendor renewals monthly; goals, pains, and a day-in-the-life quote.'
dont: Persona named after the CEO's spouse with invented hobbies and no link to target-user evidence.
example: A SaaS billing tool writes 'Admin Ana' for finance admins who reconcile invoices weekly, including goals and blockers.
source_quote: A persona is a fictional, yet realistic, description of a typical or target user of the product.
check: Does each persona read as a realistic target-user description rather than a real person or generic stock character?

rule: Choose persona scope deliberately before drafting, matching narrow or broad coverage to the project goal.
why: The source frames scope as a decision that determines whether personas fit the goal or become too vague or too narrow.
do: For a single onboarding redesign, document a narrow scope: new trial admins in mid-market SaaS, then create 3 personas.
dont: Create 12 broad personas covering every possible buyer before the team has decided what decision they need to support.
example: A web app team scoping an invite-flow redesign writes 'narrow: first-time workspace owners' before persona work starts.
source_quote: How to determine whether narrow- or broad-scope personas are better suited for your goals
check: Does the persona artifact state its scope and tie that scope to a named product goal?

rule: Select a lightweight, qualitative, or statistical persona approach before creation.
why: The source presents these as distinct creation methods with different benefits and challenges.
do: For a fast discovery sprint, choose lightweight personas and label them as working hypotheses.
dont: Mix statistical clusters, interview quotes, and invented details without declaring which persona type is being used.
example: A dashboard team picking a method writes 'qualitative personas from 8 admin interviews' before building the personas.
source_quote: 3 different ways to create personas and the benefits and challenges of each
check: Does the persona plan name the chosen type and why it fits the available data and timeline?

rule: Use personas to evaluate and compare design features when setting work priorities.
why: The source explicitly connects personas to comparing features and informing work priorities.
do: In backlog review, score each candidate feature by impact on the primary admin persona and record the rationale.
dont: Prioritize features only by loudest stakeholder request while personas sit unused in a slide deck.
example: A SaaS roadmap meeting tags each feature 'high/medium/low for Admin Ana' before choosing the next quarter's work.
source_quote: How to use personas to evaluate and compare design features to inform work priorities
check: Do feature-priority records show persona-based comparison for each candidate feature?

rule: Run scenario-mapping workshops that use personas to generate design ideas.
why: The source lists scenario mapping as a way to leverage personas for design ideation.
do: Workshop prompt: 'For Admin Ana, map the steps and pain points of adding a teammate before sketching solutions.'
dont: Hold a generic brainstorming session with no persona context and then retrofit a persona name to the ideas.
example: A web product team maps 'Manager Mia invites a contractor' scenarios and identifies missing permission steps.
source_quote: How to leverage personas to influence design in scenario-mapping workshops
check: Does the workshop record show persona-specific scenarios used to generate or evaluate design ideas?

rule: Segment website analytics by persona to uncover trends and derive UX insights.
why: The source describes using personas with website analytics to reveal data trends and UX insights.
do: Create a persona-based segment for 'trial admins' and compare activation funnel drop-off against other persona segments.
dont: Report one blended traffic dashboard and conclude all users behave the same.
example: A SaaS analytics dashboard segments signup completion by 'solo owner' vs 'team admin' to find a blocked step.
source_quote: How to use personas with website analytics to uncover trends in data and derive UX insights
check: Analytics export check counts persona-based segments used in the report; require at least two named segments.

rule: Check every page in a real browser at three viewport widths and fail the build when it reads as generic slop.
why: Layouts break between widths in ways a code-only review never shows, so the render is the only honest test.
do: Run the inspector at 375, 768 and 1440 px and block ship if any slop rule fails.
dont: Eyeball the markup on a desktop monitor and assume the mobile layout holds.
example: A SaaS pricing page looks fine on desktop; the 375 px run catches a nav overlapping the hero, so the build is held until fixed.
source_quote: Checks the page in a real browser at three widths and fails it on slop.
check: Browser run at 375, 768 and 1440 px; the count of failing slop rules must be 0.

rule: Screenshot your own build, name the top three problems, and fix them for up to three rounds.
why: Looking at the rendered page as an image exposes defects you stop seeing while writing the code.
do: Capture the page, list three concrete defects, fix them, re-capture, and stop after round three.
dont: Declare the page finished the moment the markup compiles, without a single screenshot.
example: A checkout page screenshot shows cramped button padding, a misaligned total and a stray divider; all three are fixed in round one.
source_quote: Looks at its own screenshots and fixes the top three problems, up to three rounds.
check: Number of logged screenshot review rounds (max 3) and defects fixed per round must be at least 1 each.

rule: Build dashboards with quiet panels, column-aligned figures, colour spent only on data, and a phone layout where navigation folds away.
why: Neutral chrome lets the numbers carry the page, and a collapsing nav keeps dense screens usable on a phone.
do: Use grey panel surfaces, tabular-aligned numeric columns, one accent hue reserved for chart series and deltas.
dont: Paint the sidebar and cards in loud brand colour so the charts compete with the chrome.
example: An admin analytics view ships with neutral cards, right-aligned revenue columns and a single blue used only for the trend line; on mobile the sidebar collapses into a menu button.
source_quote: checks the result with app rules: quiet panels, aligned figures, colour spent on data, a phone layout where the navigation folds away
check: Are panels neutral, figures column-aligned, and is colour used only on data or status? yes/no

rule: Check every page's frame for a clear title on the first screen, equal margins, no section shoved to one side and no random blank stretches.
why: Uneven margins and accidental gaps read as broken before a reviewer judges any content.
do: Align every section to the same container width and confirm the first screen states the page title.
dont: Run one section full-bleed while the next keeps a 40 px inset, leaving the page lopsided.
example: A settings page keeps all cards inside the same 1120 px container, and the empty gap under the last card is removed.
source_quote: checks the frame of every page (a clear title on the first screen, equal margins, no section shoved to one side, no random blank stretches)
check: Does every section share the same left and right margins with no unintended empty gaps? yes/no

rule: Write one sentence tying the client's own material to the chosen direction before any layout work starts.
why: A single binding sentence stops the build from drifting back into the average landing page.
do: State it plainly, e.g. 'a roaster's archive photographs set as the page's stacked index cards', then design to it.
dont: Open with 'modern, clean landing page for a coffee brand' and reach for a template.
example: Onboarding flow for a payments product: 'receipts as the visual grammar, each step shown as a printed slip'.
source_quote: one sentence tying the client's own material to that direction
check: Is there one written sentence naming the client's material and the chosen direction? yes/no

rule: Fill image slots with real photographs and footage from open collections, and credit them on the page.
why: Real pictures carry the art direction; placeholders quietly tell the viewer nothing was finished.
do: Pull CC BY photos from Wikimedia Commons and render an attribution line in the footer.
dont: Ship gradient blobs and grey placeholder boxes in the final build.
example: A marketing site's hero and feature rows use credited Openverse photographs, with a credits block linked from the footer.
source_quote: Builds with real pictures and footage from open collections, credited.
check: Count of image slots holding licensed real media versus placeholders; placeholders must equal 0.

rule: Deal a small set of researched art directions and commit to exactly one before designing.
why: Choosing from named directions beats defaulting to whatever layout comes to mind first.
do: Deal three of twenty documented directions and pick the one that fits the client's material.
dont: Skip options entirely and go straight to a hero, three feature cards and a CTA.
example: A developer tool site deals three directions, picks the editorial archive one, and every later decision follows it.
source_quote: A script deals three of 20 researched directions and the agent picks one.
check: Was one named direction chosen from a dealt set and stated before the build began? yes/no

rule: Keep {, }, and . out of token and group names so alias syntax stays unambiguous.
why: Aliases use brace and dot syntax, so those characters inside a name break reference parsing.
do: "color-text-primary": { "$type": "color", "$value": ... }
dont: "color.text.primary": { ... } or "color{text}": { ... }
example: A SaaS theme names a color token color.text.primary and the resolver cannot parse {color.text.primary}.
source_quote: Furthermore, due to the syntax used for token aliases the following characters MUST NOT be used anywhere in a token or group name:
check: Lint all token and group names; the count of names containing {, }, or . must be 0.

rule: Declare $type on a token or its parent group and never infer it from the value.
why: Tools must not guess, so a token with no resolvable type is invalid and cannot be translated.
do: A color group sets "$type": "color" once and every child token carries only "$value".
dont: A token with "$value": "#0066cc" and no $type anywhere in its ancestry.
example: A dashboard theme's button color token has no $type and its parent group is untyped, so the CSS exporter rejects it.
source_quote: Tools MUST NOT attempt to guess the type of a token by inspecting the contents of its value.
check: Run a token linter; count tokens with no explicit or inherited $type  -  must be 0.

rule: Never let two token names differ only by letter case.
why: Case variants collide when exported to case-insensitive targets, silently dropping one token.
do: "font-size" and "font-size-display" as distinct names.
dont: "font-size" and "FONT-SIZE" in the same group.
example: A design system exports Sass and gets two $font-size declarations, losing the 3rem token.
source_quote: having token names that differ only in case is likely to cause identical and undesirable duplicates in the output
check: Count case-insensitive duplicate token names across the file; must be 0.

rule: Never put $value on an object that also contains child tokens or groups.
why: An object is either a token or a group; mixing them is invalid and tools must report an error.
do: A group "color" holds child tokens like "primary": {"$value": ...}.
dont: "color": { "$value": "#0066cc", "primary": { "$value": "#004499" } }
example: A SaaS palette file nests primary under the same object that has $value, and the token pipeline fails validation.
source_quote: If an object contains both $value and child tokens/groups, this creates an invalid structure
check: Run the format validator; count objects with both $value and child keys  -  must be 0.

rule: Use $extends for group variants, letting local tokens replace inherited ones at the same path.
why: Deep-merge inheritance keeps variant groups consistent without duplicating every token.
do: "button-primary": { "$extends": "{button}", "background": { "$value": "#cc0066", "$type": "color" } }
dont: Copying the whole button group and editing one background, so future base changes do not propagate.
example: A component library defines button-primary by extending button and overriding only background.
source_quote: Group extension follows deep merge behavior where local properties override inherited properties at the same path
check: Resolve each $extends chain; overridden paths must equal the local value and untouched paths must equal the parent.

rule: Put vendor data under $extensions with a reverse-domain key and preserve unknown keys when saving.
why: Unpreserved extension data is lost as files move between design and translation tools.
do: "$extensions": { "org.example.tool-a": 42 }
dont: Adding a top-level "figma": {...} key or stripping $extensions on export.
example: A design file passes through a token translator; the org.example.tool-a metadata must survive the round trip.
source_quote: Tools that process design token files MUST preserve any extension data they do not themselves understand.
check: Round-trip the token file through the tool and diff $extensions keys; lost keys must be 0.

rule: Mark retiring tokens with $deprecated and explain the migration in a string instead of deleting them abruptly.
why: Consumers need warning and a replacement path before a token disappears.
do: "$deprecated": "Please use {button.activeBorder} instead."
dont: "$deprecated": true with no explanation, or silently removing the token.
example: A design system keeps Button background deprecated for one release and points to Button activeBorder.
source_quote: The $deprecated property MAY be used to mark a token as deprecated, and optionally explain the reason.
check: Does every token with $deprecated include a string explanation naming the replacement or reason?

rule: Save design token files with .tokens or .tokens.json extensions so tools can recognize them.
why: A distinct extension lets editors and token tools identify and open the file correctly.
do: tokens/colors.tokens.json
dont: tokens/colors.json (or colors.yml) with no distinct token extension.
example: A SaaS repo stores theme tokens as src/tokens/colors.tokens.json.
source_quote: Tools that can save design token files SHOULD append one of the recommended file extensions to the filename when saving.
check: Check every token file path ends with .tokens or .tokens.json; nonconforming count must be 0.

rule: Show immediate, visible feedback after every action with consequences.
why: Users learn the outcome of prior interactions and can decide next steps.
do: After a user saves billing settings, show an inline 'Saved' confirmation and update the account status label.
dont: Save settings silently with no visible change, spinner, or confirmation.
example: In a SaaS admin console, clicking 'Invite teammate' immediately shows 'Invite sent to alex@acme.com' in the row.
source_quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
check: Browser check measures time from click to visible status feedback; it must be under 1 second.

rule: Label controls and concepts with terms your users already know, not internal jargon.
why: Familiar wording reduces learnability and matches users' mental models.
do: Use 'Billing' and 'Team members' in navigation.
dont: Use 'Revenue Ops Module' and 'Provisioning entities' as visible labels.
example: In a B2B analytics app, rename 'Account Hierarchy Node' to 'Company' after research shows that term.
source_quote: The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.
check: Can a reviewer confirm every visible label uses a term from user research rather than internal jargon?

rule: Give every consequential action a clearly labeled Cancel, Back, or Undo escape.
why: Users make mistakes and need to leave unwanted actions without an extended process.
do: Put a visible Cancel button and an X in modals, and offer an Undo toast after deletion.
dont: Trap users in a multi-step wizard with no Back or Cancel control.
example: In a SaaS onboarding modal, pressing Esc or clicking Cancel closes it and preserves entered data.
source_quote: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked "emergency exit" to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.
check: Tester opens a modal, presses Esc, and confirms it closes without saving or trapping focus.

rule: Follow platform conventions and keep words and actions consistent across screens.
why: Users' experience with other products sets expectations and inconsistency adds cognitive load.
do: Use standard Save/Cancel button order and the same term for the same object everywhere.
dont: Call the same action 'Commit' on one screen and 'Save' on another.
example: In a web app, all settings pages place the primary action on the right and secondary on the left.
source_quote: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.
check: Do primary and secondary actions keep the same labels and order across comparable screens?

rule: Prevent high-cost errors with constraints, defaults, and confirmation before committing.
why: The best designs prevent problems from occurring instead of only reporting them.
do: Disable the submit button until required fields are valid, and confirm destructive deletes.
dont: Allow one-click workspace deletion with no confirmation or undo.
example: In a SaaS admin panel, deleting a project opens a confirm dialog naming the project and asks for explicit approval.
source_quote: Good error messages are important, but the best designs carefully prevent problems from occurring in the first place.
check: Tester attempts to delete a workspace and must confirm before any data is removed.

rule: Keep labels, options, and needed information visible so users do not have to memorize them.
why: Humans have limited short-term memory and visible cues reduce cognitive effort.
do: Keep field labels visible above inputs instead of using placeholder-only labels.
