dont: Hide field labels inside placeholders that disappear as soon as the user types.
example: In a checkout form, each input keeps its label visible and shows the accepted card format next to the field.
source_quote: Minimize the user's memory load by making elements, actions, and options visible.
check: Are all field labels still visible after text is entered, not only as placeholders?

rule: Remove irrelevant or rarely needed information from primary screens.
why: Every extra element competes with relevant information and lowers its visibility.
do: Keep a dashboard focused on the few KPIs tied to the primary task.
dont: Fill the dashboard with banners, tips, and widgets unrelated to the main goal.
example: In a SaaS analytics dashboard, move secondary reports behind a 'More reports' link instead of crowding the main view.
source_quote: Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed.
check: Can a reviewer identify the single primary task on the screen without competing elements?

rule: Reference functional or component color tokens instead of base color tokens in code and design.
why: Base tokens are raw values that do not respect color modes and are meant only as references for higher-level tokens.
do: Use `bgColor-default` for a card background.
dont: Use `color-scale-pink-5` for a card background.
example: A SaaS dashboard card uses `bgColor-default` so its background flips correctly between light and dark modes.
source_quote: Base color tokens don't respect color modes and should never be used directly in code or design.
check: Count `color-scale-*` base token references in stylesheets and component tokens; the count must be 0.

rule: Build every color decision to work in both light and dark modes.
why: Primer patterns are designed to work across all color modes without special-case overrides.
do: Use `fgColor-default` for body text so it resolves per mode.
dont: Hardcode `#1f2328` for body text in both modes.
example: A settings page uses semantic tokens so labels and borders remain legible when the user switches to dark mode.
source_quote: Every pattern in Primer is built to work across all color modes out of the box.
check: Does the screenshot in dark mode show text, borders, and backgrounds still legible and intentional?

rule: Pair emphasis background tokens with onEmphasis foreground tokens for text and icons.
why: Emphasis backgrounds provide stronger visual weight and require the matching onEmphasis foreground for readable contrast.
do: Use `bgColor-success-emphasis` with `fgColor-onEmphasis` for a primary button.
dont: Use `bgColor-success-emphasis` with `fgColor-default` on a primary button.
example: A billing page primary action uses an emphasis background with onEmphasis label text.
source_quote: Emphasis background colors provide a stronger emphasis for UI elements and are always combined with fgColor-onEmphasis tokens for text and icons.
check: Does every emphasis background shown in the screenshot have onEmphasis text and icons on top?

rule: Validate text and border contrast against bgColor-muted as the reference background.
why: Primer calculates all text and border contrast values against bgColor-muted so both muted and default backgrounds stay safe.
do: Check the text color against `bgColor-muted` before shipping a muted panel.
dont: Check contrast only against the default background and skip muted panels.
example: A dashboard side panel uses a muted background, and its label colors are checked against that exact background.
source_quote: All contrast values for text and borders are calculated against bgColor-muted to ensure proper contrast ratios for both muted and default.
check: Measure the WCAG contrast ratio of each text/background pair and report the lowest ratio found against bgColor-muted.

rule: Target at least 7:1 contrast for text and interactive elements in high contrast themes.
why: High contrast themes exist to raise legibility, so most text and interactive elements need a stronger ratio than the default theme.
do: Use neutral steps 11 to 13 for text in a high contrast theme.
dont: Use the default theme's muted text color in high contrast mode.
example: A high contrast theme for a task list uses darker text steps and stronger borders so labels and controls remain readable.
source_quote: For high contrast themes, the goal is to hit a minimum of 7:1 for most text and interactive elements.
check: Measure contrast ratios for text and interactive element pairs in the high contrast theme; the lowest ratio must be at least 7:1.

rule: Assign semantic colors by role such as accent, success, attention, danger, open, closed, or done rather than by hue.
why: Each semantic color carries a specific meaning, and foreground, background, and border variants exist for each role.
do: Use `danger` tokens for a form error message.
dont: Use a red token because it looks good on a success toast.
example: A CI dashboard uses `done` tokens for a completed workflow and `danger` tokens for a failed one.
source_quote: Each semantic color is tied to a role with a specific meaning. Color tokens are available for foreground, background, and border.
check: Can every semantic color in the screenshot be mapped to a named role rather than an aesthetic choice?

rule: Place each error message next to the field or control that caused it.
why: Proximity lets users connect the message to the element needing correction without scanning the page.
do: Render the error text directly beneath the invalid email field, with the field highlighted.
dont: Show a generic page-level banner at the top while the failing field sits far below.
example: In a SaaS billing form, an invalid card number error appears under the card input, not in a global alert.
source_quote: Display the error message close to the error's source. Reduce cognitive load by displaying an error indicator adjacent to the interface where the error occurred.
check: Measure vertical distance between the error element and its input; flag if greater than 48 px or outside the field group.

rule: Indicate errors with at least two cues, such as icon, text, and border, not color alone.
why: Redundant cues make errors noticeable and accessible to users with color-vision deficiency.
do: Pair a red border with an error icon and inline message.
dont: Turn only the field border red and rely on color to signal the error.
example: In a signup form, the password field gets a red border, warning icon, and 'Password too short' text.
source_quote: Use noticeable, redundant, and accessible indicators. Text and highlights that are bold, high-contrast, and red are conventional error-message visuals.
check: In a screenshot, can you identify the error using a non-color cue such as icon or text in addition to color?

rule: Wait until the user submits or clearly finishes a field before showing validation errors.
why: Premature errors punish exploration and make users feel they did something wrong before trying.
do: Validate an email field on blur only after the user has typed something, or on submit.
dont: Show 'Email is required' as soon as an empty field loses focus.
example: A SaaS signup form doesn't mark the untouched company field invalid when the user tabs through it.
source_quote: Avoid prematurely displaying errors. Timing is a crucial aspect of designing effective error messages. Presenting errors too early is a hostile pattern.
check: Tab through empty required fields without typing; confirm no error appears until submit.

rule: Write error copy that names the specific problem and gives a concrete next step.
why: Specific, constructive messages help users diagnose and recover instead of guessing.
do: Say 'Enter a ZIP code that matches your city' and offer a link to update the city.
dont: Show 'An error occurred' with no details or action.
example: A checkout form tells the user the promo code expired and offers a link to see active offers.
source_quote: Concisely and precisely describe the issue. Generic messages such as An error occurred lack context.
check: Does every error message state the problem and at least one remedy in plain language?

rule: Word errors as system guidance, not as judgments about the user.
why: Blame-focused language makes users feel accused and less able to recover.
do: Say 'That password doesn't meet the requirements yet' instead of 'You entered an invalid password.'
dont: Tell the user 'Illegal input' or 'You are wrong.'
example: In a SaaS onboarding form, the message says 'We need a work email to continue' rather than 'Invalid email.'
source_quote: Take a positive tone and don't blame the user. Write with a positive and nonjudgmental tone of voice.
check: Does the error avoid blaming words like invalid, illegal, or incorrect and speak about the requirement instead?

rule: Keep the user's entered data intact when showing an error.
why: Re-entering lost input adds effort and increases the chance users abandon the task.
do: Leave the mistyped phone number in the field and highlight the invalid segment.
dont: Clear the entire form after a failed submission.
example: A SaaS account settings form keeps all fields populated when the password change fails.
source_quote: Preserve the user's input. Let users correct errors by editing their original action instead of starting over.
check: Submit invalid data, then confirm all previous field values remain populated and editable.

rule: Offer one-click fixes or suggested corrections when the system can infer them.
why: Suggested fixes reduce the effort of correcting errors and help users recover faster.
do: When city and ZIP don't match, list matching cities as buttons.
dont: Only say 'City and ZIP code don't match' and make the user research it.
example: A shipping address form detects a ZIP mismatch and offers the matching city as a selectable fix.
source_quote: Reduce error-correction effort. If possible, guess the correct action and let users pick it from a small list of fixes.
check: For inferable errors, is there a suggested fix or corrective action offered in the message?

rule: Match the error's presentation to its severity, using inline notices for warnings and modals only for blocking failures.
why: Over-escalating minor issues interrupts flow, while under-signaling severe errors hides barriers.
do: Use a non-red inline banner for a shipping delay and a modal only for a failed payment.
dont: Open a blocking modal for a minor profile-completion reminder.
example: A dashboard shows a dismissible toast for a delayed report, but a modal for expired credentials.
source_quote: Design errors based on their impact. Design your error messages to indicate the problem's severity.
check: Does each error's UI pattern match its severity, with modals reserved for blocking errors?

rule: Show only the few most important options on the initial screen and defer advanced or rarely used features to a secondary level.
why: Progressive disclosure improves learnability, efficiency, and error rate by focusing users on what they frequently need first.
do: A SaaS invoice screen shows amount, customer, and due date; advanced tax rules, reminders, and memo fields sit behind a 'More options' control.
dont: An invoice form exposes tax rules, reminder schedules, custom fields, and payment terms all on the first screen.
example: In a project-management app, the task composer shows title, assignee, and due date; recurrence, dependencies, and custom fields live under 'More options'.
source_quote: Initially, show users only a few of the most important options.
check: Does the first screen show only core fields and hide specialized settings behind a clearly labeled secondary control?

rule: Put every frequently needed option on the initial display and keep the primary list short and free of confusing features.
why: Users should progress to secondary levels only on rare occasions, while too many or confusing primary options slow performance and dilute focus.
do: Analytics and task analysis show export and filter are used daily, so they stay on the main table toolbar; bulk archive moves to a secondary menu.
dont: A rarely used audit log sits on the main dashboard while the daily date filter is buried two clicks deep.
example: In an analytics dashboard, date range and segment filters stay visible; advanced cohort comparison is behind 'Advanced filters'.
source_quote: You have to disclose everything that users frequently need up front, so that they have to progress to the secondary display only on rare occasions.
check: Are all daily-use controls present on the initial screen, with no rarely used or confusing options competing for attention?

rule: Make the path to secondary options simple and label it so users can predict what they will find.
why: Clear mechanics and strong information scent let users decide whether advancing is worth it.
do: A 'View full specifications' link on a product page opens a details page containing specifications.
dont: A generic 'More' button opens a mixed panel of unrelated settings with no preview of content.
example: In a CRM, 'Show advanced filters' expands a panel containing exactly the advanced filter fields named on the button.
source_quote: label the button or link in a way that sets clear expectations for what users will find when they progress to the next level.
check: Can a reviewer predict the contents of the secondary screen from the label alone, and is the trigger clearly visible?

rule: Limit progressive disclosure to two levels; if you need three or more, simplify the design or group advanced features into meaningful chunks.
why: Designs beyond two disclosure levels typically have low usability because users get lost moving between levels.
do: A settings area offers main settings plus an 'Advanced' section that groups related options under clear headings.
dont: Settings nest Advanced > Expert > Diagnostic > Legacy, forcing users through three or more disclosure levels.
example: In an admin console, account settings and an Advanced panel are the only two levels; expert options are grouped inside Advanced rather than a third page.
source_quote: In practice, designs that go beyond 2 disclosure levels typically have low usability because users often get lost when moving between the levels.
check: Does the flow use no more than two disclosure levels, or if more, are advanced options chunked into clear groups?

rule: Provide one clear way to reach secondary options rather than multiple competing controls.
why: Progressive disclosure aims to expedite use of the initial display, and multiple advancement paths add complexity to that first level.
do: A report page has one 'Advanced options' button that opens all secondary report settings.
dont: A report page offers three separate 'Advanced', 'More settings', and 'Expert' buttons leading to overlapping secondary panels.
example: In a billing app, one 'Manage billing details' link opens the secondary billing screen instead of separate links for invoices, tax IDs, and payment methods.
source_quote: Because progressive disclosure's goal is to expedite use of the initial display, it's rarely a good idea to offer multiple ways to progress to secondary options.
check: Is there a single, clearly labeled control for advancing to secondary options on this screen?

rule: Use staged disclosure when a task divides into distinct sequential steps with little interaction.
why: Each step stays simple when features belonging to other steps are hidden, but interdependent steps that require back-and-forth become burdensome.
do: A checkout wizard separates shipping, payment, and review because each step is distinct and sequential.
dont: A hotel booking flow pushes room comparison, dates, and availability across multiple pages even though users adjust them together.
example: In a SaaS onboarding flow, plan selection, workspace setup, and billing are separate steps; by contrast, room comparison and pricing stay together on one screen.
source_quote: Staged disclosure is useful when you can divide a task into distinct steps that have little interaction.
check: Are sequential, low-interaction steps separated, while options users adjust together remain on one screen?

rule: Use task analysis, usage data, and observational testing to decide which features belong on the initial screen.
why: Analytics alone cannot tell whether a page is popular because users want it or because they land there by mistake.
do: Pair feature-frequency logs with moderated task tests before moving export settings off the main toolbar.
dont: Move the date filter behind 'More' based only on page views, without watching users complete real tasks.
example: In a SaaS admin tool, instrument feature use, run task tests, then keep daily actions visible and defer rare audit exports.
source_quote: you must supplement such analytics with observational usability testing to discern whether a page gets many hits because users want it or because they simply enter the page by mistake.
check: Do task-analysis notes and at least one observational usability session support the initial-versus-secondary split?

rule: Define one spacing scale and use only its values for margin and padding.
why: A fixed scale keeps vertical rhythm consistent and stops one-off pixel values from spreading through the product.
do: Apply spacing unit 6 (20px small screens, 30px large screens) for card padding.
dont: Set padding: 23px on a card because it looked right in one screenshot.
example: A SaaS dashboard settings page uses scale units 4 and 6 for all card padding instead of ad-hoc values.
source_quote: The Design System uses two different spacing scales - responsive and static.
check: Scan the stylesheet and count margin and padding values that are not on the spacing scale; target is 0 off-scale values.

rule: Use the responsive spacing scale for layout spacing that should grow on larger screens.
why: Spacing that adapts above the tablet breakpoint keeps small screens compact without cramping desktop layouts.
do: Use govuk-responsive-padding(6) so padding is 20px on small screens and 30px on large screens.
dont: Hardcode 30px padding everywhere so mobile layouts feel cramped.
example: A marketing page section uses responsive unit 8 so spacing is 30px on mobile and 50px on desktop.
source_quote: The responsive spacing scale adapts based on screen size.
check: Resize the viewport to 375px and to 1280px and measure the element padding; the large-screen value must equal the larger scale value.

rule: Keep spacing units 0 to 3 identical across all screen sizes.
why: Tight spacing around small elements like labels and icons breaks if it shifts at a breakpoint.
do: Use govuk-!-margin-bottom-2 (10px) at every viewport for label spacing.
dont: Make unit 2 shrink to 6px on mobile with a custom media query.
example: Form field labels keep a 10px bottom margin on both mobile and desktop.
source_quote: Spacing for the smallest units (0-3) stays the same for all screen sizes.
check: At 375px and 1280px, computed margin for elements using units 0 to 3 must be identical.

rule: Use static spacing when an element must keep the same spacing at every screen size.
why: Some spacing, like the inside of compact controls, should not scale or the component breaks at one breakpoint.
do: Use padding-top: govuk-spacing(6) for a fixed 30px on all screens.
dont: Use responsive unit 9 inside a small button that must keep the same height everywhere.
example: A tag component keeps 5px inner padding on mobile and desktop via the static scale.
source_quote: The static spacing scale stays the same for all screen sizes, and uses the same spacing as ‘large screens’ in the responsive spacing scale.
check: Compare computed padding at 375px and 1280px for elements using static helpers; the two values must match.

rule: Reference the spacing scale through the provided helpers instead of raw pixel values in CSS.
why: Helpers keep values on the scale and handle the responsive switch automatically.
do: Use @include govuk-responsive-margin(6, "bottom") in component styles.
dont: Write margin-bottom: 30px by hand in the component CSS.
example: A component's SCSS calls govuk-responsive-margin rather than declaring 20px directly.
source_quote: If you want to reference the spacing scale in your CSS, use the spacing helpers.
check: Grep component styles for hardcoded px values in margin and padding declarations; target is 0 occurrences outside the scale definition file.

rule: Use spacing override classes only for minor one-off adjustments, not as the main layout method.
why: Stacking override classes on components makes spacing unpredictable and hard to change later.
do: Add govuk-!-margin-bottom-0 to a single paragraph that needs its default margin removed.
dont: Build a page's whole vertical rhythm out of govuk-!-margin-* classes on every element.
example: A dashboard card adds govuk-!-padding-right-5 to one element while everything else uses component defaults.
source_quote: Occasionally, you might need to make minor adjustments like adding or removing spacing to elements of your design.
check: Does this page apply spacing override classes to more than a few elements instead of relying on component defaults?

rule: Use the zero spacing unit to remove margins instead of writing new margin: 0 rules.
why: The zero unit works at every breakpoint and stays consistent with the rest of the scale.
do: Add govuk-!-margin-0 to the last paragraph in a stack.
dont: Write a bespoke .last-item { margin: 0 } class for the same job.
example: A list's final item uses govuk-!-margin-bottom-0 to drop its trailing gap.
source_quote: govuk-!-margin-0 to remove all margins at all screen sizes
check: Search component CSS for margin: 0 rules on elements that could use the zero spacing unit; target is 0 bespoke zero-margin rules.

rule: Group dense content into smaller meaningful chunks instead of presenting one long list.
why: Working memory is limited, so chunking helps users process, understand, and remember information.
do: Split a settings page into 'Profile', 'Notifications', and 'Billing' sections, each with 4-6 related fields.
dont: Present a single 25-field settings form with no headings or grouping.
example: In a SaaS admin console, organize notification preferences into digest, alerts, and billing sections.
source_quote: Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process, understand, and memorize easily.
check: Can a reviewer point to distinct labeled groups on the screen, each containing a small set of related items?

topic: Do not cap options at seven
rule: Do not limit menus, forms, or options to seven items just because of Miller’s Law.
why: The 'magical number seven' is a memory heuristic, not a reason to impose unnecessary design limits.
do: Allow a 10-item navigation if the links are grouped and labeled clearly for users.
dont: Hide two navigation links under 'More' solely to keep the top menu at seven items.
example: A project tool's sidebar has nine links; group them under 'Work', 'Insights', and 'Admin' instead of arbitrarily hiding two.
source_quote: Don’t use the “magical number seven” to justify unnecessary design limitations.
check: Does the design avoid arbitrary 7-item caps and justify limits by grouping or user need instead?

rule: Assume working-memory capacity varies by user and context, so keep key information visible or retrievable instead of relying on recall.
why: Short-term memory capacity depends on each person's prior knowledge and situational context.
do: Keep the chosen shipping address visible in a summary panel on the payment step.
dont: Ask users to re-enter the shipping city from memory on the payment step.
example: In a multi-step checkout, show the selected plan, team size, and billing cycle in a sticky summary while users pick integrations.
source_quote: Remember that short-term memory capacity will vary per individual, based on their prior knowledge and situational context.
check: Can a reviewer confirm that key values from earlier steps or screens remain visible or retrievable without memorization?

rule: Use a skeleton screen for full-page loads that last roughly 1-10 seconds.
why: It gives users page structure without pretending to show exact progress on medium waits.
do: Show a skeleton immediately after navigation when main content takes 1.5s to load, then replace it with content.
dont: Show a skeleton for a 300ms cached dashboard load.
example: A SaaS analytics page loads report data in 2.8s; the skeleton mirrors the header, KPI cards, and chart before data appears.
source_quote: skeleton screens should be used with a wait time that’s under 10 seconds.
check: Measure navigation-to-content time; render the skeleton only when main content paint exceeds 1,000ms and remove it before 10,000ms.

rule: Suppress skeleton screens and spinners when the page reliably loads in under 1 second.
why: A flashing placeholder is more distracting than helpful on fast loads.
do: Keep a cached settings page content-first with no loading state at 400ms.
dont: Flash a skeleton for 200ms before a cached page appears.
example: A SaaS admin settings page loads from cache in 500ms; no spinner or skeleton appears.
source_quote: If a page takes less than 1 second to load, skeleton screens or spinners aren’t necessary
check: Measure p75 load time; if main content paints under 1,000ms, verify no skeleton or spinner element becomes visible.

rule: Never use a frame-display skeleton that shows only header, footer, and background.
why: It carries no layout information and feels like a broken blank page during long waits.
do: Include placeholder blocks for the title, body text, images, and cards inside the frame.
dont: Render only a page header, footer, and pulsing gray background while content loads.
example: A project dashboard skeleton shows the sidebar, project title bar, and task card rows, not just the chrome.
source_quote: Frame-display skeleton screens display no information about the page layout; they show only a header, footer, and an empty background.
check: Does the loading state show at least three content placeholder regions beyond the header and footer?

rule: Shape skeleton placeholders to mirror the final page’s content blocks and hierarchy.
why: Users form a mental model before content arrives, reducing cognitive load.
do: Use a large block for the hero image, a short thick bar for the title, and thinner bars for body text.
dont: Use five identical gray rectangles that do not map to any loaded content.
example: A Headspace-style sequence map skeleton shows step cards with title, text, and image placeholders.
source_quote: The structure of the gray boxes mimics the structure of the final page with content.
check: Can a reviewer match each skeleton placeholder to a corresponding element in the loaded page?

rule: Reserve skeleton screens for full-page loads and use progress bars or wizards for uploads, downloads, and conversions.
why: Process progress needs step or duration feedback, not a page-layout preview.
do: Show a determinate progress bar during CSV export with percentage complete.
dont: Show a skeleton of the reports page while a file upload is running in the background.
example: A SaaS invoice export shows a progress bar with '62% complete' and a cancel action.
source_quote: Whenever some other process (e.g., download, upload, convert a file) is involved, it does not make sense (and could even be confusing) to show a skeleton screen.
check: Is the indicator tied to a page load rather than a file operation or multi-step process?

rule: Switch to a progress bar or explicit duration estimate when a page load exceeds 10 seconds.
why: Users need state and remaining-time feedback once waiting becomes long.
do: Show an onboarding import screen with a progress bar and an estimated 45 seconds remaining.
dont: Keep a skeleton shimmering for 30 seconds with no progress or duration cue.
example: A SaaS data import takes 25s; the progress bar advances with 'about 20 seconds left'.
source_quote: progress bars are strongly recommended for any page that takes longer that 10 seconds to load because they give users a sense of the state of the system
check: Measure load duration; if main content exceeds 10,000ms, verify a progress bar or duration estimate is visible instead of only a skeleton.

rule: Keep skeleton animation subtle and provide a reduced-motion alternative.
why: Shimmer or pulse can distract or cause accessibility problems for some users.
do: Use a slow low-contrast shimmer and disable it under prefers-reduced-motion.
dont: Run a high-contrast full-screen pulse that cannot be turned off.
example: A DoorDash-style left-to-right shimmer on restaurant cards becomes static when reduced motion is enabled.
source_quote: Note that animations of this sort can potentially be distracting, annoying, or even create accessibility problems for some users.
check: Load with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and verify the skeleton animation is none; also verify the shimmer is low-contrast, not a full-screen flash.

rule: Match the loading indicator to scope: spinner for a single module, skeleton for the full screen.
why: A full-page skeleton is misleading when only one widget is refreshing.
do: Show a small spinner inside a dashboard card while its chart data refreshes.
dont: Replace the entire dashboard with a skeleton when only the activity feed is loading.
example: A SaaS dashboard keeps KPI cards visible and shows a spinner in the activity card.
source_quote: Spinners are typically best used on a single module, like a video or a card which is on a dashboard.
check: When only one module loads, does the loading state stay inside that module while the rest of the page remains visible?

rule: Add motion only after the static page is finished and passing inspect.mjs.
why: Animation layered on a weak layout hides nothing and cannot fix hierarchy, spacing or copy.
do: Ship the finished static page, run inspect.mjs green, then add the hero line rise and section entrances.
dont: Bolting scroll animations onto a half-built pricing page to make it feel finished.
example: SaaS pricing page: layout and copy locked and inspector-clean before any transition CSS is written.
source_quote: The static page must already be finished and passing `inspect.mjs`; motion is the last pass, never a way to rescue a weak layout.
check: inspect.mjs reports zero failures on the static build before any animation CSS or JS is added.

topic: Choreograph per section, not one uniform fade
rule: Choreograph each section's parts in reading order with a 60-90ms stagger and a 16-32px rise, once.
why: The same fade-and-slide with the same timing on every block is the most cited motion tell of generated pages.
do: Heading, text, picture and details arrive in order, about 70ms apart, rising 20px with opacity, once.
dont: Every block on the page sharing an identical 400ms fade-up with an identical delay.
example: Marketing page for a SaaS tool: feature rows arrive row by row while the product screenshot opens from a mask.
source_quote: the parts of each section arrive in reading order (heading, text, picture, details), staggered 60-90ms, rising 16-32px with opacity, once
check: Do consecutive sections use different arrival manners (list rows, masked picture, line rise) rather than one identical preset?

rule: Use ease-out for entrances, expo for reveals of 800ms or longer, ease-in-out for wipes, and never ease-in or bounce on interface.
why: Ease-in barely moves in its first frames, so interfaces feel slow and unresponsive to the eye.
do: transition: transform 800ms var(--ease-expo) on a line rise; dialog opens 300ms ease-out.
dont: transition: ease-in 500ms on a drawer, or an elastic overshoot curve on a button press.
example: Settings drawer slides in at 300ms ease-out and closes in about 210ms, quicker than it arrived.
source_quote: `ease-in` makes interfaces feel slow because the first frames barely move; do not use it.
check: Scan computed transition-timing-function and animation-timing-function values: zero ease-in, bounce or overshoot curves on interface elements.

topic: Reveal once, never strand content invisible
rule: Reveal with IntersectionObserver exactly once and gate hidden states behind html.js so content never stays invisible.
why: Scroll-listener reveals replay on re-entry and can leave blocks permanently stuck at opacity 0.
do: Add .is-in, then io.unobserve(el); keep the hidden state inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) under html.js.
dont: A scroll event listener that re-triggers the animation each time the block re-enters the viewport.
example: Content section: reveal fires when the block's top is about 88% down the viewport, then never again.
source_quote: Never attach reveals with a scroll listener, never replay them when the element re-enters, and never leave anything at `opacity: 0` if the observer fails to fire
check: Disable JavaScript and reload: all copy and images are fully visible with no element left at opacity 0.

topic: Reduced motion is the finished state
rule: Keep the finished state as the prefers-reduced-motion state and leave content visible without JavaScript.
why: Reduced-motion rules are mostly missing in the wild, and an unanimated fallback keeps the page readable for everyone.
do: Wrap masked lines, shutters and scroll scrubs in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference); reduced motion renders the final layout.
dont: A masked headline whose inner span stays translated off-screen when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is set.
example: Opening window scene: with scroll timelines unsupported or reduced motion on, the picture is simply a full-bleed screen.
source_quote: Every recipe here keeps the finished state as the reduced state.
check: Emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and disable JS: every section renders in its final state with nothing hidden or offset.

rule: Paint the message on the first frame and finish the load sequence by 1.2 seconds with no preloader.
why: Half the audited pages were still unreadable 2.5s after load, and the preloaders only cost usability.
do: Four moves at most: headline lines 100-990ms, picture opening 150-1150ms, lead sentence and CTA 420-980ms.
dont: A three-second counter intro screen before the hero headline becomes readable.
example: Product launch hero: lines rise while the hero image opens, and the CTA is clickable well under 1.2s.
source_quote: House version: no preloader, the message readable on the first frame, the load sequence over by 1.2 s.
check: Measure from navigation start: hero text readable on the first painted frame and all load animations settled at or under 1200ms.

rule: Lock scrub motion linearly to the scrollbar and keep parallax travel under 8% of the element.
why: Large parallax makes text hard to read and looks dated, and scrubbing sites lock motion to the scrollbar.
do: animation-timeline: view() with linear easing, translateY from -4% to 4% on a photo held at 106-110% in its frame.
dont: A smoothly lerped 30% parallax drift running behind body copy.
example: Hero image drifts 4% as it exits while the headline and progress bar scrub linearly with the scroll.
source_quote: Keep the travel small (under 8% of the element). Large parallax makes text hard to read and looks dated.
check: Measure the transform delta of each parallax element across its scroll range: under 8% of the element's height, with linear timing.

topic: Hover that answers, not a stuck state
rule: Put hover styles behind (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine), raise contrast, and never change font weight.
why: Touch devices fire hover on tap and leave it stuck, and weight changes reflow the text.
do: @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) { .button:hover { background: var(--accent-strong); } }
dont: An unconditional :hover that bolds the label and scales every card in the grid.
example: Pricing card CTA darkens in 180ms on desktop; on a phone it simply taps with press feedback.
source_quote: Hover styles go behind `(hover: hover)` because touch devices fire hover on tap and leave it stuck.
check: Is every :hover rule scoped inside a (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) query, with no font-weight change on hover?

rule: Use space tokens instead of raw pixel or REM values for every gap, padding and margin.
why: Tokens keep spacing consistent across apps and make later density and responsive changes possible without reworking layouts.
do: Set the card gap to space.200 (16px) in the component styles.
dont: Write gap: 17px or padding: 0.9rem directly in the component CSS.
example: A SaaS settings form uses space.150 between label and input and space.300 between form groups.
source_quote: Each space token should be used in place of the raw pixel or REM values when adding space between components or objects on a page.
check: Grep component styles for margin, padding and gap declarations with raw px or rem values; the count must be 0.

rule: Build the spacing scale on an 8px base unit and keep every value a multiple of it, from 0px to 80px.
why: A limited set of base-unit multiples gives visual consistency while still covering compact to layout-level spacing.
do: Define space.100=8px, space.200=16px, space.400=32px and space.1000=80px as the whole scale.
dont: Add 10px, 15px and 18px one-off values to the scale as needs appear.
example: A dashboard team ships 13 spacing tokens from 0px to 80px and no other spacing values in the theme.
source_quote: Each spacing value is a multiple of the base unit and ranges from 0px to 80px to allow for flexibility while still maintaining consistency across different layouts.
check: List every spacing token value in the theme file and verify each is a multiple of 8 and within 0-80px, excluding documented negative tokens.

rule: Pick spacing tokens by element size class: 0-8px for compact pieces, 12-24px for larger components, 32-80px for layout.
why: Different use cases need different spacing ranges to read correctly at their density.
do: Use space.050 between an icon and its label, and space.400 between the page header and content.
dont: Use space.800 for the icon-to-label gap inside a badge.
example: In a SaaS table, cells get space.050 icon gaps while the section above the table gets space.600.
source_quote: Different use cases require different ranges of spacing units to achieve the best outcomes.
check: Does every spacing value in the screenshot fall inside the range matching its element type (compact, component, or layout)?

rule: Place related elements closer together and unrelated elements further apart to encode their relationship.
why: Distance reads as meaning, so proximity lets users scan and group content without extra borders or labels.
do: Give 8px between a field label and its input, then 32px before the next field group.
dont: Space every form row 24px apart so labels look equally related to their own and the next input.
example: In a billing settings page, plan name and price sit 8px apart while the next plan block starts 40px down.
source_quote: Use this principle to create meaning by placing more related objects closer together, and less related objects further apart.
check: Measure the gap inside a label/control pair versus the gap between sibling groups; the intra-pair gap must be smaller than the inter-group gap.

rule: Apply identical spacing around similar items so they read as one collection.
why: Consistent spacing lends repeated elements visual similarity, which signals a shared semantic relationship.
do: Use the same row padding and gap for every item in a list.
dont: Give one list row 8px padding and the next 20px with no content reason.
example: A dashboard activity feed uses space.200 between every event card.
source_quote: Using consistent spacing around elements lends them a visual similarity that helps the user understand their semantic relationship.
check: Do repeated items in the same list or table use identical spacing values in the screenshot?

rule: Vary whitespace and scale to rank elements instead of giving everything equal spacing.
why: More whitespace around an element raises its perceived importance and steers the order users read in.
do: Give a section heading 40px above and 8px below so it binds to its content.
dont: Space every heading and paragraph 16px apart so nothing leads the page.
example: On a pricing page the plan name gets space.100 below it while the CTA button sits space.400 away.
source_quote: Similarly, varying the amount of whitespace around an element can be used to group elements together or separate them to impart greater importance.
check: Can a reviewer rank the page's elements by importance purely from their spacing and size in the screenshot?

rule: Adjust spacing off the standard scale when an element's visual weight needs balancing.
why: Equal numeric spacing does not always look equal, so optical correction keeps the page's flow harmonious.
do: Nudge a heavy filled icon 2px closer to its label so the gap looks even.
dont: Ship a visibly lopsided icon-label pair just because the token value matched the spec.
example: A sidebar's filled badge looks detached at space.100, so the designer drops the gap to space.075.
source_quote: Optical adjustments require using the spacing scale units and visual intuition to make minor changes to the spacing between objects in order to create visual harmony.
check: Does spacing look visually balanced around heavy elements in the screenshot, even where values differ from neighboring gaps?

topic: Pin the container, animate its children
rule: Animate only elements inside a pinned container, never the pinned element itself.
why: Tweening the pinned element shifts the pre-calculated measurements ScrollTrigger depends on, so the pin drifts or jitters.
do: gsap.timeline({scrollTrigger:{trigger:".panel", pin:".panel", start:"top top", end:"+=600"}}).from(".panel .card", {y:60, autoAlpha:0, stagger:0.15})
dont: gsap.to(".panel", {y:-120, opacity:0.5, scrollTrigger:{trigger:".panel", pin:".panel"}})
example: A SaaS product page pins a feature panel for 600px while three benefit cards fade in one after another.
source_quote: Warning don't animate the pinned element itself because that will throw off the measurements
check: Grep the animation files for tweens whose target selector equals the `pin:` value of the same ScrollTrigger  -  the match count must be 0.

rule: Turn on ScrollTrigger markers while dialing in start and end values, and strip them before ship.
why: Markers render the exact start, end, and trigger points so misplaced offsets are visible instead of guessed.
do: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".pricing", start: "top 80%", markers: true } while tuning, then delete the markers line before launch
dont: Shipping markers: true to production so real users see green and red debug labels painted over the pricing section
example: A marketing team tunes when the pricing table starts animating on the landing page using markers in the dev build.
source_quote: Enable visual markers during development to see exactly where the start/end/trigger points are.
check: Does a dev-mode screenshot or recording show start and end markers on the trigger being tuned?

rule: Use a numeric scrub like scrub: 1 instead of scrub: true when the scroll animation should settle smoothly.
why: A number softens the link so the playhead takes that many seconds to catch up to the scrollbar, removing jitter on wheel and trackpad scrolls.
do: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".chart-row", start: "top 75%", scrub: 1 }
dont: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".chart-row", scrub: true } on a fast trackpad, where the animation snaps hard to every scroll delta
example: A dashboard marketing page scrubs a product screenshot upward as the visitor scrolls past it.
source_quote: Soften the link between the animation and the the scrollbar so that takes a certain amount of time to "catch up"
check: In a screen recording of a fast scroll, does the scrubbed animation glide to rest over roughly the scrub duration instead of freezing the instant scrolling stops?

topic: One labeled timeline for multi-step stories
rule: Drive multi-step scroll stories from a single labeled timeline and snap to those labels.
why: A ScrollTrigger controls only one animation, and labels give snap a finite set of resting states.
do: gsap.timeline({scrollTrigger:{trigger:".story", pin:true, scrub:1, snap:{snapTo:"labels", duration:{min:0.2,max:3}}}}).addLabel("start").from(".story .step-1",{autoAlpha:0}).addLabel("step2").from(".story .step-2",{autoAlpha:0})
dont: Five independent ScrollTriggers each firing a separate tween on the same pinned section, so the steps overlap after a fast scroll
example: A SaaS homepage pinned section walks through three product steps and always rests on a whole step.
source_quote: Only one animation is controlled per ScrollTrigger, but you can wrap all your animations in a single Timeline (recommended)
check: After the user stops scrolling mid-story, does the section rest on a labeled step rather than freezing between two steps?

rule: Create ScrollTriggers top-to-bottom in page order rather than assigning refreshPriority.
why: Refresh order decides when pin spacing gets added to later triggers' start and end values, so page order keeps positions correct.
do: Instantiate the hero ScrollTrigger first, then the feature section, then the footer CTA in the same file, matching DOM order
dont: Registering the footer's pinned CTA ScrollTrigger before the hero and patching the fallout with refreshPriority values
example: A landing page with a pinned hero and a pinned mid-page demo section that both need correct start offsets.
source_quote: as long as you create your ScrollTriggers in the order they'd happen on the page
check: Call ScrollTrigger.getAll() on load and compare the trigger elements' order to their DOM order  -  the number of out-of-order entries must be 0.

topic: Clamp start and end at page bounds
rule: Wrap start and end strings in clamp() so triggers near the top or bottom of the page resolve inside the scrollable range.
why: Clamping keeps calculated positions between 0 and the max scroll, so edge-of-page triggers don't end partially scrubbed.
do: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".final-cta", start: "clamp(top bottom)", end: "clamp(bottom top)" }
dont: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".final-cta", start: "top bottom", end: "bottom top" } on the last section, leaving it stuck mid-scrub because the page has no more room to scroll
example: The last section of a SaaS landing page scrubs a card animation but the page can only scroll a few hundred pixels further.
source_quote: this ensures that any trigger elements toward the very bottom of the page won't end with partially-scrubbed animations
check: Scroll to the document bottom and read the final trigger's progress from onUpdate  -  it must reach 1.0 (within 0.01) rather than stalling short.

rule: Set anticipatePin: 1 when pinning large full-height panels that users scroll past quickly.
why: Browsers paint scroll on a separate thread, so a pinned panel can flash unpinned for a frame unless the pin is applied slightly early.
do: scrollTrigger: { trigger: ".hero", pin: true, start: "top top", end: "+=800", anticipatePin: 1 }
dont: Pinning a full-viewport hero with the default anticipatePin: 0 and watching it flash unpinned during a fast scroll
example: A landing page hero stays pinned while its headline animates and users scroll straight through it.
source_quote: A value of anticipatePin: 1 is typically fine, but you can reduce or increase that number to control how early it does the pinning.
check: In a recording of fast scrolling into the pinned panel, is any unpinned frame of that panel visible?

rule: List value, usability, feasibility, and business viability risk explicitly before committing to a solution.
why: Naming each risk prevents teams from optimizing for customer value while silently ignoring business and delivery constraints.
do: A discovery one-pager with four rows  -  Value, Usability, Feasibility, Viability  -  each with status and evidence.
dont: A single 'Risks' bullet that says 'execution risk' with no breakdown or evidence.
example: A B2B scheduling SaaS writes a discovery brief with four risk rows before the first design sprint; the viability row flags a partner-contract limit on data sharing.
source_quote: So in my new edition, I now explicitly call out the four types of risk:
check: Does the discovery doc contain four distinct risk rows  -  value, usability, feasibility, and business viability  -  each with evidence?

rule: Tackle value and business viability risk at the start of discovery, before investing in usability and feasibility detail.
why: The source says these risks are the most under-appreciated and the toughest, so discovering them late makes them expensive to fix.
do: Run customer problem interviews plus a pricing and go-to-market review in week one.
dont: Spend three sprints polishing the UI before checking whether buyers will pay or the sales channel can carry it.
example: A SaaS team delays hi-fi mockups until ten buyer interviews and a legal review of the partner contract are complete.
source_quote: Tackle the big risks early - especially value risk and business risk
check: Do the first two discovery artifacts include evidence for value (customer/buyer) and viability (GTM, legal, monetization) before any UI mockup?

rule: Assess business viability across go-to-market fit, legal/contract constraints, customer acquisition cost, monetization, and brand promise.
why: The article defines viability as broader than revenue  -  it includes channel fit, contracts, CAC, pricing, and brand consistency.
do: A viability checklist with one line each for sales channel, legal, CAC, pricing, and brand.
dont: Treating 'business viability' as a single yes/no box ticked by finance.
example: A SaaS product review flags that the new tier conflicts with an enterprise reseller contract and exceeds the target CAC.
source_quote: Business viability risk includes whether the product fits with the go-to-market or sales channel
check: Does the viability assessment address at least go-to-market fit, legal/contracts, CAC, monetization, and brand?

topic: Assign one accountable owner per risk
rule: Name a single accountable owner for each risk: PM for value and viability, designer for usability, lead engineer for feasibility.
why: The article says the PM is accountable for outcomes, the designer for the experience, and the lead engineer for delivery.
do: A risk register with an 'Owner' column showing PM, Product Designer, and Lead Engineer names.
dont: A risk list where 'the team' owns everything and no one is on the hook.
example: A SaaS discovery board shows Value → PM, Usability → Designer, Feasibility → Eng Lead, Viability → PM.
source_quote: The Product Manager is responsible for the value and viability risks, and overall accountable for the product’s outcomes.
check: Does every risk row have exactly one named owner from product, design, or engineering?

rule: Frame the work as a problem to solve with a measurable result, not as a feature list or roadmap item.
why: The source argues strong teams focus on solving problems and delivering results rather than shipping features.
do: A problem statement such as: 'Reduce time-to-first-report from 20 minutes to under 5 minutes for new admins.'
dont: A backlog item such as 'Add a wizard to the report builder' with no outcome attached.
example: A SaaS team replaces 'build CSV export' with 'let finance close the month without asking engineering for a data pull.'
source_quote: Focus on solving problems - it’s not about features or a roadmap; it’s about delivering results
check: Does each scope item state a user or business problem and a measurable result rather than only a feature name?

rule: Work the solution with engineering, design, and product together rather than handing off a finished spec.
why: The article says strong teams figure out solutions collaboratively with all three disciplines side-by-side.
do: A 90-minute working session where design sketches, engineering flags constraints, and product states the outcome.
dont: Product writes a 30-page PRD and throws it over the wall to design and engineering.
example: A SaaS onboarding redesign is scoped in a joint session; engineering surfaces an API limit that changes the flow before any mockups.
source_quote: Figure out solutions collaboratively - engineering, design, and product, working side-by-side
check: Is there a record of a solution decision made with product, design, and engineering present together?

rule: Ask one question per question page and make that question the page heading.
why: A single focused question helps users understand what is being asked and answer it accurately.
do: Page heading: 'What is your company size?' with one radio group for size options.
dont: A page titled 'Company details' asking for size, industry, and billing country at once.
example: In a SaaS onboarding flow, split 'Company details' into separate pages for company size, industry, and billing country.
source_quote: Asking just one question per question page helps users understand what you’re asking them to do, and focus on the specific question and its answer.
check: Does each question page show exactly one question in its page heading and one input group?

rule: Include a back link, page heading, and continue button on every question page.
why: These elements give users a clear way to go back, understand the question, and move forward.
do: Top of page: 'Back' link, then h1 question, then 'Continue' button after the input.
dont: A question page that starts with the form field and has no back link or submit button visible.
example: A billing address step in a checkout flow includes a back link, the h1 'What is your billing address?', and a Continue button.
source_quote: Question pages must include a: back link page heading continue button
check: Check each question page for a back-link element, exactly one h1, and a submit button; count missing required elements (must be 0).

rule: Label the primary submit button 'Continue' and align it to the left.
why: Users expect 'Continue' and a left-aligned button is not missed.
do: A left-aligned button labelled 'Continue' below the form field.
dont: A right-aligned button labelled 'Next' or 'Submit'.
example: In a multi-step signup, each step's primary action reads 'Continue' and sits at the left edge of the form column.
source_quote: Make sure your ‘Continue’ button is: labelled ‘Continue’, not ‘Next’ aligned to the left so users do not miss it
check: Measure the submit button's label text equals 'Continue' and its left edge aligns with the form fields (offset difference 0px).

rule: Mark optional fields by adding '(optional)' to the label or legend, and never mark required fields with asterisks.
why: Clear optional labelling reduces uncertainty and avoids ambiguous asterisk conventions.
do: Label: 'Phone number (optional)' on a field users can skip.
dont: Label: 'Phone number*' with a footnote explaining the asterisk.
example: A SaaS profile form labels the VAT field 'VAT number (optional)' and leaves required fields unmarked.
source_quote: in most contexts, add ‘(optional)’ to the labels of optional fields
check: Do all optional fields include '(optional)' in their label or legend, with no asterisks used for required fields?

rule: Keep hint text to a single short sentence without full stops and never put links in it.
why: Long or linked hint text is read out in full by screen readers and can frustrate users.
do: Hint: 'For example, 31 3 1980' under a date field.
dont: Hint: 'Enter the date you started. Read our guide at example.com for more details.'
example: A date-of-birth field in a signup form shows the short hint 'For example, 31 3 1980' with no link.
source_quote: Keep each hint to a single short sentence, without any full stops.
check: Count periods in each hint element (must be 0) and count anchor elements inside each hint (must be 0).

rule: Ask for each piece of information only once per journey and reuse earlier answers instead of asking again.
why: Repeating questions wastes users' time and increases errors.
do: Pre-fill the billing address with the previously entered company address, or offer it as a selectable option.
dont: Ask for the company name again on the payment page after it was entered during signup.
example: A checkout flow carries the saved shipping address into the billing step instead of showing an empty address form.
source_quote: Make sure to only ask for a piece of information once within a single journey.
check: Does the journey ask for any information more than once, unless a reuse or pre-fill option is provided?

rule: Avoid range sliders unless you also provide a non-drag way to select an answer.
why: Click-and-drag controls are difficult for some users to operate.
do: Use radio buttons or a numeric input for choosing a budget range.
dont: A slider that requires dragging to choose a number of seats, with no alternative input.
example: In a pricing configurator, replace a drag-only seat-count slider with radio options or a number field.
source_quote: Avoid using range slider questions, where the user needs to click and drag a selector across a range of answers or values.
check: If a range slider exists, is there also a non-drag input (e.g., number field or radios) that selects the same answer?

rule: Test the form without a progress indicator first and only add a simple step indicator if users still struggle.
why: Complex step indicators add clutter and often go unnoticed without improving completion.
do: Caption 'Question 3 of 9' above a single question heading.
dont: A 12-step progress bar listing all questions and allowing navigation to them.
example: A SaaS setup wizard starts without a progress bar; if testing shows confusion, it adds 'Step 2 of 5' as a caption.
source_quote: Start by testing your form without a progress indicator to see if it’s simple enough that users do not need one.
check: Is there evidence the form was tested without a progress indicator before one was added, and is any indicator a simple caption-style step count?

rule: Add novalidate to every form and never mark inputs required, relying on your own error components instead.
why: Browser-native HTML5 bubbles cannot be styled or announced consistently with the design system's accessible error summary and message components.
do: <form novalidate> with a custom error summary rendered above the fields
dont: <input required> letting the browser show its own popup bubble
example: A signup form for a SaaS trial uses novalidate so the app's own error summary component, not Chrome's tooltip, announces the problem.
source_quote: To turn off HTML5 validation, add ‘novalidate’ to your form tags.
check: Count form elements missing a novalidate attribute plus input elements carrying a required attribute  -  the total should be 0.

topic: Validate on submit, not on blur
rule: Validate only when the user submits or clicks continue, not when they leave a field.
why: Premature validation interrupts slow typists and fires errors while the answer is still being written.
do: Run validation in the submit handler and render errors only after the request
dont: Attach an onblur validator that throws 'Invalid email' as soon as the field loses focus
example: A checkout address form in a web shop only shows errors after 'Continue to payment' is pressed, not when tabbing out of the postcode field.
source_quote: Do not validate when the user moves away from a field. Wait until they try to move to the next part of the service
check: Tab through every field without submitting and confirm zero error messages appear; then submit and confirm errors render.

rule: Re-render the failed form with every field still holding what the user typed.
why: Keeping the answers lets users see the mistake, edit it, and avoids retyping the whole form.
do: Echo submitted values back into the inputs alongside the error messages
dont: Reset the form to empty placeholders after a validation failure
example: A password-reset form returns the user's email still filled in when only the confirm-password field failed.
source_quote: show them the page again, with the form fields as the user filled them in
check: Does a screenshot of the re-displayed error page show the user's submitted values still in the fields?

rule: Prefix the page title with 'Error: ' when validation fails so assistive tech announces it immediately.
why: Screen readers read the title first on page load, so the prefix signals the failure without extra navigation.
do: <title>Error: Enter your date of birth - Service name</title>
dont: <title>Enter your date of birth - Service name</title> left unchanged after a failed submit
example: A dashboard's account-settings save fails and the tab title becomes 'Error: Change your email address - Acme'.
source_quote: add ‘Error: ’ to the beginning of the page <title> so screen readers read it out as soon as possible
check: Assert document.title starts with 'Error: ' after a failed submission.

rule: Show an error summary at the top of the page and move keyboard focus to it after a failed submit.
why: Focusing the summary takes keyboard and screen reader users straight to the list of problems.
do: Render the error summary component and call focus() on it once the page loads
dont: Render the summary but leave focus on the submit button at the bottom of the page
example: A support-ticket form fails and focus lands on the 'There is a problem' summary listing each missing field.
source_quote: show an Error summary component at the top of the page, and move keyboard focus to it
check: After a failed submit, is document.activeElement the error summary container?

rule: Always validate on the server even when client-side validation is present.
why: Client-side checks can be bypassed or fail to load, so the server is the only trustworthy gate.
do: Repeat the same rules in the API or controller and return field errors from there
dont: Trust a JavaScript-only check and save whatever the request body contains
example: A billing form validates card numbers in the browser but the payment endpoint re-checks before charging.
source_quote: You’ll always need to carry out server side validation, even if you use client side validation.
check: Send a request that bypasses the browser with invalid data and confirm the server returns a validation error, not a 2xx.

rule: Strip spaces, hyphens and invisible characters from answers instead of rejecting them as errors.
why: Users paste and dictate data with stray characters, and an error they cannot see is nearly impossible to fix.
do: Normalise 'SW1A 1AA' and 'sw1a1aa' to the same value before validating
dont: Reject a card number the user entered with spaces as containing invalid characters
example: A signup form accepts a phone number typed with spaces and dashes and stores only the digits.
source_quote: Use validation to ignore unwanted characters, unless it would make the information too unclear for you to use.
check: Submit the same valid value with and without spaces or hyphens and confirm both are accepted.

rule: Return visible feedback to every user action within 400 ms.
why: Interactions under 400 ms keep users’ attention and increase productivity.
do: Show a pressed button state and spinner immediately on click.
dont: Freeze the UI for 2 seconds after submit with no visible change.
example: In a SaaS invite flow, clicking “Send invite” instantly shows a pending row and toast while the request runs.
source_quote: Provide system feedback within 400 ms in order to keep users’ attention and increase productivity.
check: Measure milliseconds from click event to first visible DOM change; assert <= 400 ms.

rule: Use perceived performance tactics to shorten the felt wait.
why: Perceived performance improves response time and reduces the perception of waiting.
do: Optimistically render a new list item before the server confirms it.
dont: Show a blank screen until the full server response returns.
example: In a project tracker, a newly added task appears immediately with a subtle syncing indicator.
source_quote: Use perceived performance to improve response time and reduce the perception of waiting.
check: Does the interface show an immediate placeholder or optimistic state while the response is pending?

rule: Animate loading states to visually engage users during background processing.
why: Animation is one way to visually engage people while loading or processing is happening in the background.
do: Use skeleton shimmer and progress motion during a data fetch.
dont: Leave a static blank panel during a 3-second fetch.
example: A dashboard widget shows skeleton rows and a subtle pulse while metrics load.
source_quote: Animation is one way to visually engage people while loading or processing is happening in the background.
check: During a load over 400 ms, is there visible motion or skeleton content instead of a static blank area?

rule: Show a progress bar for waits that exceed the instant-feedback threshold.
why: Progress bars help make wait times tolerable, regardless of their accuracy.
do: Display step progress for a multi-second file import.
dont: Use an indeterminate spinner for a 20-second file import.
example: A CSV import in a SaaS admin shows “Step 2 of 4” and a filled progress bar until complete.
source_quote: Progress bars help make wait times tolerable, regardless of their accuracy.
check: For any wait longer than 400 ms, is a progress indicator visible?

rule: Add a deliberate short delay only where extra perceived value or trust is the goal.
why: Purposefully adding a delay to a process can actually increase its perceived value and instill a sense of trust, even when the process itself actually takes much less time.
do: Show a 1-second verification step for sensitive account changes.
dont: Add artificial delay to every save action.
example: A password reset confirmation pauses briefly with “Verifying…” before showing success.
source_quote: Purposefully adding a delay to a process can actually increase its perceived value and instill a sense of trust, even when the process itself actually takes much less time.
check: Is every intentional delay tied to a high-value or trust-sensitive moment and accompanied by status feedback?

rule: Pair red error styling with a visible text message (and icon) so invalid state is not conveyed by color alone.
why: Color-only errors exclude people with color vision deficiencies or custom color settings.
do: Red border plus warning icon plus text 'Address cannot be empty.' below the field.
dont: Only a red border on the input with no text or icon.
example: In a SaaS billing form, the ZIP field turns red and shows 'ZIP code is required' so every user knows what failed.
source_quote: using it alone is not enough, as defended by WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color.
check: Does the invalid field show a visible text error message in addition to any color change?

rule: Attach field hints and error text to the input with aria-describedby referencing their element IDs.
why: Screen readers announce described text automatically when the input receives focus.
do: Include door and apartment.
dont: Place hint text next to the input without any aria-describedby link.
example: In a signup form, the password field's 'At least 12 characters' hint is linked via aria-describedby so screen reader users hear it on focus.
source_quote: we can connect the description to the input by using the aria-describedby attribute, which accepts an id pointing to the description element.
check: DOM check: count inputs with helper text that lack aria-describedby to an existing ID; expected 0.

rule: Use aria-required="true" on inputs when building custom validation instead of the native required attribute.
why: aria-required keeps required semantics for assistive tech without triggering unstylable native tooltips and focus jumps.
do: <input id="email" type="email" aria-required="true">
dont: <input id="email" type="email" required> with custom error handling.
example: In a SaaS invite form, the email field is marked aria-required so VoiceOver says 'required' while the app controls its own error display.
source_quote: The first step is to replace required with aria-required, which will keep the input required semantics without modifying its style or behavior.
check: DOM check: count inputs with native required plus custom validation; expected 0 (use aria-required instead).

rule: Set aria-invalid="true" on invalid inputs and reference the error message via aria-describedby.
why: Screen readers announce the invalid state and the specific error when the field is focused.
do: Address cannot be empty.
dont: Style the input red without aria-invalid or an associated error message.
example: In a checkout form, the card number field gets aria-invalid and its error text is announced on focus after a failed submit.
source_quote: To mark a field as invalid, we use the ARIA attribute aria-invalid="true", which will make the SR announce that the field is invalid when it’s focused.
check: DOM check: count visible error messages whose input lacks aria-invalid="true" or aria-describedby; expected 0.

rule: Add aria-live="assertive" to error elements that appear dynamically during instant or blur validation.
why: Without a live region, screen readers do not announce new error text unless the user navigates to it.
do: Enter a valid email address.
dont: Insert or update an error paragraph visually without aria-live during inline validation.
example: In a signup form, typing an invalid email shows an error that is both visible and announced because its container has aria-live="assertive".
source_quote: To do so, we must turn the error element in a Live Region, by using aria-live="assertive".
check: DOM check: count dynamically shown inline error elements without aria-live="assertive"; expected 0.

topic: One live error summary on submit
rule: On submit validation of long forms, put aria-live="assertive" only on a single error summary, not on every inline error.
why: Announcing all inline errors at once is noisy and some screen readers only announce the first live region.
do:
Failed to save because 2 fields are invalid.

Failed to save because 2 fields are invalid.
dont: Give every inline error message aria-live="assertive" after a submit.
example: In a long SaaS onboarding form, submit shows one screen-reader-only summary and visual inline errors without live regions.
source_quote: Instead, I add the aria-live="assertive" only to the error summary.
check: DOM check after submit: count aria-live="assertive" regions among inline errors; expected 0, and summary regions; expected 1.

rule: Leave the submit button enabled and show an accessible error message with instructions instead of disabling it.
why: A disabled button hides why submission is blocked and how to fix it, adding cognitive effort.
do: Enabled 'Save' button that on click shows 'Address cannot be empty' and focuses/links to the field.
dont: Disabled 'Save' button until all fields pass validation.
example: In a SaaS settings form, users can click Save at any time and receive inline field errors rather than a mysteriously disabled button.
source_quote: Whenever possible, avoid disabled buttons. Let people click buttons at any time and show them the error message with instructions.
check: Is the submit button enabled before the form is valid, with errors shown after click?

rule: Test custom form validation manually with at least one screen reader before shipping.
why: Automated accessibility tools catch only about 20-25% of issues and miss interactive validation bugs.
do: Run a VoiceOver or NVDA pass through submit, inline error, and correction flow; record the announcement order.
dont: Rely only on an automated axe scan to sign off form validation.
example: Before release, a product team runs VoiceOver on the signup form to confirm required, invalid, and error-summary announcements.
source_quote: Automated accessibility tools catch only around 20-25% of A11Y issues; the more interactive your webpage is, the fewer bugs it catches.
check: A recorded screen reader session demonstrates the invalid field, error message, and required state are announced for each validation moment.

rule: Wrap the app in MotionConfig with reducedMotion="user" so transform and layout animations are disabled automatically for people who ask for less motion.
why: This single setting respects the OS-level preference everywhere, rather than relying on each component to opt in.
do: <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user">{children}</MotionConfig> at the app root
dont: Shipping motion.div slide-in panels with no MotionConfig and no reduced-motion check anywhere
example: A SaaS dashboard wraps its root layout in MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"; a customer with Reduced Motion enabled sees panels fade instead of sliding off-screen.
source_quote: By setting reducedMotion it to "user", all motion components will automatically disable transform and layout animations, while preserving the animation of other values like opacity and backgroundColor.
check: Grep the app root file for a MotionConfig element with reducedMotion="user"; the match count must be at least 1.

rule: Replace transform, scale and x/y animations on large elements with opacity transitions when reduced motion is enabled.
why: Large moving surfaces are the main trigger for motion sickness, while a fade still communicates that the state changed.
do: animate = shouldReduceMotion ? { opacity: 1 } : { x: 0 }
dont: animate={{ x: isOpen ? 0 : "-100%" }} with no reduced-motion branch
example: A slide-over settings panel in a SaaS app fades in place of sliding 100% from the left for users with Reduced Motion on.
source_quote: That means replacing transform animations on large elements with opacity transitions, disabling auto-playing videos, and disabling parallax animations.
check: With Reduced Motion enabled, does the large panel appear by fading without any horizontal or scale movement?

rule: Use the useReducedMotion boolean to set autoplay to false on background and decorative video.
why: Auto-playing video is continuous motion the user did not start, which is exactly what the reduced-motion setting is meant to stop.
do: <video autoplay={!shouldReduceMotion} />
dont: <video autoplay muted loop /> shipped unconditionally in the hero
example: A marketing landing page's looping product demo stays paused on its poster frame for visitors who prefer reduced motion.
source_quote: useReducedMotion isn’t only compatible with the Motion. It returns a simple boolean, so you can use it for any purpose, like disabling the autoplay of a background video element:
check: Grep every <video autoplay occurrence; the number of those not guarded by a useReducedMotion boolean must be 0.

rule: Conditionally pass a static value instead of a scroll-driven MotionValue when useReducedMotion returns true.
why: Parallax layers move against the scroll direction, which is uncomfortable for people prone to motion sickness.
do: style={{ y: shouldReduceMotion ? 0 : y }}
dont: style={{ y: useTransform(scrollY, [0, 1], [0, -0.2]) }} applied unconditionally
example: A landing page hero image keeps a fixed vertical offset across the whole scroll for reduced-motion visitors.
source_quote: Parallax animations can be very unpleasant for people pre-disposed to motion sickness.
check: Record the element's bounding-box y at scroll 0 and at scroll 500px with Reduced Motion on; the delta must be 0px.

rule: Offer an in-product setting that lets a user force reducedMotion to "always" or "never" for your site.
why: A person's site-level preference may differ from their OS setting, and honoring an explicit choice keeps the experience predictable.
do: <MotionConfig reducedMotion={userSetting}> where userSetting is "always" | "never" | "user"
dont: Reading the OS preference once at load and never letting the user change it
example: A SaaS app's Accessibility settings page has a "Reduce motion" toggle stored on the user profile and fed into MotionConfig.
source_quote: Additionally, you can allow a user to override Reduced Motion for just your site by setting reducedMotion to "always" or "never" based on their profile.
check: Is there a user-facing control whose stored value is passed into MotionConfig reducedMotion?

rule: Preserve transitions that explain a state change, converting them to fades rather than removing animation entirely.
why: Motion carries meaning about where content came from; deleting it can make context switches confusing for the same users.
do: Crossfade between onboarding steps when reduced motion is on
dont: Setting all transition durations to 0 and making views swap instantly with no fade
example: A multi-step signup form crossfades between steps instead of sliding, so reduced-motion users still see that the step changed.
source_quote: The main takeaways are that for users with "Reduced Motion" enabled, we should keep educational transitions but be aware of motion sickness.
check: With Reduced Motion enabled, does each state change still have a visible non-motion cue such as an opacity fade?

rule: Call useReducedMotion inside components that need custom reduced-motion behavior outside Motion's built-in options.
why: The hook exposes the preference as a plain boolean, so you can adapt any React API, not just motion components.
do: const shouldReduceMotion = useReducedMotion() and branch the animate object
dont: Hardcoding a media query string in each component and duplicating the logic
example: A data-viz widget reads useReducedMotion to swap an animated bar growth for an instant height set.
source_quote: This hook returns true/false depending on whether your visitor has Reduced Motion enabled.
check: Count files importing useReducedMotion; must be at least 1 wherever a custom non-Motion animation exists.

topic: Shaping fidelity: rough sketch, not wireframe
rule: Shape the concept with rough sketches that fix how it works, not with wireframes or hi-fi mockups that fix how it looks.
why: Wireframes over-specify the design early and leave designers no room to rethink and no room for creativity.
do: A hand-drawn box grid plus three labelled annotations showing dots, an event list below, and click-to-scroll.
dont: A pixel-perfect Figma mockup with final type scale, spacing tokens, and hover states for the calendar view.
example: Before building a 'weekly digest' feature in a SaaS app, sketch three boxes and an arrow on paper instead of opening the design tool.
source_quote: When we shape the work, we need to do it at the right level of abstraction: not too vague and not too concrete.
check: Does the concept artifact stay at sketch fidelity, with no final color, spacing, or component specs decided?

rule: Keep shaping artifacts visibly unfinished so the builder can see where their own judgement goes.
why: Work that is too fine too early commits everyone to the wrong details before real trade-offs are discovered.
do: A sketch with a note 'layout here is TBD  -  designer decides' next to a boxed area.
dont: A flow doc that dictates every empty state string and every interaction before the builder starts.
example: A one-page feature sketch for 'add group notifications' leaves the settings screen as an empty box labelled 'TBD'.
source_quote: Work in the shaping stage is rough. Everyone can tell by looking at it that it’s unfinished. They can see the open spaces where their contributions will go.
check: Can a reviewer point to at least one area the sketch deliberately leaves open for the builder?
