rule: Make the shaped concept complete at the macro level so all main elements connect into one working solution.
why: Under-specified projects grow out of control because the team has no direction and must guess what was meant.
do: Sketch showing dots on the grid, the event list below, and the click behaviour that links them, end to end.
dont: A note saying 'build a calendar view' with no decision about what happens when a day with events is clicked.
example: A 'team activity feed' concept states what counts as an event, where it appears, and what clicking it opens  -  before any code.
source_quote: Despite being rough and unfinished, shaped work has been thought through. All the main elements of the solution are there at the macro level and they connect together.
check: Can a reviewer trace how every main element of the concept connects to the others with no undefined macro-level gap?

rule: State what the team will not do and the fixed time appetite, so scope is limited by definition.
why: Limiting scope is what makes it possible to finish within a fixed amount of time instead of expanding indefinitely.
do: 'Two-month read-only grid; no dragging events, no multi-day spanning, no color categories; six weeks.'
dont: 'Build a full calendar with all the usual views' with no list of exclusions and no time cap.
example: A 'CSV export' shaping doc lists inclusion of the export button and CSV format, and explicitly excludes scheduling, filters, and email delivery.
source_quote: shaped work indicates what not to do. It tells the team where to stop.
check: Count explicit exclusions and the time appetite in the shaping doc: at least 3 named exclusions and 1 stated appetite.

topic: Kill rabbit holes before the build
rule: Review the shaped solution for holes, unanswered questions, and risky spots, then cut or specify those spots before the team starts.
why: Unresolved rabbit holes get the team stuck or wasting time once building begins.
do: Note 'multi-day events: skip, just repeat the dot' as an explicit cut written into the concept.
dont: Leaving 'what happens with events spanning the month edge?' open for whoever hits it during the build.
example: Before a 'bulk import' build starts, the team decides to cap files at 500 rows and exclude duplicate merging, removing both open questions.
source_quote: we take a hard look at it to find holes or unanswered questions that could trip up the team.
check: Does the concept name each known risk and either cut it or specify the exact behaviour, with no open questions left unlisted?

topic: Package the shape as a pitch
rule: Write the shaped concept into a pitch that covers the problem, constraints, solution, rabbit holes, and limitations.
why: The pitch is what gets considered for a bet and later reused at kick-off to explain the project to the team.
do: A one-page write-up: the customer ask, the six-week appetite, the dot grid solution, excluded features, and the known risks.
dont: Handing the team a sketch with no problem statement, no constraints, and no list of what was left out.
example: A 'shared inbox' proposal ships as a short doc with five headed sections, reused verbatim at the kick-off meeting.
source_quote: The pitch summarizes the problem, constraints, solution, rabbit holes, and limitations.
check: Count the pitch sections present: all 5 of problem, constraints, solution, rabbit holes, limitations must be found.

rule: Cut the number of choices on screens where response time matters down to one clear action.
why: Decision time grows with the number and complexity of the options in front of the user.
do: A payment step showing one 'Pay $49' button plus a quiet 'Back' link.
dont: A payment step offering 'Pay', 'Save draft', 'Apply coupon', 'Chat with sales' and 'Compare plans' at equal weight.
example: A SaaS upgrade modal shows one plan and a 'Continue' button instead of four plan cards with five add-on toggles.
source_quote: Minimize choices when response times are critical to decrease decision time.
check: Count clickable CTAs of equal visual weight inside the primary decision panel of the critical screen; target is 2 or fewer.

rule: Split long or complex tasks into smaller sequential steps instead of one dense screen.
why: Smaller steps reduce the cognitive load of holding and comparing many inputs at once.
do: A 4-step setup wizard with three fields per step and a progress indicator.
dont: One 18-field 'Create account' form the user must scan top to bottom.
example: A SaaS workspace setup asks name, then team size, then integrations, then invites  -  one question group per screen.
source_quote: Break complex tasks into smaller steps in order to decrease cognitive load.
check: Count visible input fields per step in the flow; every step should have 5 or fewer fields.

rule: Mark one recommended option visually instead of presenting all choices at equal weight.
why: A clear recommendation removes a comparison decision the user would otherwise have to make.
do: A pricing page badges one plan 'Recommended' and gives it the only filled button.
dont: Four identically styled plans with identical buttons and no guidance.
example: A SaaS plan picker highlights 'Team' with a badge and a filled CTA while the other plans keep outline buttons.
source_quote: Avoid overwhelming users by highlighting recommended options.
check: Is exactly one option on the choice screen visually marked as recommended (badge, fill, or label)?

rule: Show new users only the core feature and reveal the rest as they learn it.
why: Hiding non-essential features keeps the first session's choice set within what a beginner can handle.
do: First-run workspace with just the message composer; navigation items unlock after the first message.
dont: Dropping a brand-new account into the full dashboard with every module, tab and setting enabled.
example: A project tool opens on a single 'Create your first task' input and adds boards, reports and automations later.
source_quote: Use progressive onboarding to minimize cognitive load for new users.
check: Walk a fresh account through first run and count enabled primary features on the first screen; target is 2 or fewer.

rule: Move secondary settings off the main surface and disclose them progressively inside menus or detail views.
why: Transferring complexity to deeper layers keeps the primary screen's decision set small and organized.
do: A settings hub listing five grouped sections that each open their own page.
dont: One settings page with sixty toggles and dropdowns stacked in a single scroll.
example: A SaaS admin screen shows five categories (Members, Billing, Integrations, Security, Notifications) instead of every switch inline.
source_quote: By transferring complexity to the TV interface itself, information can be effectively organized and progressively disclosed within menus.
check: Count interactive controls on the default view of the settings surface; target is 12 or fewer before any drill-down.

rule: Keep labels concrete and recognizable when you cut options rather than compressing them into abstractions.
why: Simplification that strips meaning forces users to decode the interface, adding back the effort you removed.
do: Nav labels 'Billing', 'Members', 'Integrations' kept as words next to their icons.
dont: Replacing the same nav with three unlabeled glyph icons and a 'More' catch-all.
example: A SaaS sidebar keeps short text labels beside icons so a new user can name each destination.
source_quote: Be careful not to simplify to the point of abstraction.
check: Can a first-time user state what each remaining control does from its label alone, without hovering or guessing?

rule: Turn the one-line idea into a brief with vision, the user, MVP features, tech stack and a project structure outline before research.
why: The workflow starts with a written vision and MVP list, so later steps have something to test.
do: idea.md lists vision, who it is for, 3 to 5 MVP features, stack, folder outline, next step.
dont: Jumping from "a CRM for agencies" straight to screens.
source_quote: the ideation output has Project Vision, Key Features (MVP), Tech Stack, Project Structure Outline, and Next Step
check: check-record --base: the idea record has Vision, User, MVP, Out of scope and Next step headings with text under each.

rule: Write a project rules file (stack, folders, naming, tokens, banned patterns) before the first line of build code.
why: Step 8 of the workflow; rules keep many AI sessions consistent.
do: PROJECT-RULES.md with stack, folder map, naming, token file path and the ban list.
dont: Each build session re-deciding folder names and colors.
source_quote: 8 PROJECT RULES, 9 TASK BREAKDOWN, 10 SETUP
check: check-record --base: a ARCHITECTURE.md has Project rules with Stack, Folders and Banned lines.

rule: Run a security review against the OWASP Top 10 before shipping anything with accounts, forms or data.
why: Step 13 of the workflow; broken access control is the top web risk.
do: Ship check lists each OWASP item as checked, not applicable, or open.
dont: Shipping a login form with no note on access control or input handling.
source_quote: The OWASP Top 10 is the reference standard for the most critical web application security risks.
check: check-record --ship: the ship record has a Security section naming access control and input validation.

rule: Deploy every change to a preview URL and QA it there before production.
why: Steps 15 to 17: preview, QA, then production.
do: Ship record links the preview URL and the QA pass on it.
dont: Merging to main and testing on the live site.
source_quote: 14 CODE REVIEW, 15 PREVIEW DEPLOYMENT, 16 QA TESTING, 17 PRODUCTION DEPLOY
check: check-record --ship: the ship record has Preview and QA sections, QA lists the screens and states tested.

rule: Name what you will watch after launch: errors, latency, traffic and saturation, and who looks.
why: Step 18 of the workflow; the four golden signals are the minimum.
do: Ship record: "Errors: runtime logs daily. Latency: p95 page load. Owner: Altaz."
dont: Launching with no plan to see breakage.
source_quote: The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
check: check-record --ship: the ship record has a Monitoring section with at least errors and an owner.

rule: Keep phone tap targets at least 44px and spaced apart, with main actions in thumb reach.
why: Small, crowded targets cause mis-taps (synsation_ Build for Good UX Pt 19).
do: Bottom action bar with 48px buttons and 8px gaps.
dont: Three 28px icon buttons touching in the top corner.
source_quote: small tap targets placed close together cause mis-taps; mind thumb reach
check: check-ui small-targets / touch-targets at 390.

rule: Pick the loading pattern by context: skeleton for page or list loads with known layout, spinner only for short single actions.
why: synsation_ Pt 3; skeletons show structure and feel faster.
do: Leads table shows 8 skeleton rows while loading.
dont: A full-page spinner over the dashboard for every load.
source_quote: choose the loading pattern by context, skeleton screen vs spinner
check: check-record --base: every screen lists a loading state naming skeleton or spinner.

rule: If you use glass, keep text contrast at 4.5:1 over the busiest part of the background, and use it on one layer only.
why: Glass is returning (synsation_), but blur over busy media fails contrast.
do: One frosted nav over a calm photo, tested for contrast.
dont: Every card frosted over a gradient blob.
source_quote: Skeuomorphism to flat to glass history; glass is coming back
check: Is glass used on at most one layer, with readable text over the busiest part?

rule: For cursor, magnetic and trail effects, start from a maintained library example (Motion.dev, Anime.js) and add a reduced-motion path.
why: Resource post from @avani.codes; libraries handle timing and cleanup.
do: Magnetic button from a Motion example with prefers-reduced-motion off switch.
dont: Hand-rolled rAF cursor that never stops on reduced motion.
source_quote: Anime.js (animation engine), Motion.dev (UI animation and interaction examples, e.g. cursor effects, magnetic, trails)
check: check-ui premium-reduced-content passes with reduced motion.

rule: A heading must not name a color or tone that contradicts the background it sits on.
why: 1.3.1 bug: "One step is black" sat on a black band and read as a mistake.
do: "Here the band turns light" on a light band.
dont: "One step is black" on a #000 band.
source_quote: Nothing automated catches the wrong "One step is black" wording on a black band
check: check-ui heading-color-word.

rule: Keep a pinned scroll scene to at most 3 screens of scroll per pinned step, and never more than 6 screens total.
why: 1.3.1 hole: long pins feel stuck and nothing checked length.
do: 5 steps pinned over 2.5 screens each.
dont: A hero pin that eats 12 screens of scroll.
source_quote: nothing checks pin length
check: check-ui pin-length.
